docs.title: Background: how Python runs your code (Sections 1.2 and 1.3)
docs.text:
There is no code in these sections, but one idea is needed for everything that follows.

A computer cannot run Python text directly. Some program has to turn your code into actions. There are two ways to do this.

  • Compiler: reads the whole program first, translates all of it into a new file (object code or an executable), and only then is that file run. C++ works this way.
  • Interpreter: reads your program a little at a time and runs each part straight away. There is no separate translated file for you to manage. Python works this way.

Path A is an interpreted language like Python. Path B is a compiled language like C++.

Because Python is interpreted, you can use it in two ways:

Interactive mode (command line) Script mode (.py file) How you use it Type one line, press Enter, see the result at once Write many lines in a file, save it, then run the whole file Good for Quick tests, trying out an idea, using Python as a calculator Real programs you want to keep, share and run again Is your code saved? No Yes

A notebook like this one sits in between. Each cell can be run on its own, like interactive mode. But all the cells are saved in one file, like a script.

docs.title: Section 1.8: Using Python as a calculator
docs.text:
The book shows four small calculations typed into a Jupyter Notebook (Figure 1.4). Examples 1 to 4 below are the same four cells.

In each cell, Python works out the expression and shows the answer below the cell. You do not need print() here. A notebook, like the interactive shell, automatically shows the value of the last line of a cell.

The four operators used here are:

Operator Meaning Example Result + Addition 2 + 4 6 * Multiplication 2 * 4 8 ** Power (raise to) 2 ** 4 16 / Division 2 / 4 0.5

Subtraction (-) works the same way. You can also use round brackets ( ) to group parts of an expression, just as in school maths.

docs.title: Example 1: Addition, and your first comment
docs.text:
What it does: adds 2 and 4 and shows 6.

How it does it:

  • Line 1 starts with #. Everything after a # up to the end of that line is a comment. Python skips it completely.
  • Line 2 is 2+4. Python works out the sum. The part # Addition is again a comment, so Python ignores it.
  • Because 2+4 is the last line of the cell, the notebook shows its value.

Why: comments let you leave notes for people who read your code. Python does not read them at all.

Learning points:

  • A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line.
  • A comment can take a full line (line 1) or sit at the end of a line of code (line 2).
  • In a notebook, the value of the last line is shown on its own.

docs.title: Example 2: Multiplication
docs.text:
What it does: multiplies 2 by 4 and shows 8.

How: Python uses * (the star, or asterisk) for multiplication. It does not use x, because x is a letter and can be a variable name.

Learning point: the multiplication sign in Python is *.

docs.title: Example 3: Power
docs.text:
What it does: works out 2 raised to the power 4, which is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16.

How: two stars ** mean "raise to the power of". The number on the left is the base. The number on the right is the power.

Learning point: ** is the power operator. Be careful: 2*4 is 8, but 2**4 is 16. One extra star changes the answer.

docs.title: Example 4: Division
docs.text:
What it does: divides 2 by 4 and shows 0.5.

How: a single slash / means division. In Python 3, / always gives a decimal answer (a float), even when both numbers are whole numbers.

Learning point: the result of / is always a float.

docs.title: Notes on Example 4 (and Examples 1 to 3)
docs.text:
1. Division in Python is not the same as in C. In C or C++, dividing two whole numbers throws away the decimal part, so 2/4 gives 0. Python 3 does not do this. It keeps the decimal part.

Expression Result in Python 3 Type of the result 2/4 0.5 float 4/2 2.0 float (not 2) 7//2 3 int (// drops the decimal part) 7%2 1 int (% gives the remainder)

You will meet // and % in the chapter on operators. Try them now if you like: add a new cell and type 7//2.

2. Spaces in expressions. 2+4# Addition works, but it is a little squeezed. The Python style guide (PEP 8, see Example 14) suggests spaces around operators and two spaces before an end-of-line comment:

2 + 4  # Addition

Both versions give exactly the same result. Spacing only makes code easier to read.

3. Try it yourself. Change the numbers in Examples 1 to 4 and run the cells again. Then try (2 + 4) * 3 and 2 + 4 * 3. Why are the answers different?

docs.title: Example 5: Printing text and a result together
docs.text:
What it does: prints a piece of text followed by the answer to 2+2:

The result of 2 + 2 is:-> 4

How it does it:

  • print is a built-in function. To call (use) a function, you write its name followed by round brackets ( ).
  • Inside the brackets you give the things you want printed. These are called arguments. Here there are two, separated by a comma:
  • "The result of 2 + 2 is:->" is text inside double quotes. Text in quotes is called a string. It is printed exactly as it is.
  • 2+2 is not in quotes, so Python works it out first and gets 4.
  • print() puts one space between its arguments and moves to a new line at the end.

Why: in a script (a .py file), Python does not show values on its own the way a notebook does. print() is how a program shows results to the user.

Learning points:

  • Anything inside quotes is printed as it is. "2 + 2" inside the string stays as the text 2 + 2.
  • Anything outside quotes is worked out first. 2+2 becomes 4.
  • Double quotes " " and single quotes ' ' both make strings.
  • Commas separate the arguments, and print() adds a space between them.

Signature of print() (the full list of what it accepts):

print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n', file=None, flush=False)
Parameter What it means Default *objects Any number of values to print, separated by commas nothing (prints an empty line) sep What to put between the values one space ' ' end What to put after the last value a new line '\n' file Where to send the output the screen flush Send the output out at once False

For now you only need *objects. The "Beyond the Book" section shows sep and end.

docs.title: Section 1.10: Running Python from a file (a script)
Example 6: The one-line script hello.py
docs.text:
What it does: prints the message Hello from a Python script!.

How it is meant to be used: in the book, this line is saved in a file named hello.py. The file is then run from a terminal (command prompt) by typing:

python hello.py

On some computers (mostly macOS and Linux) the command is python3 hello.py.

Here, in the notebook, we simply run the line in a cell. The output is the same.

Why: a script is saved. You can run it again tomorrow, share it with a friend, or make it longer. Lines typed in the interactive shell are lost when you close it.

Learning points:

  • Any file whose name ends in .py is a Python script.
  • A script is run as a whole, from the first line to the last.
  • In a script, you must use print() to see anything. A script does not show values automatically.

Want to create and run a real hello.py file inside Colab? See "Beyond the Book", Extra 1.

docs.title: Notes on Example 6
docs.text:
Why use a script? Use a script when:

  • you want to keep your code,
  • the program is long,
  • you want to use functions, loops and modules,
  • someone else needs to run your program,
  • you want the computer to run it on its own, for example at a set time every day.

Shell or script: a quick comparison

Feature Python shell (command line) Python script (.py file) Saves your code No Yes Good for testing a line or two Yes Not ideal Suitable for full programs No Yes Can be run again later No Yes

docs.title: Section 1.11: Comments
docs.text:
Python has two ways to write notes inside code:

Hash # Triple quotes """...""" or '''...''' What it really is A true comment A string (text value) What Python does with it Skips it completely Creates the string, then throws it away if it is not used Covers From # to the end of that line As many lines as you like Main use Explaining how the code works, line by line Docstrings: describing what a function, class or module does and how to use it Read by People reading the code People and tools that build documentation (like help())

docs.title: Example 7: A comment over two lines using #
docs.text:
What it does: nothing that you can see. Both lines are comments, so Python skips them. The cell runs without any output.

How: a # comment only covers one line. To write a note that goes over two lines, you put a # at the start of each line.

Why: this is the normal way to write a longer note in Python code.

Learning points:

  • Every comment line needs its own #.
  • If you forget the # on the second line, Python will try to run that text as code and you will get an error. Try it: delete the # at the start of line 2 and run the cell.

docs.title: Example 8: Triple quotes used as a multi-line comment
docs.text:
What it does: creates a string that spans three lines.

How: text that starts with three quote marks (""" or ''') and ends with the same three quote marks can run over many lines. This is called a triple-quoted string.

Why: people often use triple quotes as a multi-line comment, because Python does nothing harmful with a string that is not stored or used.

Learning points:

  • Triple quotes make a real string. They are not a true comment.
  • When a triple-quoted string is the first line inside a function, class or module, it becomes a docstring. Tools such as help() read docstrings to build documentation.

Run the cell and then read the note below it. The output may surprise you.

docs.title: Notes on Example 8: why did the notebook show the text?
docs.text:
A true comment (#) never produces output. But this cell did show something like:

' Multi-line quote
... continues
.... ends'

The reason:

  1. The triple-quoted text is a string value, just like 2+4 is a number value.
  2. It is the last line of the cell. A notebook always shows the value of the last line.
  3. So the notebook shows the string. The marks show where each new line starts inside the string.

In a .py script, nothing would be shown, because a script does not show values on its own. That is why triple-quoted strings behave like comments inside scripts.

Remember: use # for comments. Keep triple quotes for docstrings.

docs.title: Section 1.11.1: Statements over many lines, and many statements on one line
docs.text:
A statement is one instruction that Python can run. For example, x = 10 is an assignment statement. if, for and while statements are other kinds.

Normally, a statement ends where the line ends. The next four examples show how to bend this rule, and when you should not.

Way How it looks Needs a special character? Recommended? Explicit line continuation End the line with a backslash \ Yes, \ Only when there is no better way Implicit line continuation Keep the statement inside ( ), [ ] or { } No Yes, the preferred way Many statements on one line Separate them with semicolons ; Yes, ; No, avoid it One statement per line The normal way No Yes

docs.title: Example 9: Explicit line continuation with a backslash
docs.text:
What it does: works out 2 + 3 + 4 and shows 9, even though the sum is split over two lines.

How it does it:

  • The first three lines are comments. Python skips them.
  • Line 4 ends with a backslash \. This tells Python: "the statement is not finished, carry on to the next line."
  • Python joins line 4 and line 5 and reads them as 2 + 3 + 4.

Why: it lets you break a very long statement into shorter lines that fit on the screen.

Learning points:

  • The backslash must be the very last character on the line. Nothing can come after it: not a comment, and not even a space. Otherwise Python raises SyntaxError: unexpected character after line continuation character.
  • This is why the comment is written on separate lines above the code, and not after the \.

docs.title: Notes on Example 9
docs.text: Try it: put a space after the backslash on line 4 and run the cell. Then put # test after the backslash. Read the error each time, then undo your change.

docs.title: Example 10: Implicit line continuation inside brackets
docs.text:
What it does: adds 10 + 20 + 30 + 40 and prints 100.

How it does it:

  1. Line 1 opens a round bracket (.
  2. As long as a bracket is open, Python knows the statement is not finished. It keeps reading the next lines.
  3. At the closing bracket ) on line 4, the statement is complete. Python adds the numbers and stores 100 in result.
  4. Line 5 prints result.

Why: this is the clean, preferred way to split a long line. You do not need a backslash, and a stray space at the end of a line cannot break it.

Learning points:

  • An open (, [ or { lets a statement continue over many lines.
  • Python waits for the matching closing bracket before it treats the statement as complete.
  • The indentation of lines 2 and 3 is only for looks. Inside brackets, Python does not care about it.

docs.title: Example 11: Many statements on one line with semicolons
docs.text:
What it does: stores 5 in a, stores 6 in b, and prints their sum 11. All three steps are on one line.

How it does it: a semicolon ; separates statements. Python runs them one after the other, from left to right:

  1. a = 5 puts the value 5 in the variable a.
  2. b = 6 puts the value 6 in the variable b.
  3. print(a + b) adds them and prints 11.

Why it is shown: so that you can recognise it when you see it. It is allowed, but it is not good practice.

Learning point: a semicolon lets you put several statements on one line. Avoid it, because:

  • the code is harder to read,
  • errors are harder to find, since one line now holds several steps,
  • the logic is hidden, and mistakes are easier to miss.

docs.title: Example 12: The better version, one statement per line
docs.text:
What it does: the same work as Example 11, and prints 11.

How: each statement is on its own line. No semicolons are needed.

Why: the Python style guide (PEP 8) recommends one statement per line. Each line does one job, so the code is easy to read and to fix.

Learning point: Examples 11 and 12 give the same result. The difference is only readability, and readability matters a lot when you or someone else comes back to the code later.

docs.title: Section 1.12: Indentation (no code in the book)
docs.text:
Most languages such as C, C++ and Java use braces { } to mark a block of code. Python uses indentation instead: the spaces at the start of a line.

  • A block (for example, the body of an if or a function) starts when lines are indented.
  • The block ends at the first line that goes back to the earlier indentation.
  • Use 4 spaces per level. This is the common style.
  • Do not mix tabs and spaces. It can cause errors or strange behaviour.

You can see indentation at work in Example 14 below, inside the functions, classes and if statements.

docs.title: Section 1.13: Python keywords
docs.text:
Keywords are words that Python keeps for itself. Each one has a fixed meaning in the grammar of the language. You cannot use a keyword as the name of a variable, a function, a class, or anything else you create.

Keywords are case-sensitive. True is a keyword, but true is not. if is a keyword, but If is not.

docs.title: Example 13: Printing the list of all keywords
docs.text:
What it does: prints every keyword of the Python version you are using.

How it does it:

  1. import keyword loads a small module (a ready-made file of Python code) named keyword. It comes with Python, so you do not need to install it.
  2. Inside that module there is a list named kwlist that holds all the keywords.
  3. print(keyword.kwlist) prints that list. The dot in keyword.kwlist means "the kwlist that lives inside keyword".

Why: you do not need to learn the list by heart. You can always ask Python for it. The list can change a little between Python versions, and this code always gives the correct list for your version.

Learning points:

  • import gives you access to a module.
  • A dot (.) is used to reach something inside a module.
  • kwlist is a list, not a function, so there are no brackets after it.

What is inside the keyword module:

Name Kind What it gives you keyword.kwlist list All keywords of your Python version keyword.iskeyword(s) function True if the text s is a keyword, otherwise False keyword.softkwlist list "Soft" keywords (see Beyond the Book, Extra 3)

docs.title: Notes on Example 13
docs.text:
1. Your output may differ a little from the book. The list depends on the Python version. Python 3.10 and later versions have 35 keywords. To see which version you are using, run import sys and then print(sys.version) in a new cell. For example, Python 3.9 also showed a special entry named __peg_parser__. It was removed in Python 3.10, so you will not see it in Colab.

2. print and exec are not keywords in Python 3. They were keywords in the old Python 2. In Python 3 they are built-in functions. That is why you call them with brackets, like print("Hi"), and why they do not appear in the list above.

3. The 35 keywords grouped by what they do. You do not need to learn these now. You will meet each group in later chapters.

Group Keywords Special values True, False, None Logic and testing and, or, not, is, in Making decisions if, elif, else Loops for, while, break, continue Functions def, return, lambda, yield Classes class Using modules import, from, as Handling errors try, except, finally, raise, assert Managing resources with Scope of names global, nonlocal Running tasks side by side async, await Other pass, del

Notice that only True, False and None start with a capital letter.

docs.title: Sections 1.14 and 1.15: Identifiers, naming conventions and PEP 8
docs.text:
An identifier is a name you give to something in your code: a variable, a function, a class, a module and so on.

There are two kinds of naming rules:

  1. Legal rules. Python checks these. Break one and your code will not run.
  2. Conventions. Python does not check these. They are good habits that most Python programmers follow, mostly taken from PEP 8. Your code will run if you ignore them, but it will be harder for others to read.

docs.title: The legal rules
docs.text:
Rule What it means Valid examples Invalid examples 1. Allowed characters Only letters (a-z, A-Z), digits (0-9) and the underscore _ total_marks, value2, Student_Name hello-world, age@school 2. First character Must be a letter or an underscore, never a digit value1, _count, name2 1value, 2ndNumber 3. No keywords A keyword cannot be used as a name (none) for, while, class, break 4. No special symbols Symbols like @, $, !, #, % and - are not allowed (none) first-name, price$, value#1 5. Case matters Names that differ only in capital letters are different names student, Student, STUDENT are three separate names (none)

A word of care about print: it is not a keyword in Python 3, so print = 10 is legal. But it is a very bad idea. After that line, print means 10, and print("Hi") stops working until you restart the notebook. The same goes for other built-in names such as list, str, type and id.

docs.title: PEP and PEP 8
docs.text:
• PEP stands for Python Enhancement Proposal. A PEP is a document that proposes or describes something about Python.
  • PEP 8 is the official style guide for Python code. It covers naming, spacing, line length and more.

The main naming conventions from PEP 8:

What you are naming Style Example Avoid Variables snake_case: lowercase words joined by underscores student_age StudentAge, studentage Functions snake_case calculate_average CalculateAverage Constants (values that should not change) UPPER_CASE with underscores MAX_LIMIT maxlimit Classes PascalCase: each word starts with a capital, no underscores StudentRecord studentRecord, Attendance_Manager Names meant for use only inside a module A single leading underscore _internal_utility_function (no underscore, if it is meant to be internal)

About camelCase: in camelCase the first word is lowercase and each later word starts with a capital, as in myAge. The capital letter looks like the hump of a camel. camelCase is common in Java and JavaScript. PEP 8 prefers snake_case (my_age) for variables and functions in Python.

Also choose names that tell you what they hold. n = 10 is legal, but number_of_students = 10 explains itself.

docs.title: Example 14: PEP 8 style versus non-PEP 8 style
docs.text:
This script is not printed in the book. It supports Sections 1.14 and 1.15, where the book points to the online resource for more on PEP 8.

What it does: shows, side by side, the right way (PEP 8) and the way to avoid (non-PEP 8) for five kinds of code. It prints one line for each section.

How it does it: the script has five parts. Each part has a "PEP 8 STYLE (CORRECT)" block and a "NON-PEP 8 STYLE (AVOID)" block.

Part Topic The PEP 8 way The way to avoid 1 Variables and constants student_age, MAX_LIMIT StudentAge, totalScore, maxlimit 2 Functions def calculate_average(...) with the body on its own indented lines CalculateAverage, with the whole body squeezed onto the def line with semicolons 3 Classes StudentRecord, AttendanceManager studentRecord, Attendance_Manager 4 if statements Spaces around > and ==, body on its own indented line if x>5: print("x>5") on one line 5 Internal names _internal_utility_function with a leading underscore (not shown)

Why: code is read far more often than it is written. When everyone follows the same style, anyone can pick up anyone's code and read it quickly.

Learning points:

  • Both styles run. Python does not check style. The "AVOID" code runs without any error. You can even see its output: the line x>5 is printed by the squeezed if statement.
  • PEP 8 is about readability, not about whether code works.
  • Some things in the script, such as functions, classes and if, are covered in later chapters. For now, just look at how the names are written and how the code is spaced out.
  • pass is a keyword that means "do nothing". It is used here because a class body cannot be empty.

docs.title: Notes on Example 14
docs.text:
1. Reading the output line by line

Output line Printed by Section 1: Variable naming conventions demonstrated. The print() at the end of part 1 Section 2: Average is 90.0 calculate_average(80, 90, 100) works out (80 + 90 + 100) / 3 = 90.0. It is a float because / always gives a float Section 3: Class naming (PascalCase) demonstrated. The print() at the end of part 3 Section 4: x is greater than 5 The PEP 8 if statement, because x is 10 x>5 The squeezed, non-PEP 8 if statement. It runs fine, it is just hard to read Section 5: This is a hidden helper function. The value returned by _internal_utility_function()

2. Why is there no output from CalculateAverage? It is defined, but never called. A function only runs when it is called.

3. About the last comment in the script. The closing comment says that all the code is PEP 8 compliant. Read it as "all the code runs without errors". The "AVOID" blocks are left in on purpose to show bad style, so they are not PEP 8 compliant.

4. The f before some strings. In f"Section 2: Average is {calculate_average(80, 90, 100)}", the f makes an f-string. The part inside the curly braces { } is worked out and its value is put into the text. You will learn f-strings properly in the chapter on strings.

5. A tip. Tools called "linters" (for example flake8 or pylint) and formatters (for example black) can check or fix PEP 8 style for you. VS Code can run them as you type.

docs.title: Section 1.16: Variables, literals, references and built-in types
docs.text: Some ideas in this part may feel new if you have never programmed before. Do not worry. Run each example, look at the output, and they will become clear.

docs.title: A variable is a tag, not a box
docs.text:
A variable is a name that refers to a value (an object) stored in memory. The way this works is different in C++ and Python.

  • In C++, a variable is like a box. Each box is made for one kind of thing, just as a shoe box is made for shoes and a match box for matches. You must say what kind of box it is (int, float and so on) before you use it, and it keeps that kind for life.
  • In Python, a variable is like a price tag. The tag has no type of its own. You can take it off a shoe and tie it to a book. The object the tag is tied to has the type.
Feature C++ (statically typed) Python (dynamically typed) What a variable is A box that holds a value A tag (label) tied to a value Must you declare the type? Yes (int, float, string ...) No Who has the type? The box (the variable) The object (the value) Can the same name later refer to a different type? No. An int variable cannot later hold a string Yes. The same name can point to any type Everyday picture Boxes for shoes, boxes for matches A price tag that can be tied to any item

Static and dynamic typing. C++ is called statically typed, because the type of each variable is fixed when you write the code. Python is dynamically typed, because Python works out the type from the object at the moment the code runs.

Python is also strongly typed. Dynamic does not mean careless. Python will not quietly mix types that do not fit together. For example, "5" + 5 gives an error instead of guessing what you meant. (See Beyond the Book, Extra 4.)

docs.title: Example 15: Two tags on one object, then one tag moves
docs.text:
What it does: prints 2 and then 3.

How it does it, step by step:

  1. x = 2: Python creates the object 2 and ties the tag x to it.
  2. y = x: Python does not copy the number. It ties a second tag, y, to the same object 2.
  3. y = 3: Python creates the object 3 and moves the tag y to it. Tag x is not touched. It is still on 2.
  4. print(x) prints 2, and print(y) prints 3.

Why: many beginners expect x to change to 3 as well. It does not, because y = 3 only moves the tag y.

Learning points:

  • = means "tie this name to that object". It does not mean "equal" as in maths.
  • y = x makes both names refer to the same object. It does not create a copy.
  • Giving a new value to one name never changes another name.

docs.title: Example 16: The same name, two different types
docs.text:
What it does: prints the type of x twice. First it is a string (str), then a whole number (int).

How it does it:

  1. x = 'abc' ties the tag x to the string 'abc'.
  2. type(x) asks: "what type is the object that x points to?" The answer is <class 'str'="">.
  3. x=5 moves the tag x to the integer 5. The string 'abc' is left without a tag.
  4. type(x) now answers <class 'int'="">.

Why: this is dynamic typing in action. You never told Python the type. It looked at the object each time and worked it out.

Learning points:

  • type() reports the type of the object, not of the name.
  • The same name can point to objects of different types at different times.
  • In Python every type is a class, which is why the output says class.

Signature of type() (the one-argument form used here):

type(object)
Part Meaning object Any value or variable Returns The type (class) of that object, for example <class 'int'="">

docs.title: Notes on Example 16
docs.text:
Python shows a space after class: the real output is <class 'str'=""> and <class 'int'="">.

Also, x=5 has no spaces around =. It works the same as x = 5, but PEP 8 prefers the spaced version.

Some common types you will meet soon:

Example value type() shows Name of the type 5 <class 'int'=""> integer (whole number) 78.11 <class 'float'=""> floating-point (decimal) number 'abc' <class 'str'=""> string (text) True <class 'bool'=""> Boolean (True or False) None <class 'nonetype'=""> the "no value" value

docs.title: Example 17: Casting a float to an int
docs.text:
Casting (or type conversion) means making a new object of one type from an object of another type.

What it does: turns the float 78.11 into the whole number 78, and prints the id (identity number) of each object.

How it does it:

  1. my_float = 78.11 creates a float object and ties the tag my_float to it.
  2. id(my_float) gives the identity number of that float object.
  3. int(my_float) builds a new integer object from it. The decimal part .11 is dropped. The tag my_int is tied to this new object 78.
  4. print(my_int) prints 78.
  5. id(my_int) gives the identity of the integer object. It is a different number from step 2, because it is a different object.
  6. id(78) gives the same number as id(my_int). This shows that my_int points to the object 78.

Why: in Python it is the object that is converted, not the name. int() does not change the float. It makes a new integer, and the float stays as it was. Numbers cannot be changed in place (they are immutable), so converting always creates a new object.

Learning points:

  • int() drops the decimal part. It does not round: int(78.99) is also 78.
  • The original object (78.11) stays unchanged. Check it by printing my_float after the conversion.
  • The comments in the code mention myInt. They mean the variable my_int.

Signature of int():

int(x=0)
int(x, base=10)
Parameter Meaning x The value to convert, for example a float such as 78.11 or a string such as "78" base Only used when x is a string. The number base, for example 2 for binary. Default is 10 Returns A new int object. int() with nothing inside gives 0

docs.title: Notes on Example 17
docs.text:
1. Your id numbers will be different. The long numbers in the comments are the ones the author got. An id depends on where the object sits in memory on that computer at that moment. Your numbers will be different, and they change each time the notebook is restarted. What matters is the pattern:

  • id(my_float) is different from id(my_int): two different objects.
  • id(my_int) is the same as id(78): one and the same object.

2. Why are id(my_int) and id(78) the same? The standard version of Python (called CPython) keeps one ready-made object for each small whole number from -5 to 256. Every time you use 78, you get that same object. This saves memory. It is a hidden detail of CPython. Your programs should not depend on it.

3. Try it: add print(my_float) at the end of the cell. It still prints 78.11, which proves the original float was not changed.

docs.title: Section 1.16.3: What happens in an assignment
docs.text:
When you write x = 3, Python does three things:

  1. It creates the object 3 (an int) in memory.
  2. It creates the name x, if it does not exist yet. The name has no type of its own.
  3. It ties the name x to the object 3. This link is called a reference.

If you now ask type(x), you get int. That is the type of the object x refers to, not a type of x itself.

docs.title: Example 18: A simple assignment
docs.text:
What it does: ties the name x to the integer 3. There is no output, because there is no print() and an assignment has no value to show.

Learning point: an assignment creates a reference from a name to an object.

docs.title: Section 1.16.4: Shared references
docs.text: When two or more names point to the same object, the object has a shared reference.

docs.title: Example 19: Two names, one object
docs.text:
What it does: makes x and y point to the same object. There is no output.

How it does it:

  1. x = 3: tag x is tied to the object 3.
  2. y = 2: tag y is tied to the object 2.
  3. y = x: tag y is moved to whatever x points to, which is the object 3.

After line 3, both x and y refer to the object 3. The object 3 now has a shared reference.

The object 2 has no tag left. Python notices this and frees that memory on its own. This is the automatic memory management (garbage collection) described in Section 1.3.2.

Learning point: y = x makes y point to the object that x points to, here 3.

docs.title: Example 20: Changing one name does not change the other
docs.text:
Run Example 19 first. This cell needs x and y from it.

What it does: adds 2 to x and prints 5 and 3.

How it does it:

  1. Before this cell, x and y both point to 3.
  2. x = x + 2: Python first works out the right-hand side. It reads the value of x (3), adds 2, and creates a new object 5.
  3. The tag x is moved to the new object 5.
  4. The tag y is not touched. It still points to 3.
  5. So print(x) shows 5, and print(y) shows 3.

Why: the object 3 is not changed into 5. Whole numbers cannot be changed in place (they are immutable). Python makes a new object and moves only the tag x. That is why y does not change.

Learning points:

  • In x = x + 2, the right-hand side is worked out first, using the old value of x.
  • Changing what one name points to does not affect the other names.
  • Mutable objects (like lists) can behave differently with shared references. You will see this in the chapter on lists.

docs.title: Section 1.16.5: Variable versus identifier
docs.text:
People often use the words "variable" and "identifier" as if they meant the same thing. They do not.

  • An identifier is just a name.
  • A variable is a name that is tied to a value. So it has a name, a value, the type of that value, and a scope (the part of the program where the name can be used).
Identifier Variable What it is A name only A name plus a value (with its type) plus a scope Can name Variables, functions, classes, modules and more Data only Example calculate_average (a function name), StudentRecord (a class name), age age = 10

So every variable has an identifier, but not every identifier is a variable.

A variable must be defined (given a value) before you use it. If you use a name that has never been given a value, Python stops with a NameError. Example 21 shows this.

docs.title: Helper cell (not from the book)
docs.text:
In this notebook, x was already given a value in Examples 15 to 20. So if you ran x now, you would see 5, not an error. The cell below removes the name x, so that Example 21 behaves as it does in the book.

  • x = None makes sure x exists. This way the next line works even if you skipped the earlier cells.
  • del x deletes the name x. (del is one of the keywords from Example 13.)

docs.title: Example 21: Using a name that has no value (this cell gives an error on purpose)
docs.text:
What it does: tries to show the value of x. Since x does not exist, Python stops and reports a NameError.

How: Python looks up the name x. It cannot find it, so it cannot go on.

Why: this is one of the most common errors for beginners. It usually means a spelling mistake, or a cell that was not run yet.

Learning points:

  • You must give a name a value before you use it.
  • The last line of the error message is the most useful part: NameError: name 'x' is not defined.
  • In the book, the error comes from a script file, so the message names the file (c:\test11\ch1.py). In Colab, the message names the notebook cell instead. The last line is the same.

docs.title: Notes on Example 21
docs.text:
If you used Runtime > Run all, the notebook stopped here. That is expected. Click the next code cell and choose Runtime > Run after to run the rest.

How to fix a NameError:

  1. Check the spelling. Age and age are different names.
  2. Make sure the cell that creates the name has been run.
  3. Make sure the name is given a value before the line that uses it.

docs.title: Example 22: Looking at an object's identity with id()
docs.text:
Every object in Python has three things:

Property What it is How to see it Identity A number that is unique to the object while it exists id(obj) Type The kind of object, such as int or str type(obj) Value The data it holds, such as 10 print(obj)

A name has one more property: its scope, meaning where in the program the name can be used. You will learn about scope in the chapter on functions.

What the code does: prints the id of the object 10, then ties the name age to 10 and prints its id. Both ids are the same.

How it does it:

  1. id(10) works out the id of 10, but the result is not printed. This is not the last line of the cell, so the notebook does not show it.
  2. print(id(10)) prints the id of the object 10.
  3. age = 10 ties the tag age to the object 10.
  4. print(id(age)) prints the id of the object that age points to. It is the same number as in step 2.

Why: this shows that a variable is only a label for an object. age has no id of its own. id(age) gives the id of the object that age refers to.

Learning points:

  • id() gives the identity of an object. In standard Python (CPython), this number is the object's address in memory.
  • If two names give the same id, they refer to the same object.
  • The same id here also comes from the small-number store described in the notes on Example 17: CPython keeps one shared object for each whole number from -5 to 256.
  • Your id numbers will not match the numbers in the comments. That is normal.

Signature of id():

id(object)
Part Meaning object Any value or variable Returns An integer. It is unique for that object as long as the object exists

docs.title: Extra 1: Create and run a real script file inside Colab
docs.text:
In Example 6 we ran the print() line directly. Here we will do what the book describes: save the line in a file named hello.py, and then run that file.

How it works:

  • The first cell starts with %%writefile hello.py. This is a special notebook command, not Python. It saves the rest of the cell into a file named hello.py, instead of running it.
  • The second cell starts with !. In a notebook, ! sends the rest of the line to the computer's terminal. So !python hello.py runs the file exactly as you would in a terminal.

To see the file, click the folder icon on the left side of Colab. Note that files in Colab are deleted when the session ends.

docs.title: Extra 2: The sep and end options of print()
docs.text:
The signature of print() (see Example 5) has two useful options:

  • sep sets what goes between the values. The default is one space.
  • end sets what goes after the last value. The default is a new line.

The cell below shows both. Compare each output line with the code that made it.

docs.title: Extra 3: Let Python check a name for you
docs.text:
Two small tools help you check the naming rules from Section 1.14:

Tool What it checks "some_name".isidentifier() Is the text built from legal characters, and does it not start with a digit? keyword.iskeyword("some_name") Is the text a keyword?

A name can be used only if the first gives True and the second gives False.

The code uses a for loop, which you will learn in the chapter on flow control. For now, read it as: "for each name in the list, check it and print the answer."

The last line prints the soft keywords. These are words like match and case that act as keywords only in certain places. Elsewhere they can still be used as names, but it is better to avoid them.

docs.title: Extra 4: Dynamic, but also strong (the last line gives an error on purpose)
docs.text:
Python lets a name point to any type (dynamic typing). But it does not guess when you mix types that do not fit together (strong typing).

  • Line 1 turns the number 5 into the text "5" with str(), then joins two strings: 55.
  • Line 2 turns the text "5" into the number 5 with int(), then adds two numbers: 10.
  • Line 3 tries to add text and a number without converting. Python refuses and raises a TypeError.

Some languages, such as JavaScript, would quietly turn "5" + 5 into "55". Python makes you say clearly what you want.

    This module provides access to the mathematical functions

        Return the arc cosine (measured in radians) of x.

        Return the inverse hyperbolic cosine of x.

        Return the arc sine (measured in radians) of x.

        The result is between -pi/2 and pi/2.

        Return the inverse hyperbolic sine of x.

    atan(x, /)
        Return the arc tangent (measured in radians) of x.

        The result is between -pi/2 and pi/2.

    atan2(y, x, /)
        Return the arc tangent (measured in radians) of y/x.

        Unlike atan(y/x), the signs of both x and y are considered.

    atanh(x, /)
        Return the inverse hyperbolic tangent of x.

    cbrt(x, /)
        Return the cube root of x.

    ceil(x, /)
        Return the ceiling of x as an Integral.

        This is the smallest integer >= x.

    comb(n, k, /)
        Number of ways to choose k items from n items without repetition and without order.

        Evaluates to n! / (k! * (n - k)!) when k <= n and evaluates
        to zero when k > n.

        Also called the binomial coefficient because it is equivalent
        to the coefficient of k-th term in polynomial expansion of the
        expression (1 + x)**n.

        Raises TypeError if either of the arguments are not integers.
        Raises ValueError if either of the arguments are negative.

    copysign(x, y, /)
        Return a float with the magnitude (absolute value) of x but the sign of y.

        On platforms that support signed zeros, copysign(1.0, -0.0)

        Return the cosine of x (measured in radians).

        Return the hyperbolic cosine of x.

        Return the Euclidean distance between two points p and q.

# Script 2: Reading Documentation of Third-Party Python Modules

# This script demonstrates how to:
# 1. Check whether a third-party module is installed
# 2. Read its documentation safely
# 3. Use help(), dir(), and docstrings
# 4. Use pydoc programmatically
# We use try / except so that the program does NOT crash
# if a third-party module is not installed.

# A. Reading documentation for NumPy (third-party module)

try:
    import numpy as np

    print("\nNumPy module found!")  # Will print if NumPy is imported successfully
    print("Exploring NumPy documentation...\n")

    # dir() lists all top-level names in the module
    print("Listing some NumPy attributes and functions:")
    print(dir(np))     # Shows array, zeros, ones, random, etc.

    print("\nHelp on numpy.array:")
    help(np.array)     # Detailed documentation for array()

    print("\nDocstring of numpy.array:")
    print(np.array.__doc__)   # Short description of array constructor

except ModuleNotFoundError:
    print("NumPy is NOT installed.")
    print("Install it using: pip install numpy")

array(...)
    array(object, dtype=None, *, copy=True, order='K', subok=False, ndmin=0,
          like=None)

    Create an array.

    Parameters
    ----------
    object : array_like
        An array, any object exposing the array interface, an object whose
        ``__array__`` method returns an array, or any (nested) sequence.
        If object is a scalar, a 0-dimensional array containing object is
        returned.
    dtype : data-type, optional
        The desired data-type for the array. If not given, NumPy will try to use
        a default ``dtype`` that can represent the values (by applying promotion
        rules when necessary.)
    copy : bool, optional
        If ``True`` (default), then the array data is copied. If ``None``,
        a copy will only be made if ``__array__`` returns a copy, if obj is
        a nested sequence, or if a copy is needed to satisfy any of the other
        requirements (``dtype``, ``order``, etc.). Note that any copy of
        the data is shallow, i.e., for arrays with object dtype, the new
        array will point to the same objects. See Examples for `ndarray.copy`.
        For ``False`` it raises a ``ValueError`` if a copy cannot be avoided.
        Default: ``True``.
    order : {'K', 'A', 'C', 'F'}, optional
        Specify the memory layout of the array. If object is not an array, the
        newly created array will be in C order (row major) unless 'F' is
        specified, in which case it will be in Fortran order (column major).
        If object is an array the following holds.

        ===== ========= ===================================================
        order  no copy                     copy=True
        ===== ========= ===================================================
        'K'   unchanged F & C order preserved, otherwise most similar order
        'A'   unchanged F order if input is F and not C, otherwise C order
        'C'   C order   C order
        'F'   F order   F order
        ===== ========= ===================================================

        When ``copy=None`` and a copy is made for other reasons, the result is
        the same as if ``copy=True``, with some exceptions for 'A', see the
        Notes section. The default order is 'K'.
    subok : bool, optional
        If True, then sub-classes will be passed-through, otherwise
        the returned array will be forced to be a base-class array (default).
    ndmin : int, optional
        Specifies the minimum number of dimensions that the resulting
        array should have.  Ones will be prepended to the shape as
        needed to meet this requirement.
    like : array_like, optional
        Reference object to allow the creation of arrays which are not
        NumPy arrays. If an array-like passed in as ``like`` supports
        the ``__array_function__`` protocol, the result will be defined
        by it. In this case, it ensures the creation of an array object
        compatible with that passed in via this argument.

        .. versionadded:: 1.20.0

    Returns
    -------
    out : ndarray
        An array object satisfying the specified requirements.

    See Also
    --------
    empty_like : Return an empty array with shape and type of input.
    ones_like : Return an array of ones with shape and type of input.
    zeros_like : Return an array of zeros with shape and type of input.
    full_like : Return a new array with shape of input filled with value.
    empty : Return a new uninitialized array.
    ones : Return a new array setting values to one.
    zeros : Return a new array setting values to zero.
    full : Return a new array of given shape filled with value.
    copy: Return an array copy of the given object.


    Notes
    -----
    When order is 'A' and ``object`` is an array in neither 'C' nor 'F' order,
    and a copy is forced by a change in dtype, then the order of the result is
    not necessarily 'C' as expected. This is likely a bug.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> np.array([1, 2, 3])
    array([1, 2, 3])

    Upcasting:

    >>> np.array([1, 2, 3.0])
    array([ 1.,  2.,  3.])

    More than one dimension:

    >>> np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
    array([[1, 2],
           [3, 4]])

    Minimum dimensions 2:

    >>> np.array([1, 2, 3], ndmin=2)
    array([[1, 2, 3]])

    Type provided:

    >>> np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype=complex)
    array([ 1.+0.j,  2.+0.j,  3.+0.j])

    Data-type consisting of more than one element:

    >>> x = np.array([(1,2),(3,4)],dtype=[('a','<i4'),('b','<i4')])
    >>> x['a']
    array([1, 3])

    Creating an array from sub-classes:

    >>> np.array(np.asmatrix('1 2; 3 4'))
    array([[1, 2],
           [3, 4]])

    >>> np.array(np.asmatrix('1 2; 3 4'), subok=True)
    matrix([[1, 2],
            [3, 4]])
