docs.title: 3.1 Introduction
docs.text:
A calculation is made of operators and operands.

  • An operator is a symbol (or a word) that tells Python to do something: +, -, *, /, ==, and, in, is and so on.
  • An operand is a value or variable that the operator works on.

In 3 + 4, the operator is + and the operands are 3 and 4.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.2 Assignment
docs.text:
In Python, = is the assignment operator. x = 5 means "take the value on the right and tie the name on the left to it". It helps to read = as an arrow pointing left:

You write Read it as a = 5 a gets 5 (a ← 5) a = a + 5 a gets (the old a) + 5

As you saw in Chapter 1, the name a is a tag, and the value 5 is the object the tag is tied to.

= is not the "equals" of school maths.

  • x = 12 is fine: the name x now refers to 12.
  • 12 = x is an error: you cannot assign anything to the number 12, because 12 is a literal, not a name.
  • To test whether two values are equal, Python uses a different operator, == (see Section 3.9).

Re-assignment. A statement such as a = a + 5 may look strange at first. Python runs it in two steps:

  1. It works out the right-hand side, using the current value of a.
  2. It ties the name on the left to the result.

Because the right-hand side is worked out first, a must already have a value. If a has never been given a value, a = a + 5 stops with a NameError.

The rules of assignment in Python:

No. Rule 1 The value on the right side is worked out first 2 The result is then stored in the name on the left side 3 = assigns. It does not compare 4 A variable can refer to any type of value 5 A variable is created automatically the first time it is assigned

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.3 Operators and operands
docs.text:
In short: operators are the tools that do the work, and operands are the values they work on.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.3.1 Why are operators needed?
docs.text:
Operators let a program:

  1. do calculations,
  2. compare values,
  3. make logical decisions,
  4. check whether data is present,
  5. check whether two names refer to the same object in memory, and
  6. work with the individual bits of a number.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.4 Compound (augmented) assignment operators
docs.text:
A compound assignment operator does a calculation and an assignment in one go. For example, a += 15 means "add 15 to a and store the result back in a". It is a short form of a = a + 15.

Operator Example Same as What it does = a = 10 (plain assignment) a gets 10 += a += 15 a = a + 15 Increase a by 15 -= a -= 5 a = a - 5 Decrease a by 5 *= a *= 15 a = a * 15 Multiply a by 15 /= a /= 15 a = a / 15 Divide a by 15. The result is always a float %= a %= 5 a = a % 5 a gets the remainder of a divided by 5 //= a //= 5 a = a // 5 a gets the result of floor division of a by 5 **= a **= 5 a = a ** 5 a gets a raised to the power 5

As with a = a + 5, the variable must already have a value before you use a compound operator on it. "Beyond the Book", Extra 1 runs all of these in one cell.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.5 Categories of operators
docs.text:
Python's operators fall into seven groups:

No. Category Purpose Examples 1 Arithmetic Maths +, -, *, /, //, %, ** 2 Assignment Giving values to names =, +=, -=, *=, /= and so on 3 Comparison Comparing values ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= 4 Logical Combining conditions and, or, not 5 Bit-wise Working on individual bits &, \|, ^, ~, <<, >> 6 Identity Checking whether two names refer to the same object is, is not 7 Membership Checking whether a value is inside a collection in, not in

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.6 Arithmetic operators
docs.text:
Arithmetic operators work on numbers. Most take two operands (binary form, as in x + y). + and - can also take one operand (unary form, as in -20).

No. Operator Meaning Example Result 1 + Add two operands 7 + 2 9 Unary plus +20 20 2 - Subtract the right operand from the left 7 - 2 5 Unary minus -20 -20 3 * Multiply 7 * 2 14 4 / Divide. The result is always a float 6 / 2 3.0 (not 3) 5 % Modulus: the remainder after division 13 % 8 5 6 // Floor division: divide, then round down to the next whole number on the number line 7 // 3 2 (not 2.5) Rounding down also applies to negative results -7 // 3 -3 (not -2) 7 ** Power: the left operand raised to the right operand 2 ** 5 32

% works with floats too: 7.5 % 2 gives 1.5.

Spaces around an operator do not matter. 2+3, 2 + 3 and 2 + 3 all give 5. But an operator made of two characters must be written without a space inside it. 2 ** 3 is 8, while 2 * * 3 is a SyntaxError. The same goes for //, ==, !=, <=, >=, += and the other two-character operators.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: The sign of the remainder
docs.text:
What it does: works out three remainders where one or both numbers are negative: -7 % 3, 7 % -3 and -7 % -3.

How it does it: Python finds the remainder in two steps:

  1. It does floor division first: q = a // b. This divides and then rounds down (towards minus infinity).
  2. The remainder is whatever is left: r = a - b * q.
Expression a // b (rounded down) a - b * q Remainder -7 % 3 -7 // 3 = -3 -7 - (3 * -3) = -7 + 9 2 7 % -3 7 // -3 = -3 7 - (-3 * -3) = 7 - 9 -2 -7 % -3 -7 // -3 = 2 -7 - (-3 * 2) = -7 + 6 -1

Why: because // always rounds down, the remainder in Python always has the same sign as the divisor (the number on the right), or is zero. C and Java work differently: there, the remainder takes the sign of the number on the left, so -7 % 3 gives -1 in C.

Learning points:

  • a % b has the same sign as b.
  • (a // b) * b + (a % b) always gives back a. This is true for every pair of numbers (as long as b is not zero). Check it for each line of the table.
  • This rule is handy. For example, n % 7 is always between 0 and 6 for any whole number n, even a negative one, which makes it easy to work out days of the week.

docs.title: 3.7 Order of precedence of operators
docs.text:
When an expression has more than one operator, Python must decide which one to work out first. This is decided by precedence. The rules are the same ones you learned in school maths, extended to Python's other operators.

  • Parentheses come first. Anything inside ( ) is worked out before the rest. 2 * (3 - 1) is 4. Brackets are also useful just to make an expression easier to read, even when they do not change the result, as in (minute * 100) / 60.
  • Power comes next. 2 ** 1 + 1 is 3, not 4, and 3 * 1 ** 3 is 3, not 27, because the power is worked out before the + or *.
  • Multiplication and division (*, /, //, %) come before addition and subtraction. 2 * 3 - 1 is 5, not 4, and 5 - 2 * 2 is 1, not 6.
  • Operators with the same precedence are worked out from left to right. They are called left-associative. So 6 - 3 + 2 is (6 - 3) + 2, which is 5. Working from right to left would give 6 - (3 + 2), which is 1.
  • There is one exception: the power operator ** is worked out from right to left. So 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** (3 ** 2), which is 2 ** 9 = 512, not (2 ** 3) ** 2 = 64.

The full order, from highest (done first) to lowest (done last):

Level Operators Meaning 1 (highest) ( ) Parentheses 2 ** Power (right to left) 3 +x, -x, ~x Unary plus, unary minus, bit-wise NOT 4 *, /, //, %, @ Multiplication, division, floor division, remainder, matrix multiplication 5 +, - Addition, subtraction 6 <<, >> Bit shifts 7 & Bit-wise AND 8 ^ Bit-wise XOR 9 \| Bit-wise OR 10 ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, is, is not, in, not in Comparisons, identity, membership 11 not Logical NOT 12 and Logical AND 13 (lowest) or Logical OR

Watch out: -2 ** 2 is -4, not 4. The power is worked out before the minus sign on its left. Write (-2) ** 2 if you want 4.

When in doubt, add brackets. They cost nothing and make your meaning clear. "Beyond the Book", Extra 2 lets you test all of these rules.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.8 Types of operands and the type of the result
docs.text:
When an operator works on two operands, three things can happen:

Case Example Result Both operands have the same type, and so does the result 2 + 3 (int + int) 5 (int) Both operands have the same type, but the result has a different type 6 / 3 (int / int) 2.0 (float) The operands have different types; the result has the type of one of them 2.5 * 4 (float * int) 10.0 (float)

So always be aware of what type of result an operation gives. (This links to type casting, which you met in Chapter 2.)

You can check the type of any value or variable with the built-in function type(), for example type(6 / 3) gives float.

The same operator can do different jobs. + adds numbers, but it joins (concatenates) strings: 5 + 3 is 8, while "5" + "3" is "53". * multiplies numbers, but repeats strings, lists and tuples. Example 2 shows this.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: + and * on different types
docs.text:
What it does: uses + and * on numbers, strings, lists and tuples, and prints the seven results.

How it does it: Python looks at the types of the operands and picks the matching job:

No. Code Types Job done Result 1 5 + 3 int + int Addition 8 2 "Hello, " + "world!" str + str Joining Hello, world! 3 [1, 2] + [3, 4] list + list Joining [1, 2, 3, 4] 4 4 * 2 int * int Multiplication 8 5 "abc " * 3 str * int Repetition abc abc abc 6 [1, 2, 3] * 3 list * int Repetition the list three times 7 (4, 5) * 2 tuple * int Repetition (4, 5, 4, 5)

Why: the meaning of an operator depends on the types of its operands. This is called operator overloading.

Learning points:

  • + joins two sequences of the same type. [1, 2] + (3, 4) (a list and a tuple) is an error, and so is "5" + 3.
  • * repeats a sequence only when the other operand is a whole number.
  • In block 5 the string is "abc ", with a space at the end, so the output ends with a space too.

docs.title: 3.9 Comparison operators
docs.text:
A comparison operator compares two values and always gives back a Boolean: True if the comparison holds, False if it does not. Just as + takes two numbers and gives back their sum, a comparison operator takes two values and gives back True or False.

No. Operator Meaning True when Example Result 1 < Less than the left operand is strictly less than the right 3 < 5 True 2 <= Less than or equal to the left operand is less than or equal to the right 5 <= 5 True 3 > Greater than the left operand is strictly greater than the right 10 > 2 True 4 >= Greater than or equal to the left operand is greater than or equal to the right 7 >= 9 False 5 == Equal to both operands have the same value 4 == 4 True 6 != Not equal to the operands have different values 8 != 3 True

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: The six comparison operators
docs.text:
What it does: runs one example of each comparison operator and prints True or False.

How: each print() line compares two numbers. The comment on the same line gives the expected answer and the reason.

Why: comparisons are the heart of every decision a program makes. Every if and every while uses one.

Learning points:

  • A comparison always gives back True or False, never a number.
  • == (two equals signs) compares. = (one equals sign) assigns. Mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
  • <= and >= include equality: 5 <= 5 is True, but 5 < 5 is False.
  • Comparisons also work on other types. Strings are compared letter by letter in dictionary order: "apple" < "banana" is True.

docs.title: 3.10 Identity operators
docs.text:
Identity operators check whether two names refer to the very same object in memory. They do not compare values. Python has two:

No. Operator Meaning True when Example Result 1 is Same object both names refer to the same object x = [1, 2], y = x, then x is y True 2 is not Not the same object the names refer to different objects a = [1, 2], b = [1, 2], then a is not b True (two separate lists)

When should you use is? Only when you really care about identity, not value. The two common cases are:

  1. checking for None: if x is None:
  2. checking whether two names refer to the same list or other object.

is compared with ==:

== (equality) is (identity) Question it asks "Are the values equal?" "Are both names tied to the same object?" Kind of test Value comparison Reference comparison [1, 2] == [1, 2] True [1, 2] is [1, 2] False (two different list objects) a = 5; b = 5 a == b is True a is b is True here because of interning (see Example 4), but this is not guaranteed in every case

Two different objects can have the same value and still not be the same object. That is why:

  • use == to check equality, and
  • use is to check identity.

Small integers and short strings can look "identical" because Python reuses (interns) some objects to save memory. So a is b may happen to be True when you did not expect it. Never rely on that. Example 4 explores this.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: Interning, and why is can surprise you
docs.text:
This example goes a little deeper than the book. It supports the note on interning in Section 3.10.

What it does: compares six pairs of values with both is and ==: small integers, large integers, short strings, long strings and lists.

How it works: interning is a memory-saving trick. For some immutable values, Python keeps one shared object and hands out that same object every time, instead of making a new copy.

Block Values What standard Python (CPython) does is result in this notebook == result 1 256 and 256 Whole numbers from -5 to 256 are always shared True True 2 10000 and 10000 Not always shared False True 3 1000000 and 1000000 Not always shared False True 4 "hello" and "hello" Short strings that look like names are usually shared True True 5 "a" * 1000 twice Long strings are usually not shared False True 6 [1, 2, 3] twice Lists are never shared: each list is a new object False True

Why: this shows why is must not be used to compare values. The is results depend on hidden details of Python. The == results are always True, because the values really are equal.

Learning points:

  • == compares values. is compares identity.
  • The comments say "False in some implementations". The results of blocks 2, 3 and 5 can change: if you put the same code in a .py file and run it as a script, Python may reuse the same object and print True. Your code must never depend on this.
  • The only safe everyday uses of is are x is None and checking whether two names point to the same object.

docs.title: 3.11 Membership operators
docs.text:
Membership operators check whether a value is found inside a collection. There are two:

No. Operator Meaning Returns True when Example Result 1 in Is a member the value is found in the collection x = [1, 2, 3], then 2 in x True 2 not in Is not a member the value is not found in the collection x = [1, 2, 3], then 4 not in x True

Points to note:

  • They always give back True or False.
  • They work with strings, lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. Strings, lists and tuples are sequences; sets and dictionaries are not, but membership works for them too.
  • With a string, in looks for a piece of text: "ell" in "hello" is True.
  • With a dictionary, in checks the keys only, not the values.
  • They are very useful in if statements and loops.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.12 Logical operators
docs.text:
Logical operators combine conditions. Each gives back a Boolean.

No. Operator Meaning Example 1 and True only if both operands are True x and y is True only when both x and y are True 2 or True if at least one operand is True x or y is True when either x or y (or both) is True 3 not Works on one operand and flips it not x is True when x is False, and False when x is True

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.12.1 Understanding and with a simple example
docs.text:
Think of and as "both conditions must be met". A student is promoted only if they pass both English and Science:

English Science Promoted? In Python Fail Fail No False and False gives False Fail Pass No False and True gives False Pass Fail No True and False gives False Pass Pass Yes True and True gives True

A table like this, listing every possible input with its result, is called a truth table. Here are the truth tables for or and not:

x y x or y False False False False True True True False True True True True x not x False True True False

"Beyond the Book", Extra 3 lets you run these operators.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.13 Bit-wise operators
docs.text:
Bit-wise operators work on whole numbers as if they were strings of binary digits (bits: 0s and 1s), one bit at a time. They are used in low-level work, such as handling on/off flags, controlling devices, network code and fast calculations.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.13.1 Bit-wise operators, a simple explanation
docs.text:
Operator Name Rule for each pair of bits & AND The result bit is 1 only if both bits are 1 \| OR The result bit is 1 if at least one bit is 1 ^ XOR (exclusive OR) The result bit is 1 only if the two bits are different ~ NOT Flips every bit. For any whole number A, ~A equals -(A + 1) << Left shift Moves the bits to the left and fills with 0s on the right. Each shift by one place multiplies by 2 >> Right shift Moves the bits to the right and drops the rightmost bits. Each shift by one place divides by 2 (floor division)

The easiest way to follow a bit-wise operation is to write both numbers in binary, line up the bits, and work column by column. Here the numbers are written in 8 bits (1 byte):

Bits Decimal 6 0 0 0 0 0 1 1 0 6 5 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 1 5 6 & 5 (both 1) 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 0 4 6 \| 5 (at least one 1) 0 0 0 0 0 1 1 1 7 6 ^ 5 (different) 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 1 3

More results:

No. Example How it works 1 6 << 2 gives 24 00000110 shifted left by 2 places becomes 00011000, which is 16 + 8 = 24. It is the same as 6 * 2 * 2 2 6 >> 2 gives 1 00000110 shifted right by 2 places becomes 00000001, which is 1. It is the same as 6 // 4 3 ~6 gives -7 Flipping every bit of 00000110 gives 11111001. In the "two's complement" system used for negative numbers, the leftmost bit counts as -128, so this is -128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 1 = -7. The quick rule is ~A = -(A + 1)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 5: The six bit-wise operators
docs.text:
What it does: applies each bit-wise operator to the numbers 6 and 5 (or to 6 alone) and prints the result.

How: the comments above each print() show the binary working. Compare them with the tables above.

Block Code Binary working Result 1 6 & 5 00000110 & 00000101 = 00000100 4 2 6 \| 5 00000110 \| 00000101 = 00000111 7 3 6 ^ 5 00000110 ^ 00000101 = 00000011 3 4 ~6 flip 00000110 to get 11111001 -7 5 6 << 1 00000110 becomes 00001100 12 6 6 >> 1 00000110 becomes 00000011 3

Why: these operators are fast and compact. For example, a single number can store eight yes/no settings, one in each bit.

Learning points:

  • Bit-wise operators work only on whole numbers (and Booleans), not on floats.
  • x << n is the same as x * 2**n, and x >> n is the same as x // 2**n.
  • You can see the binary form of a number with bin(): bin(6) gives '0b110'.

docs.title: 3.14 Boolean operators compared with bit-wise operators
docs.text:
• Bit-wise operators (&, |, ^, ~) work on the individual bits of whole numbers.
  • Logical operators (and, or, not) work on truth values (True and False).

Python has keywords for logical and, or and not, but it has no keyword for logical XOR. XOR ("exclusive or") is True when exactly one of the two operands is True:

Operand 1 Operand 2 Logical XOR result False False False False True True True False True True True False

Even without a keyword, you can build logical XOR of two variables a and b from the operators you have: (a and not b) or (not a and b). For two Booleans, a != b gives the same answer and is shorter. "Beyond the Book", Extra 3 tries both.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.15 Special operators: identity and membership
docs.text:
Python's identity operators (is, is not) and membership operators (in, not in) are sometimes called special operators, because they behave differently from ordinary comparisons.

Membership operators (in, not in):

  • in is True if the value exists in the collection.
  • not in is True if the value does not exist.
  • They work with strings, lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries. With dictionaries, they check the keys only, not the values.

Identity operators (is, is not):

  1. They check whether two names refer to the same object in memory, not whether their contents are equal.
  2. is is True if both names refer to the same object; is not is True if they refer to different objects.
  3. Identity is about the object itself, not its value. You can see an object's identity number with the built-in function id().
  4. Two objects can have equal values (== gives True) but different identities (is gives False).
  5. An object's identity never changes while it exists.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: Identity and membership together
docs.text:
What it does: shows three things: the difference between is and ==, membership in a string and a list, and membership in a dictionary.

How it does it:

Block Code Result Reason 1 a = b = [1, 2, 3] One list is created, and both a and b are tied to it c = [1, 2, 3] A second, separate list with the same values a is b True Same object a is c False Different objects a == c True Same values 2 'a' in 'abcd' True The letter is found in the string 5 not in [1, 2, 3] True 5 is not in the list 3 'x' in my_dict True 'x' is a key 10 in my_dict False 10 is a value, not a key

Learning points:

  • a = b = [1, 2, 3] is a chained assignment: one object, two names. If you now do b.append(4), then a changes too, because it is the same list.
  • To check whether a dictionary contains a value, use .values(): 10 in my_dict.values() gives True.

docs.title: 3.16 Some more operators and concepts
docs.text:
Recent versions of Python have added a few more handy operators and forms.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 3.16.1 The walrus operator := (Python 3.8 and later)
docs.text:
The walrus operator := assigns a value to a variable as part of an expression. (It is called "walrus" because := looks like the eyes and tusks of a walrus.) It helps you avoid working out the same value twice, and can make code shorter.

It is meant for use inside a larger expression, such as the condition of an if statement or a while loop. Written on its own as a plain statement, as in n := 5, it is a SyntaxError. Use the ordinary n = 5 there.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 7: The walrus operator in an if statement
docs.text:
What it does: works out the length of "hello", stores it in n, checks whether it is greater than 3, and prints 5.

How it does it:

  1. len("hello") gives 5.
  2. n := ... stores 5 in n, and at the same time passes 5 on to the rest of the expression.
  3. 5 > 3 is True, so the if block runs.
  4. print(n) prints 5.

The brackets around (n := len("hello")) are needed. Without them, Python would work out len("hello") > 3 first and store True in n.

Why: without the walrus operator, you would need two lines: n = len("hello") and then if n > 3:. With it, you assign and test in one step.

Learning points:

  • = is a statement; it cannot be used inside an expression. := is an operator; it can.
  • Keep walrus expressions short and simple. If they make the line hard to read, use two lines instead.

docs.title: 3.16.2 Chained comparisons
docs.text:
A chained comparison compares several values in one expression, just as you would write it in maths: 1 < x < 10 means "x is between 1 and 10".

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: Chained comparisons
docs.text:
What it does: checks whether x is between 1 and 10, and whether y is between 10 and 20 (inclusive), and prints a message for each.

How it does it:

  • 1 < x < 10 is worked out as (1 < x) and (x < 10). Both parts must be True for the whole expression to be True.
  • 10 <= y <= 20 works the same way, with <= so that 10 and 20 themselves count as "between".
  • The messages use f-strings: the {x} inside f"..." is replaced by the value of x.

Why: a chained comparison is shorter and easier to read than joining two comparisons with and.

Learning points:

  • Any comparison operators can be chained, including == and !=. For example, a == b == c is True when all three are equal.
  • In a chain, the middle value is worked out only once.
  • If the first comparison is False, Python does not check the rest. The whole chain is already False.

docs.title: 3.16.3 The ternary conditional operator
docs.text:
The ternary conditional operator lets you write a simple if-else choice on one line. It is called "ternary" because it has three parts: a value if true, a condition, and a value if false.

Syntax:

value_if_true if condition else value_if_false

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 9: Choosing between two values in one line
docs.text:
What it does: stores "Adult" in status if age is 18 or more, and "Minor" otherwise. Since age is 20, it prints Adult.

How it does it:

  1. Python checks the condition in the middle: age >= 18.
  2. If it is True, the whole expression gives the value on the left, "Adult".
  3. If it is False, it gives the value on the right, "Minor".
  4. The chosen value is stored in status.

Why: it is a compact way to pick one of two values. The same thing written as a full if statement takes four lines:

if age >= 18:
    status = "Adult"
else:
    status = "Minor"

Learning point: use the ternary operator only for simple choices. For anything longer, a full if statement is easier to read.

docs.title: Beyond the Text
docs.text:
The book's "Beyond the Text" section asks you to study two more operators: the matrix multiplication operator @ and the set operators. The two examples below cover them.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: The matrix multiplication operator @
docs.text:
The @ operator was added in Python 3.5. It multiplies matrices and vectors. It is mostly used with the NumPy library, which is already installed in Colab.

To multiply matrix A by matrix B, the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B. Each entry of the result is made by taking a row of A and a column of B, multiplying the matching numbers, and adding them up:

For A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[5, 6], [7, 8]]:

Result position Row of A Column of B Working Value Row 1, column 1 [1, 2] [5, 7] 15 + 27 19 Row 1, column 2 [1, 2] [6, 8] 16 + 28 22 Row 2, column 1 [3, 4] [5, 7] 35 + 47 43 Row 2, column 2 [3, 4] [6, 8] 36 + 48 50

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: Matrix multiplication with @
docs.text:
What it does: multiplies two 2 by 2 matrices, and then a matrix by a vector, and prints everything.

How it does it:

  1. import numpy as np loads NumPy under the short name np.
  2. np.array(...) turns nested lists into NumPy arrays (matrices).
  3. A @ B multiplies the two matrices and gives [[19, 22], [43, 50]], as worked out in the table above.
  4. M @ v multiplies a matrix by a vector: 15 + 26 = 17 and 35 + 46 = 39, so the result is [17, 39].

Why: matrix multiplication is at the heart of graphics, engineering, statistics and machine learning. A @ B reads almost like the maths.

Learning points:

  • A @ B is matrix multiplication. A * B with NumPy arrays is something different: it multiplies matching entries one by one ([[5, 12], [21, 32]] here). Try it.
  • The order matters: A @ B is usually not the same as B @ A.
  • @ does not work on ordinary Python lists. [[1, 2]] @ [[3], [4]] gives a TypeError. That is why NumPy arrays are used.

docs.title: Set operators
docs.text:
Sets (Chapter 2) have their own operators:

Operator Name Result With set_a = {1, 2, 3} and set_b = {3, 4, 5} \| Union Items in either set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} & Intersection Items in both sets {3} - Difference Items in the first set but not in the second {1, 2} ^ Symmetric difference Items in exactly one of the two sets {1, 2, 4, 5}

Notice that |, & and ^ are the same symbols as the bit-wise operators. With sets they do the matching job on items instead of bits: ^ keeps the items that are in one set or the other, but not in both, just as bit-wise XOR keeps the bits that differ.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 11: The four set operators
docs.text:
What it does: builds two small sets and prints their union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference.

How: the triple-quoted text at the top is just a note listing the operators. It is a string that is not stored anywhere, so Python ignores it. Each example then uses one operator and prints the result.

Learning points:

  • Each operator gives back a new set. set_a and set_b are not changed.
  • set_a - set_b is not the same as set_b - set_a. Try it: the second gives {4, 5}.
  • The same results are available as methods: set_a.union(set_b), set_a.intersection(set_b), set_a.difference(set_b) and set_a.symmetric_difference(set_b).

docs.title: Extra 4: Checking the floor division and remainder rule
docs.text:
Example 1 said that (a // b) * b + (a % b) always gives back a. This cell checks it for all four sign combinations.

  • The for line takes each pair of numbers from the list in turn (you will learn loops in the next chapter).
  • q, r = a // b, a % b works out the quotient and the remainder in one line.
  • The last column prints True if the rule holds.

Python also has a built-in function that gives both at once: divmod(-7, 3) returns (-3, 2).

docs.title: Chapter 4: Flow Control
docs.text:
# --- STEP 1: Get User Input ---
user_entry = input("Enter a number: ")

# --- STEP 2: Convert to Integer ---
# We convert the input string directly to a number using int().
# Note: Will raise an error if input not a valid integer,
# but we are skipping error handling for simplicity.
num = int(user_entry)

# --- STEP 3: The Decision Structure (Selection Flow) ---
if num > 0:
    # Runs if num is greater than zero
    print(f"Success: {num} is a positive number.")

elif num < 0:
    # Runs if num is less than zero
    print(f"Success: {num} is a negative number.")

else:
    # Runs only if the number is exactly zero
    print("Success: The number is zero.")

# --- STEP 4: End of Script ---
print("Program execution finished.")

Enter a number: -6
Success: -6 is a negative number.
Program execution finished.

Back to the Table of Contents

# --- STEP 1: Get User Input ---
# We use input() to get a string from the user and int() to convert it
user_entry = input("Enter a whole number to check: ")
num = int(user_entry)

# --- STEP 2: The Two-Way Decision (Selection Flow) ---
# We use the Modulo Operator (%) to find the remainder.
# If a number divided by 2 has a remainder of 0, it is EVEN.

if num % 2 == 0:
    # This block executes if the boolean expression evaluates to True
    print(f"The number {num} is Even.")
else:
    # This block executes if the boolean expression evaluates to False
    print(f"The number {num} is Odd.")

# --- STEP 3: Sequential Flow Resumes ---
print("Flow Control test complete.")

The number 3 is Odd.
Flow Control test complete.

# --- STEP 1: Get User Input ---
# We convert the input to an integer immediately
my_age = int(input("Enter Age: "))

# --- STEP 2: The Nested Logic ---
# Each 'else' block contains a new 'if' statement,
# pushing the logic deeper into the nest.
if my_age >= 18:
    my_comment = 'You can vote'
else:
    # First level of nesting: Happens if age is < 18
    if my_age >= 13:
        my_comment = 'You are a teenager'
    else:
        # Second level of nesting: Happens if age is < 13
        if my_age >= 10:
            my_comment = 'You are in middle school'
        else:
            # Third level of nesting: Happens if age is < 10
            if my_age >= 6:
                my_comment = 'You are in primary school'
            else:
                # The deepest part of the nest
                my_comment = 'You are too small to learn Python'

# --- STEP 3: Sequential Flow Resumes ---
# This line is unindented, so it always executes at the end.
print(f"At age: {my_age} -> {my_comment}")

At age: 3 -> You are too small to learn Python

# --- STEP 1: Get User Input ---
# We convert the inputs to integers to perform the modulo calculation.
num1 = int(input('Enter the first number: '))
num2 = int(input('Enter the second number: '))

# --- STEP 2: Multi-way Decision using 'and' ---
# Each 'elif' represents a specific combination of conditions.

if (num1 % 2 == 0) and (num2 % 2 == 0):
    # Runs only if BOTH numbers have a remainder of 0
    print('Both numbers are Even.')

elif (num1 % 2 != 0) and (num2 % 2 == 0):
    # Runs if num1 is Odd AND num2 is Even
    print('First number is Odd, second number is Even.')

    # Runs if num1 is Even AND num2 is Odd
    print('First number is Even, second number is Odd.')

else:
    # If none of the above are True, both must be Odd.
    # Note: No boolean expression is needed for 'else'.
    print('Both numbers are Odd.')

# --- STEP 1: Initialize the Counter ---
# We start x at 1. This variable controls how many times the loop repeats.
x = 1

# --- STEP 2: Print the Table Header ---
# \t is an 'escape character' that acts like the Tab key on your keyboard.
print('Number\tSquare')
print('------\t------')

# --- STEP 3: The while Loop ---
# The condition (x <= 5) is checked BEFORE every iteration.
while x <= 5:

    # Calculate the square (x to the power of 2)
    square = x ** 2

    # Print the result using an f-string (formatted string).
    # This automatically converts numbers to strings for us!
    print(f"{x}\t{square}")

    # --- STEP 4: Update the Counter ---
    # We add 1 to x so the loop eventually reaches 6 and stops.
    # If we forgot this line, the loop would run forever (Infinite Loop)!
    x = x + 1

# --- STEP 5: Loop Exit ---
# This line is unindented, so it only runs once the loop is finished.
print('Done!')

1   1
2   4
3   9
4   16
5   25
Done!

# --- STEP 1: Define the initial string ---
s1 = '112233'

# --- STEP 2: The Loop Condition ---
# In Python, an empty string '' is considered False.
# A string with characters is considered True.
# Therefore, 'while s1:' means 'Keep going until the string is empty'.
while s1:
    # Print the current state of the string
    print(s1)

    # --- STEP 3: String Slicing (The Update) ---
    # s1[2:] creates a NEW string starting from index 2 to the end.
    # This effectively "chops off" the first two characters.
    s1 = s1[2:]

# --- STEP 4: Loop Exit ---
print("The string is now empty!")

# 2233
# 33
# The string is now empty!

x = 0
print("Starting the loop...")

while x < 10:
    x = x + 1

    # 1. BREAK STATEMENT Exits loop immediately even if condition is still True.
    if x == 8:
        print(f"--- Found {x}: Breaking (Exiting loop entirely) ---")
        break

    # 2. CONTINUE STATEMENT Skips rest of current iteration. Moves to next
    if x == 5:
        print(f"--- Found {x}: Continuing (Skipping rest of this iteration) ---")
        continue

    # 3. THE PASS STATEMENT Does nothing, acts as a placeholder.
    if x == 3:
        # We know 3 is special, but we haven't decided what to do yet.
        # 'pass' keeps the code from crashing.
        pass
        print(f"--- Found {x}: Pass was used, but execution continues below ---")

    # This print statement is skipped when 'continue' or 'break' is triggered
    print(f"Current number is: {x}")

print("Loop is finished!")

        break

    # 3. This runs only if the 'if' condition was False (break didn't happen)
    print('Error: You did not enter a valid integer. Please try again.\n')

print('Program continues...')

# Example: Identifying Dead Code

# --- Type 1: Post-Termination Code ---
while True:
    print("This line runs!")
    break
    print("DEAD CODE: This will never print because of the break above.")

# --- Type 2: Impossible Conditions ---
x = 10
if x < 5 and x > 15:
    print("DEAD CODE: A number cannot be less than 5 AND greater than 15.")

# --- Type 3: Redundant Logic ---
# Imagine a student's score is 95
score = 95
# 1. This condition is checked first.
# Since 95 is greater than 50, this block executes.
if score > 50:
    print("You passed!")

# 2. DEAD CODE / REDUNDANT BLOCK:
# Even though 95 is also greater than 90, Python will NEVER look at this elif.
# Once the first 'if' is True, Python skips all related 'elif' and 'else' blocks.
elif score > 90:
    print("Excellent! You got an A!")

# 3. This else is also skipped because the first 'if' was True.
else:
    print("Better luck next time.")

print("Program finished.")

# ==========================================================
# Demonstrating various usages of the range() function
# ==========================================================

# 1. Using range() with a SINGLE argument (stop)
# Starts at 0 by default. Ends at (stop - 1).
print("Single argument (0 to 4):")
print(list(range(5)))         # Output: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

# 2. Using range() with START and STOP arguments
# Starts at 2. Ends at (6 - 1 = 5).
print("\nStart and Stop (2 to 5):")
print(list(range(2, 6)))      # Output: [2, 3, 4, 5]

# 3. Using range() with START, STOP, and STEP arguments
# Starts at 0. Increments by 3. Stops before 12.
print("\nWith positive step (0 to 9):")
print(list(range(0, 12, 3)))  # Output: [0, 3, 6, 9]

# 4. Using range() with NEGATIVE STEP (Counting Backwards)
# Starts at 0. Decrements by 1. Stops before -5.
print("\nNegative step (0 to -4):")
print(list(range(0, -5, -1))) # Output: [0, -1, -2, -3, -4]

# 5. Negative START and STOP with NEGATIVE STEP
# Starts at -2. Decrements by 2. Stops before -12.
print("\nNegative start/stop/step (-2 to -10):")
print(list(range(-2, -12, -2))) # Output: [-2, -4, -6, -8, -10]

# ----------------------------------------------------------
# LOGIC TRAPS: Why some ranges return an empty list []
# ----------------------------------------------------------

# 6. Impossible Range: Negative start/stop with POSITIVE step
# Logic: You cannot count UP from -2 to reach -12.
print("\nImpossible (Start > Stop with positive step):")
print(list(range(-2, -12, 2)))  # Output: []

# 7. Impossible Range: Positive start/stop with NEGATIVE step
# Logic: You cannot count DOWN from 2 to reach 8.
print("\nImpossible (Start < Stop with negative step):")
print(list(range(2, 8, -1)))    # Output: []

print("\n--- End of Demonstration ---")

docs.title: 4.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Flow control is about the order in which the statements of a program run. By default, Python runs statements one after another, from top to bottom. Flow control lets a program choose a path, repeat work, or jump out early.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: The three building blocks of flow
docs.text:
No. Building block What it does Python keywords 1 Selection (conditionals) Chooses between paths, based on whether a condition is True or False if, elif, else, match 2 Iteration (loops) Repeats a block of code until a job is finished while, for 3 Transfer statements Change the flow in the middle, for example to leave a loop early break, continue, return

(pass is also covered in this chapter. It does not change the flow at all. It is a placeholder that does nothing.)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: A real-world picture: taking cash from an ATM
docs.text:
A visit to an ATM uses all three kinds of flow:

  1. Sequential flow: insert your card, enter your PIN, choose "Withdraw Cash". Each step must finish before the next one starts.
  2. Conditional flow: is there enough money in your account? If yes, the machine pays out. If no, it shows "Insufficient Funds".
  3. Iterative flow: the machine counts out one Rs 100 note at a time, and keeps going while the total counted is less than the amount you asked for.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 4.2 The if...elif...else decision structure
docs.text:
The if...elif...else statement lets a program choose exactly one path out of several.

The general form is:

if condition_1:# condition_1 must be a Bool expression and eval to True or False
    statement_block_1
elif condition_2:   # condition_2 also must be a bool expression
    statement_block_2
else:
    statement_block_3

(This is a pattern, not a program you can run, so it is shown as text.)

Key rules:

No. Rule What it means 1 Conditions are Boolean Every condition after if or elif must work out to True or False 2 Only one block runs Python checks the conditions from the top. It runs the block of the first condition that is True, and then jumps past the whole structure 3 else is the catch-all else has no condition. It runs only if every condition above it was False 4 Indentation marks a block All the statements in a block must be indented by the same amount, usually 4 spaces. The first line that is not indented ends the block 5 Any number of elif, at most one else You may have many elif blocks, but only one else, and it must come last

elif is short for "else if".

Truthiness. A condition does not have to be a real Boolean. Python treats any non-zero number (including negative numbers) as True, and treats 0, 0.0, None, False and empty containers such as "" and [] as False. (You met this in Chapter 2.)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: Is a number positive, negative or zero?
docs.text:
What it does: asks you for a number and tells you whether it is positive, negative or zero.

How it does it:

  1. input() reads what you type, as a string.
  2. int() turns that string into a whole number.
  3. if num > 0: checks for a positive number. If this is True, Python prints the "positive" message and skips the rest of the structure.
  4. Otherwise elif num < 0: checks for a negative number.
  5. If both tests are False, the number can only be zero, so the else block runs.
  6. The last print() is not indented, so it runs in every case.

Why: this is the classic three-way choice. Exactly one of the three messages is printed.

Learning points:

  • The else block does not need a test. By the time Python reaches it, only one possibility is left.
  • Try 0, 7 and -3 to see all three paths.
  • If you type something like abc or 2.5, int() raises a ValueError. The comment in the code warns about this.

docs.title: 4.3 if...else statement (without elif)
docs.text:
When there are only two possible paths, you need just if and else:

if bool_expression:   #bool_expression must eval to True or False
    #Code block for bool_expression True
    pass
else:
    # Code block for bool_expression False
    pass

(pass is a placeholder that means "do nothing". It is used here only because a block cannot be empty. See Section 4.8.)

Key rules:

  • The colon: both the if line and the else line must end with a colon :. It tells Python that a block is starting.
  • Indentation: all statements in each block must be indented by the same amount.
  • One or the other: Python runs either the if block or the else block, never both.
  • No condition on else: it simply handles every case that the if did not.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: Even or odd?
docs.text:
What it does: asks for a whole number and says whether it is even or odd.

How it does it:

  • num % 2 is the remainder when num is divided by 2. For an even number it is 0 (for example 10 % 2 is 0). For an odd number it is 1 (for example 11 % 2 is 1).
  • if num % 2 == 0: is True for an even number, so the "Even" message is printed. Otherwise the else block prints "Odd".

Why: a number is either even or odd, never both. With exactly two paths, if...else is the natural choice.

Learning points:

  • == compares. = assigns. Writing if num % 2 = 0: is a SyntaxError.
  • % (the remainder operator) is the standard way to test whether one number divides another.

docs.title: 4.4 Omitting the else clause (the "one-way" decision)
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to act only when a condition is True, and do nothing at all when it is False. Then you leave out the else completely.

  • True case: the indented block runs, and then the program carries on with the rest of the script.
  • False case: Python skips the indented block and goes straight to the first line after it that is not indented.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: Switching on the air conditioner
docs.text:
What it does: switches the air conditioner on only if the temperature is above 25 degrees. Either way, it then prints "Monitoring system is active...".

How it does it:

  1. temp = 30 sets the temperature.
  2. if temp > 25: is True (30 is more than 25), so the two indented print() lines run.
  3. The last print() is not indented. It is outside the if, so it always runs.

Why: like a thermostat, you only need to act when it is hot. When it is cool, there is nothing special to do.

Learning points:

  • An if does not need an else.
  • Indentation decides which lines belong to the if.
  • Change temp to 20 and run the cell again. Only the last line is printed.

docs.title: 4.5 Nested if...else statements
docs.text:
Nesting means putting an if...elif...else statement inside a block of another one. Python lets you nest as deeply as you like. Each level of nesting is shown by one more level of indentation.

The problem with nesting: deep nesting pushes the code further and further to the right, and it becomes hard to read and to change. A good rule of thumb: if your code starts drifting far to the right, look for a simpler way to write it, for example with elif or with logical operators (Section 4.6).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: A staircase of nested checks on age
docs.text:
What it does: asks for your age and prints a comment, such as "You can vote" or "You are a teenager".

How it does it: each else block contains a new if. So each check happens only when all the checks above it were False:

Age typed First test that is True Comment 18 or more my_age >= 18 You can vote 13 to 17 my_age >= 13 You are a teenager 10 to 12 my_age >= 10 You are in middle school 6 to 9 my_age >= 6 You are in primary school Below 6 (none) You are too small to learn Python

The comment is stored in my_comment. The last line, which is not indented, prints the age and the comment.

Why: it shows how nesting works, and also why deep nesting gets hard to read. Each level moves the code four spaces to the right.

Learning points:

  • The order of the checks matters. Checking from the largest age downwards means each test only has to check a lower limit.
  • The same logic can be written flat, with one if, several elif and one else. Try rewriting it that way. It is much easier to read.

docs.title: Example 5: Two numbers, each even or odd (nested version)
docs.text:
What it does: asks for two numbers and says, for each one, whether it is even or odd.

How it does it:

  1. The outer if checks the first number.
  2. Inside both branches of the outer if, an inner if...else checks the second number.
  3. So there are four possible paths, and each one prints two lines.

Why: it shows nesting two levels deep. Notice that the inner check on num2 is written twice, once in each branch. This repetition is a sign that the code could be simpler, as Example 7 shows.

Learning points:

  • Here input() gives a string, and int(num1) converts it each time it is used. Converting once, straight after input(), is tidier.
  • (int(num1) % 2) == 0 has extra brackets. They are not needed, but they make the order of working clear.

docs.title: 4.6 How to avoid nested if statements (good programming technique)
docs.text:
As programs grow, nesting (if statements inside other if statements) makes code hard to read and maintain. A good way to simplify is to combine conditions with the logical operators and, or and not. This reduces the indentation and makes the logic clear at a glance. and is especially useful, because it needs both conditions to be True at the same time.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: The "teenager" check in one line
docs.text:
What it does: checks whether age (set to 15) is between 13 and 19, first with and and then with a chained comparison. Both print a message.

How it does it:

  • Option 1: age > 12 and age < 20 combines a lower limit and an upper limit into one condition. It is True only when both parts are True.
  • Option 2: 12 < age < 20 is a chained comparison (Chapter 3). Python reads it as (12 < age) and (age < 20).

Why: instead of a "staircase" of two if statements, one inside the other, you get a single, readable line.

Style Code Levels of indentation Nested if age > 12: then, inside it, if age < 20: 2 With and if age > 12 and age < 20: 1 Chained if 12 < age < 20: 1

Learning point: change age to 25 or 10 and run the cell again. Neither message is printed.

docs.title: Example 7: Two numbers, even or odd, without nesting
docs.text:
What it does: the same job as Example 5, but with one flat if...elif...else structure instead of nesting.

How it does it: each branch tests one of the four possible combinations:

Branch Condition num1 num2 if (num1 % 2 == 0) and (num2 % 2 == 0) even even first elif (num1 % 2 != 0) and (num2 % 2 == 0) odd even second elif (num1 % 2 == 0) and (num2 % 2 != 0) even odd else (no condition needed) odd odd

Why: the code is flatter, each branch says exactly which case it handles, and there is no repeated inner check.

Learning points:

  • With four combinations of two yes-or-no questions, three conditions are enough. The fourth case is whatever is left, so else handles it.
  • The inputs are converted with int() straight away, so the conditions stay short.

docs.title: 4.7 The while loop (iterative flow)
docs.text:
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as a condition stays True. An if statement checks its condition once. A while loop checks the condition, runs the body, and then goes back to check the condition again.

How it works:

Stage What happens The pre-check The condition is checked before each round, including the first. If it is False at the very start, the body never runs The iteration If the condition is True, the indented body runs. Then Python goes back to the while line and checks the condition again The exit As soon as the condition is False, Python skips the body and carries on with the first line after the loop Indentation As with if, the body of the loop is marked by indentation

The syntax, with the optional else part:

while test_condition:   # Must evaluate to True or False
    # Loop body: Runs repeatedly while condition is True
    statements
else:
    # Optional: Runs once when the condition becomes False
    statements

The else part is explained in Section 4.11.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: Numbers and their squares
docs.text:
What it does: prints the numbers 1 to 5 and their squares in two columns, then prints "Done!".

How it does it:

  1. x = 1 sets up the counter, the variable that controls the loop.
  2. Two print() lines print the column headings. \t is an escape character that works like the Tab key, so the columns line up.
  3. while x <= 5: checks the condition before every round.
  4. Inside the loop, x ** 2 works out the square, and the f-string prints x, a tab, and the square.
  5. x = x + 1 moves the counter on. After the round with x = 5, x becomes 6, the condition is False, and the loop ends.
  6. print('Done!') is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.

Why: this is the standard pattern for a counting loop: set up a counter, test it, do the work, and update the counter.

Learning points:

  • Always update the counter. If you delete x = x + 1, x stays 1 forever and the loop never ends. This is called an infinite loop. (In Colab, stop a runaway cell with the Stop button on the left of the cell, or Runtime > Interrupt execution.)
  • f-strings turn numbers into text for you, so you do not need str().
Round x at the start x <= 5? Printed x at the end 1 1 True 1 and 1 2 2 2 True 2 and 4 3 3 3 True 3 and 9 4 4 4 True 4 and 16 5 5 5 True 5 and 25 6 (check) 6 False the loop ends

docs.title: Example 9: Chopping a string, two characters at a time
docs.text:
What it does: prints '112233', then removes the first two characters and prints what is left, again and again until the string is empty.

How it does it:

  1. while s1: uses truthiness. A string with characters counts as True; the empty string '' counts as False. So the loop runs while s1 still has characters.
  2. print(s1) shows the string.
  3. s1 = s1[2:] is a slice from index 2 to the end. It makes a new, shorter string and ties s1 to it.
  4. After three rounds, s1 is '', the condition is False, and the loop ends.
Round s1 at the start Printed s1 at the end 1 '112233' 112233 '2233' 2 '2233' 2233 '33' 3 '33' 33 '' (check) '' the loop ends

Why: it shows how a loop can process data step by step, and how truthiness keeps the condition short.

Learning points:

  • Implicit Boolean check: you do not need to write while s1 != "":. while s1: does the same job and is the "Pythonic" way.
  • Slicing does not delete anything. Strings cannot be changed (they are immutable), so s1[2:] builds a new string, and the name s1 is moved to it.
  • The exit condition: the loop stops because the slicing eventually produces an empty string.

docs.title: 4.8 Control flow tools: break, continue and pass
docs.text:
Sometimes you need finer control over a loop. Python has three keywords for this:

Keyword Nickname Effect on this round Effect on later rounds Typical use break The emergency exit Stops at once None: the loop ends completely Stop as soon as you find what you are looking for continue The skip button Stops at once The loop goes on with the next round Skip bad data or particular values pass The placeholder Does nothing None Keep a place for code you have not written yet

After a break, Python carries on with the first line after the loop.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: break, continue and pass in one loop
docs.text:
What it does: counts x up from 1. It behaves differently at 3 (pass), 5 (continue) and 8 (break).

How it does it: at the top of each round, x = x + 1. Then three if tests are checked, in this order:

x What happens Is "Current number is: x" printed? 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 None of the tests match Yes 3 pass does nothing. The note is printed, and the round carries on as normal Yes 5 The note is printed, then continue jumps straight back to the while line No 8 The note is printed, then break ends the loop at once No 9, 10 Never reached: the loop already ended at 8

Why: it puts the three keywords side by side, so you can see exactly how they differ.

Learning points:

  • pass changes nothing about the flow. Here the print() after it still runs.
  • continue skips only the rest of this round.
  • break ends the whole loop, even though x < 10 is still True.

docs.title: 4.9 The continue statement
docs.text:
break ends the loop. continue is gentler: it says "stop this round here, ignore the code below me, and go on with the next item".

  • The jump: when Python reaches continue, it goes straight to the next round.
  • Use it to skip bad data or particular values, without stopping the whole process.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 11: Skipping the unlucky 7
docs.text:
What it does: goes through the numbers 1 to 10 and prints each one, except 7, which it skips with a message.

How it does it:

  1. for num in range(1, 11): gives num the values 1, 2, ..., 10 in turn. (for and range() are explained in Sections 4.12 and 4.16.)
  2. When num == 7, the skip message is printed and continue sends Python to the next number.
  3. For every other number, the "Processing number" line runs.

Learning points:

  • continue works the same way in for loops and while loops.
  • Replace continue with break and run the cell again. Now the loop stops at 7, and 8, 9 and 10 are never processed.

docs.title: 4.10 The match statement (Python 3.10 and later)
docs.text:
match is Python's version of the "switch" statement found in C++ and Java. It was added in Python 3.10. Its full name is structural pattern matching. It is a cleaner alternative to a long chain of if...elif...else, and is handy for menu-driven programs.

Key ideas:

Part Meaning The subject The value after match, which is compared with each pattern The cases Each case line gives a pattern to look for. Python tries them from the top and runs the first one that matches The wildcard _ case _: matches anything. It works like else, and should come last A guard An if after a pattern, as in case char if .... The case matches only if the guard is also True

The general shape:

match subject:
    case pattern_1:
        statements
    case pattern_2 if condition:   # a pattern with a guard
        statements
    case _:                        # the wildcard: anything else
        statements

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 12: What kind of key did you press?
docs.text:
What it does: asks you to press one key (then Enter), and tells you whether it was a letter, a digit, or something else.

How it does it:

  1. case char if char.isalpha() and len(char) == 1: The pattern char on its own matches any value and gives it the name char. The guard then checks that it is a single letter.
  2. case num if num.isdigit() and len(num) == 1: works the same way for a single digit.
  3. case _: catches everything else: a symbol, a space, several keys, or nothing at all.
Method Returns True when s.isalpha() every character of s is a letter, and s is not empty s.isdigit() every character of s is a digit, and s is not empty

Why: the three cases read like a list of rules, which is easier to follow than a chain of elifs.

Learning points:

  • A bare name in a case (like char) captures the value. It does not compare with a variable of that name.
  • Only the first matching case runs. There is no "fall through" to the next case, as there is in C.
  • Try a, 7, # and ab.

docs.title: 4.11 The while...else statement
docs.text:
while...else is a feature found in Python but not in most languages. It looks odd at first, but it becomes useful once you know the "exit rule".

Key ideas:

Rule Meaning The "condition False" trigger The else block runs when the while condition becomes False The "break" rule If the loop is ended by break, the else block is skipped Think "completed" else means: "if the loop finished normally, without being stopped early, run this" The exception rule If an error stops the program inside the loop, the else block does not run either

if...else compared with while...else:

Feature if...else while...else Logic Runs the if block or the else block, once Runs the body again and again, then runs else once at the end When else runs When the condition is False When the condition becomes False in the normal way Effect of break Not used The else block is skipped

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 13: Using while to act like if
docs.text:
What it does: asks for a number and says whether it is even or odd, using while...else instead of if...else.

How it does it:

  • Even number: the condition num % 2 == 0 is True, so the body prints "even". Then break ends the loop, and because of break, the else block is skipped.
  • Odd number: the condition is False from the start, so the body never runs. The loop ends normally, and the else block prints "odd".

Why: this is an unusual way to write an if-else, and you would not normally do it. It is here because it shows the break rule very clearly.

Learning points:

  • The break is essential. Without it, num would stay even for ever, and the loop would print "even" without stopping.
  • else after a loop means "no break happened".

docs.title: Example 14: A practical use: searching
docs.text:
What it does: looks for the letter 'z' in the word "Python". It is not there, so the else block prints "No 'z' was found".

How it does it:

  1. index starts at 0 and the loop runs while index < len(word), so it visits every position of the word.
  2. If word[index] == 'z', it prints "Found a 'z'!" and break ends the loop. The else is skipped.
  3. Otherwise index += 1 moves on to the next letter.
  4. If the loop reaches the end of the word without a break, the condition becomes False and the else block runs.

Why: this is where while...else really helps. It lets you say: "I looked at everything, and since I never found it (never used break), now I will run the else part". Without else, you would need an extra variable to remember whether the letter was found.

Learning points:

  • Change word to "pizza" and run the cell again. The loop now finds a 'z', and the else message is not printed.
  • The comment suggests "Zebra". Try it too. The search compares exactly, and 'Z' is not the same as 'z', so no 'z' is found.

docs.title: 4.11.1 Simulating a do...until loop in Python
docs.text:
Languages such as Visual Basic and C++ have a do...until or do...while loop. In those loops the body always runs at least once, and the condition is checked at the end. Python has no such loop. Instead, you use while True: together with an if...break at the point where you want to stop.

The pattern:

Part Job while True: Starts a loop that will never end on its own The body Runs at once, at least one time The exit condition An if checks whether it is time to stop break Leaves the loop when the condition is met

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 15: The input trap
docs.text:
What it does: keeps asking for your age until you type only digits. Then it prints a success message and moves on.

How it does it:

  1. while True: starts a loop whose condition is always True.
  2. input() asks for your age. This always happens at least once.
  3. my_age.isdigit() checks whether the text is made only of the digits 0 to 9.
  4. If it is, the success message is printed, and break leaves the loop.
  5. If not, the error message is printed, and the loop goes round again to ask once more.

Why: this is a very common real use: input validation. The user is "trapped" in the loop until they give the right kind of data.

Learning points:

  • The "at least once" rule: the prompt is always shown once, because the check comes after input().
  • \n at the end of the error message adds a blank line, which separates the failed attempts.
  • isdigit() is False for -5 and for 3.5, because - and . are not digits. Try them, and then try abc, and finally a proper age.

docs.title: 4.12 The for loop: iterating over a sequence
docs.text:
A for loop steps through the items of a sequence or collection, such as a string, a list, a tuple or a range, one item at a time.

  • A while loop is indefinite: it runs as long as a condition is True, and you may not know in advance how many rounds that will take.
  • A for loop is definite: the number of rounds is fixed by the size of the collection.

Key ideas:

Idea Meaning Sequence-based It "steps through" the items of a string, list, tuple, range and so on Automatic progress You do not need a counter like x = x + 1. Python moves to the next item for you The loop variable In each round, the current item is put into the loop variable (also called the target variable) Optional else As with while, an else block runs once after the loop ends normally, without a break

The general syntax:

for item in collection:
    # This code runs for every single item in the collection
    statements
else:
    # Optional: Runs once after the loop finishes naturally
    statements

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 16: Spelling a word, one letter at a time
docs.text:
What it does: prints each letter of "Python" on its own line, then a closing message from the else block, then "Program continues...".

How it does it:

  1. for letter in word: puts 'P' into letter in round 1, 'y' in round 2, and so on, up to 'n'.
  2. After the last letter, the loop ends normally, so the else block runs.
  3. The last print() is outside the loop and runs once.

Why: walking through a string letter by letter is one of the most common uses of for.

Learning points:

  • The same kind of loop works over lists, tuples and dictionaries. (Over a dictionary, the loop variable gets the keys.)
  • There is no counter to forget, so there is no risk of an infinite loop.

docs.title: 4.13 Nested for loops
docs.text:
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. It is useful when you need to compare every item of one collection with every item of another.

Think of a clock: the minute hand (the inner loop) must go all the way round before the hour hand (the outer loop) moves on by one step.

Key ideas:

  • Each-to-each comparison: for every single item of the first collection, the whole second collection is scanned from start to finish.
  • Execution order: the inner loop runs much more often than the outer loop.
  • Cost: the total number of comparisons is the length of the first collection multiplied by the length of the second. For large collections, nested loops can be slow.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 17: Finding matching characters
docs.text:
What it does: compares every letter of "hello" with every letter of "world", and prints each match.

How it does it:

  1. The outer loop takes one letter ch1 from "hello".
  2. For that ch1, the inner loop takes each letter ch2 of "world" in turn.
  3. If ch1 == ch2, a match is printed.
  4. When the inner loop has used every letter of "world", the outer loop moves to the next letter of "hello".
ch1 from "hello" Matches found in "world" h none e none l l l l o o

So there are 5 x 5 = 25 comparisons and 3 matches.

Why: it shows the "every item against every item" pattern that nested loops are used for.

Learning point: 'l' is printed twice because it appears twice in "hello". The loops report every match, not just unique ones. (With sets from Chapter 2, set(str1) & set(str2) gives just the unique common letters: {'l', 'o'}.)

docs.title: 4.14 Choosing your tool: for or while
docs.text:
Both loops can often do the same job, but each has a "natural home" where it is shorter and clearer.

Feature for loop while loop Kind of repetition Definite: the number of rounds is known or fixed Indefinite: the number of rounds depends on a condition Driven by A sequence (list, string, range and so on) A Boolean condition Moving on Automatic: Python hands you the next item Manual: you must update the variable yourself, for example x += 1 Main purpose Process every item in a collection Repeat until something changes Risk of an infinite loop Very low: it ends when the items run out Higher: it never ends if the condition stays True Reads best for Counting and walking through sequences Open-ended logic, waiting for something to happen Does the body always run at least once? No, not if the collection is empty No, not if the condition is False at the start Typical example "Print every name in this list" "Keep asking for a password until it is correct"

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 4.15 Dead code (unreachable code)
docs.text:
Dead code (also called unreachable code) is code that can never run, whatever happens. It does not break the program, but it makes the script messy and confusing, because a reader may think it does something.

Dead code usually falls into one of three groups:

No. Kind Example Why it never runs 1 Code after an exit statement a line after break, continue, return or raise in the same block Python has already left the block 2 An impossible condition if 1 > 2: or if x < 5 and x > 15: The condition can never be True 3 A shadowed (redundant) branch if x > 0: followed by elif x > 10: Any value that passes the second test has already passed the first, so the elif is never reached

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 18: Three kinds of dead code
docs.text:
What it does: contains one example of each kind of dead code. Only three lines are printed: "This line runs!", "You passed!" and "Program finished.".

How it does it:

Type Code What happens 1. After an exit a print() after break break leaves the loop first, so that print() is never reached 2. Impossible condition if x < 5 and x > 15: No number is both below 5 and above 15, so the block never runs 3. Redundant logic if score > 50: then elif score > 90: 95 passes the first test, so Python never looks at the elif. In fact every score above 90 is also above 50, so the elif can never run for any score

Why: knowing these patterns helps you spot mistakes in your own code.

Learning point: the fix for type 3 is to put the stricter test first:

if score > 90:
    print("Excellent! You got an A!")
elif score > 50:
    print("You passed!")
else:
    print("Better luck next time.")

docs.title: 4.16 The range() function
docs.text:
range() creates a sequence of whole numbers. It is very memory-efficient: it does not store all the numbers at once, but produces each one when it is needed.

Signature:

range(stop)
range(start, stop)
range(start, stop, step)
Parameter Meaning Default start The first number 0 stop The sequence stops before this number. stop itself is never included (required) step How much to add each time. It can be negative, to count down, but it cannot be 0 1

All three must be whole numbers. A step of 0 raises a ValueError.

The "up to but not including" rule: if you want the numbers to reach 10, stop must be 11.

How the values are worked out: the number at position i is start + step * i, for i = 0, 1, 2, ....

  • With a positive step, the sequence continues while the value is less than stop.
  • With a negative step, it continues while the value is greater than stop.
  • If the step points the wrong way (start below stop with a negative step, or start above stop with a positive step), the range is empty.
Call Numbers produced Why range(5) 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 start defaults to 0, step to 1 range(2, 7) 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 starts at 2 and stops before 7 range(1, 10, 2) 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 starts at 1 and goes up in steps of 2 range(10, 0, -2) 10, 8, 6, 4, 2 a negative step counts down; 0 is not included range(5, 1, 1) (empty) you cannot go down from 5 to 1 with a positive step range(1, 5, -1) (empty) you cannot go up from 1 to 5 with a negative step

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 19: The different ways to use range()
docs.text:
What it does: shows seven ranges, from simple to tricky, and prints each one as a list.

How it does it: list(range(...)) turns the range into a list, so that you can see all its numbers at once. (Printing range(5) directly just shows range(0, 5).)

No. Call Result 1 range(5) [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] 2 range(2, 6) [2, 3, 4, 5] 3 range(0, 12, 3) [0, 3, 6, 9] 4 range(0, -5, -1) [0, -1, -2, -3, -4] 5 range(-2, -12, -2) [-2, -4, -6, -8, -10] 6 range(-2, -12, 2) []: you cannot count up from -2 to -12 7 range(2, 8, -1) []: you cannot count down from 2 to 8

Learning points:

  • An empty range is not an error. A loop over it simply does not run.
  • Check the direction: a negative step needs start greater than stop.

docs.title: 4.17 Using the range() function in a loop
Example 20: range() in for loops
docs.text:
What it does: uses range() in nine small for loops: six that print something and three that print nothing.

How it does it:

Part Loop What it shows 1 for i in range(len(s)): Loops over the positions of a string. len(s) is 6, so i goes 0 to 5, and s[i] gives the letter at each position 2 for i in range(len(my_list)): The same idea for a list 3 range(0, 10, 2) Counts in twos: 0 2 4 6 8 4 range(10, 0, -1) Counts down from 10 to 1 (0 is not included) 5 range(-1, -6, -1) Counts down through negative numbers: -1 to -5 6 range(1, 10, 15) The step is bigger than the whole range, so only 1 is printed A range(3, 3) Start equals stop: nothing to loop over B range(1, 5, -1) Wrong direction: empty C range(0) Zero rounds

About end=" ": normally print() moves to a new line after each call. print(i, end=" ") puts a space after the value instead, so the numbers appear on one line. The \n\n at the start of the next heading then moves down two lines.

Learning points:

  • range(len(...)) is useful when you need the position as well as the item. (Python also has enumerate(), which gives both at once. See "Beyond the Book", Extra 3.)
  • An empty range never causes an error.
  • A step of 0 does. That line is commented out at the end of the cell. Remove the # from the for line and the print(i) line to see the ValueError, then put them back.

docs.title: Beyond the Text
docs.text:
The book asks you to study two more topics. Here is a short guide to each.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Dead code in different situations
docs.text:
Section 4.15 showed three kinds of dead code. The same ideas turn up in other places too:

Situation Example Why the code is dead Inside a function, after return return total followed by print(total) return leaves the function first After an unconditional raise raise ValueError("bad") followed by more lines The error leaves the block first A branch that can never be True if False: or while False: The condition is fixed A branch hidden by an earlier one if n % 2 == 0: then elif n % 4 == 0: Every multiple of 4 is also even, so it is always caught by the first test An else after a loop that always breaks while True: with a break, followed by else: A while True loop can only end with break, and break always skips the else

Tools called linters (such as pylint or flake8) and some editors, such as VS Code, can point out unreachable code for you.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: The iterator protocol: how a for loop really works
docs.text:
How does a for loop "talk" to a list? It uses the iterator protocol.

Term Meaning Examples Iterable Any object you can loop over strings, lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, ranges Iterator An object that hands out the items of an iterable one at a time and remembers where it has got to what iter() returns iter(obj) Makes an iterator from an iterable it = iter([10, 20]) next(it) Gets the next item from the iterator. When there are no items left, it raises StopIteration next(it) gives 10, then 20

When you write for x in my_list:, Python quietly does this:

  1. It calls iter(my_list) to get an iterator.
  2. It calls next() on the iterator again and again, putting each item into x and running the body.
  3. When next() raises StopIteration, the loop ends. (If there is an else, it runs now.)

The next cell does the same thing by hand.

  • The first three next() calls give 'a', 'b' and 'c'.
  • The fourth call would raise StopIteration. To keep the notebook running, it is written as next(it, "no more items"). The second argument is a default value that next() returns instead of raising the error.

docs.title: Beyond the Book
docs.text:
Three short extras on ideas from this chapter. They are optional.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Extra 1: for...else with break
docs.text:
Example 16 used else after a for loop that always finishes. The else is most useful together with break, as in the search of Example 14. This cell looks for the first number greater than 50 in a list. The else runs only if no such number is found.

Change 50 to 100 and run the cell again to see the else message.

docs.title: Extra 2: A range is a lazy sequence
docs.text:
Section 4.16 said that range() does not store all its numbers. You can still ask it questions as if it were a list, and it answers without building the list:

Question Code How many numbers? len(r) Is a number in it? in What is at a position? r[index] (negative positions work too)

range(0, 1_000_000_000, 7) holds over 142 million numbers, but it takes only a few bytes of memory. (The underscores in 1_000_000_000 just make a long number easier to read.)

docs.title: Extra 3: enumerate() gives the position and the item together
docs.text:
Example 20 used range(len(s)) to get the positions of a string. enumerate() gives you both the position and the item in each round, which is shorter and easier to read.

for i, ch in enumerate(s): unpacks each (position, item) pair into two names, just like tuple unpacking in Chapter 2.

# Example 1:- Builtin len() returns number of items in an object.

import random

# Example 1:- random.random(). # It generates a random number
# in semi-open range [0.0, 1.0). The square bracket means
# "closed interval on the left" and the round parenthesis means

def make_counter():
    # 1. Variable count belongs to the ENCLOSING scope.
    # It acts as the "Private Memory" for the closure.
    count = 0

    def counter():
        # 2. The 'nonlocal' keyword is essential here.
        # It allows the inner function to MODIFY 'count'.
        # Without it, Python would treat 'count' as a new local variable.
        nonlocal count

        count += 1
        return count

    # 3. Return the function object to create the Closure
    return counter

# --- INDEPENDENT STATE ---
# Each call to make_counter() creates a brand new "Private Memory" box.
counter_a = make_counter()
counter_b = make_counter()

print(f"Counter A: {counter_a()}")  # Output: 1
print(f"Counter A: {counter_a()}")  # Output: 2

# Advanced: How to see the "hidden" memory
# Each function object has a __closure__ attribute
cell = counter_a.__closure__[0]
print(f"The hidden value in counter_a is: {cell.cell_contents}")
# Output: The hidden value in counter_a is: 2

# Counter B starts fresh; it cannot see or touch Counter A's memory.
print(f"Counter B: {counter_b()}")  # Output: 1

# Counter A still remembers where it left off.
print(f"Counter A: {counter_a()}")  # Output: 3

Counter A: 1
Counter A: 2
The hidden value in counter_a is: 2
Counter B: 1
Counter A: 3
