docs.title: 5.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Functions go by many names in programming: subroutines, routines, procedures, methods or subprograms.

A function is a named block of statements that does a job. You write the block once, give it a name, and then use it again and again just by calling that name. A function can also:

  • take parameters (inputs), and
  • return a result (a value or an object).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.2 Why do we need functions?
docs.text:
• Reuse: write the code once and use it many times. Python's own modules are examples of this. The random module, for instance, is a ready-made set of functions for random numbers.
  • Decomposition: break a problem into smaller units, each with one job.
  • Readability: a long, complicated script becomes a set of short, named parts.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.3 Basics of functions
docs.text:
Python has three broad kinds of functions:

Kind Where it comes from Needs import? Examples Built-in Part of Python itself, always available No print(), len(), type() Module Stored in separate .py files called modules Yes math.sqrt(), random.randint() User-defined Written by you, with the def keyword No (if in the same file) any function you write

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.3.1 Built-in functions
docs.text:
Built-in functions are always ready to use. Python has about 70 of them. They include:

Group Examples Maths abs(), round(), max(), min(), sum(), pow() Type conversion int(), float(), str(), bool(), list() Input and output input(), print() Other len(), id(), type(), range()

(Python 2 had a separate raw_input(). In Python 3 it is just input().)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.3.2 Functions in modules
docs.text:
A module is a separate .py file. You reach its functions with a dot, as in math.sqrt(16). Python keeps only the most useful functions built in, and puts the rest in modules that you import when you need them. This keeps the core language small.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.3.3 User-defined functions
docs.text:
These are the functions you write yourself. Sections 5.8 onwards show how.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.4 Calling a function (as opposed to defining one)
docs.text:
Built-in and module functions have already been written for you. You only need to call them. For a built-in function you just use its name. For a module function you first import the module and then use the dot.

When it is called, a function:

  1. may or may not take arguments,
  2. may or may not do something useful (a function that does nothing is of little use, but see pass in Example 6), and
  3. always returns something. If it does not say what, it returns None.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text:
Category Function Meaning Example Returns Sequence len() Number of items len("Hello") gives 5 int Utility type() The type of a value type(12) gives <class 'int'=""> a type object Utility input() Reads what the user types input("Name: ") str Utility print() Shows output print("Hi") None Conversion int() Converts to a whole number int("5") gives 5 int Conversion float() Converts to a float float("3.5") gives 3.5 float Conversion str() Converts to a string str(9) gives '9' str Conversion bool() Converts to True or False bool(0) gives False bool Conversion list() Converts to a list list("Hi") gives ['H', 'i'] list Sequence range() Makes a sequence of whole numbers range(1, 5) a range object Maths max() The largest value max(2, 8, 5) gives 8 same type as the items Maths min() The smallest value min(3, 7, 1) gives 1 same type as the items Maths sum() Adds up the items sum([1, 2, 3]) gives 6 int or float

How it does it:

Example Call Result Meaning 10 range(5) in a for loop 0 1 2 3 4, one per line Makes the numbers 0 to 4 11 max([10, 20, 5, 30]) 30 The largest item 12 min([10, 20, 5, 30]) 5 The smallest item 13 sum([10, 20, 30]) 60 Adds up the items 14 abs(-15) 15 Removes the minus sign 15 round(3.567, 2) 3.57 Rounds to 2 decimal places

docs.title: Notes on Example 2: lazy evaluation
docs.text:
range() saves memory with a trick called lazy evaluation. Suppose you need the numbers 1 to 10. You could store them all in a list, but the list takes up memory. range(1, 11) instead works out each number only when it is needed.

A range is a special lazy sequence. It is not a list, and it is not a generator either. (Generators are another kind of lazy object that you will meet later in the book.) Chapter 4, "Beyond the Book", showed how a range can answer len(), in and indexing without building a list.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.6 The math module
docs.text:
The math module is part of Python's standard library. It needs no installation, but you must import it before using it. Its functions fall into these groups:

Group Examples Basic maths math.sqrt(), math.factorial(), math.fabs() Powers and logarithms math.pow(), math.exp(), math.log(), math.log10() Trigonometry math.sin(), math.cos(), math.tan() Angle conversion math.degrees(), math.radians() Rounding math.ceil(), math.floor(), math.trunc() Constants math.pi, math.e, math.tau, math.inf

These functions do not work with complex numbers. For complex numbers, use the functions of the same name in the cmath module.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: Common math functions
docs.text:
What it does: uses six math functions and the constant math.pi.

How it does it:

Example Call Result Note 1 math.sqrt(16) 4.0 Square root. Always a float 2 math.factorial(5) 120 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 3 math.pow(2, 3) 8.0 Always a float. (2 ** 3 gives the int 8) 4 math.ceil(4.3) 5 Rounds up to the next whole number 5 math.floor(4.7) 4 Rounds down 6 math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) True The safe way to compare floats (see Chapter 2) 7 math.pi * 5 ** 2 78.539... Area of a circle of radius 5

Learning point: ceil() and floor() also work for negative numbers: math.ceil(-4.3) is -4 and math.floor(-4.3) is -5. Rounding "up" means towards plus infinity.

docs.title: 5.7 The random module
docs.text:
The random module makes pseudo-random numbers: numbers that look random but are really produced by a fixed formula.

Common uses:

  1. games, such as rolling a die or shuffling a pack of cards,
  2. simulations,
  3. testing, for example making random test data, and
  4. machine learning, for example picking random samples.
Category Function What it does Example Sample output Random float random.random() A float from 0.0 up to, but not including, 1.0 random.random() 0.3748 Random whole number random.randint(a, b) A whole number from a to b, both included random.randint(1, 6) a value from 1 to 6 Random whole number random.randrange(start, stop, step) One number picked from range(start, stop, step) random.randrange(0, 10, 2) 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 Random float random.uniform(a, b) A float between a and b random.uniform(1.5, 5.5) 3.21... Pick one item random.choice(seq) One random item from a sequence random.choice([2, 4, 6]) 4 Pick several (repeats allowed) random.choices(seq, k=n) n items, the same item may come more than once random.choices([1, 2, 3], k=4) [3, 1, 3, 2] Pick several (no repeats) random.sample(seq, k) k different items random.sample([1, 2, 3, 4], 2) [3, 1] Shuffle random.shuffle(lst) Mixes up a list in place. Returns None random.shuffle(L) L becomes [3, 1, 2] Repeatable results random.seed(x) Sets the starting point of the generator random.seed(5) then random.random() always 0.6229... Random bits random.getrandbits(k) A whole number made of k random bits random.getrandbits(8) 0 to 255

Why "pseudo-random"? Python uses a formula called the Mersenne Twister. It starts from a value called the seed. The same seed always gives the same sequence of numbers, so the numbers are not truly random: they only appear random. A real die is different: you cannot predict the next roll. If you do not set a seed, Python picks one for you (from the operating system's source of randomness, or from the current time), so each run is different.

random.seed() is sometimes called a "bookkeeping" function, because it does not produce a random number itself. It only sets up the generator so that the other functions can work. "Beyond the Book", Extra 1 shows how a seed makes results repeatable.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: Six random functions
docs.text:
What it does: makes a random float, a random whole number, a random choice, a shuffled list, a random sample and a random float in a range.

How it does it:

Example Call What you get 1 random.random() A float in [0.0, 1.0) 2 random.randint(1, 10) A whole number from 1 to 10 3 random.choice(my_list) One of East, West, North, South 4 random.shuffle(my_numbers) The same list, in a new order 5 random.sample(range(1, 21), 5) 5 different numbers from 1 to 20 6 random.uniform(1.5, 5.5) A float between 1.5 and 5.5

About [0.0, 1.0): a square bracket means the end is included; a round bracket means it is not. So 0.0 can come up, but every number is less than 1.0.

Learning points:

  • Your output will be different from the saved output, and different every time you run the cell. That is the point of random numbers.
  • shuffle() changes the list itself and returns None. So write random.shuffle(my_numbers) and then print my_numbers. Writing print(random.shuffle(my_numbers)) would just print None.
  • sample() never repeats an item; choices() can.

docs.title: 5.7.1 Note on randrange()
docs.text:
Signature:

random.randrange(stop)
random.randrange(start, stop)
random.randrange(start, stop, step)
Parameter Meaning Default start The first possible value. It can be picked 0 stop The end. It is never picked (required) step The gap between the possible values 1

range() compared with randrange(): range() makes the whole sequence of numbers. randrange() picks one number from that sequence at random.

Call What it gives range(3, 10, 2) the sequence 3, 5, 7, 9 random.randrange(3, 10, 2) one of 3, 5, 7 or 9

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 5: randrange() with one, two and three arguments
docs.text:
What it does: picks a random number three times, with different ranges.

Example Call Possible results 1 randrange(10) 0 to 9 2 randrange(5, 15) 5 to 14 3 randrange(0, 30, 5) 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25 (never 30)

Learning point: random.randint(a, b) includes b, but random.randrange(a, b) does not. randint(1, 10) can give 10; randrange(1, 10) cannot.

docs.title: 5.8 Defining a function
docs.text:
Besides using built-in and module functions, you can write your own. A program that does this has two parts:

  1. the definition, which creates the function, and
  2. the call, which uses it.

Calling your own function works exactly like calling a built-in one.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.8.1 Function syntax
docs.text:
def func_name(arg1, arg2, ..., argN):
    statements
    return value     # optional

(This is a pattern, so it is shown as text. The names inside the brackets are really parameters; see below.)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.8.2 Components of a Python function
docs.text:
No. Part What to know 1 The keyword def Starts every function definition. Defining a function does not run it; you must call it 2 The function name Follows the normal rules for names (letters, digits, underscores). Choose a name that says what it does 3 Parameters Names inside the brackets that will receive values when the function is called 4 The colon : Ends the header line. Always required 5 The body One or more statements, indented the same amount (usually 4 spaces) 6 return (optional) Sends a value back to the caller and ends the function at once

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: The smallest possible function
docs.text:
What it does: defines a function called calculate_sum that does nothing yet. There is no output.

How: a function body cannot be empty, so pass (a statement that does nothing) fills the space.

Why: it shows the bare shape of a definition: def, a name, brackets, a colon, and an indented body. Programmers often write empty functions like this first, as a plan, and fill them in later.

Learning points:

  • Running this cell only creates the function. Nothing is printed.
  • Add a new cell with print(calculate_sum()). It prints None, because the function returns nothing.

docs.title: Parameters and arguments
docs.text:
These two words are often mixed up. They are two sides of the same coin:

  • A parameter is a name in the def line. It is an empty box (a "reserved seat") waiting for a value.
  • An argument is the actual value you pass in when you call the function.
Term Role Where you find it Example Parameter Placeholder In the def line def greet(name): (name is the parameter) Argument Actual value In the function call greet("Alice") ("Alice" is the argument)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 7: A parameter and an argument
docs.text:
What it does: defines greet(name) and calls it with "Bobby". It prints Hello Bobby.

How it does it:

  1. def greet(name): creates the function. name is the parameter.
  2. greet("Bobby") calls it. The argument "Bobby" is placed in name.
  3. The body runs: print("Hello", name) prints Hello Bobby.

Learning point: call it again with a different argument, for example greet("Asha"). The same code now prints a different name. This is what makes functions reusable.

docs.title: The return statement
docs.text:
return is the "exit door" of a function. It does two things at once:

  1. It sends a value back to the line that called the function.
  2. It ends the function. Any code after return in the same block never runs. (It is dead code, as in Chapter 4.)

A Python function always returns something:

Case What the caller gets return value that value a bare return None no return at all None

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: The three cases of return
docs.text:
What it does: defines three functions, one for each case, and prints what each one returns.

How it does it:

Function How it ends Printed inside the function Value returned add_numbers(5, 3) return a + b nothing 8 print_message() a bare return Hello, World! None greet("Alice") and greet("Bob") no return Hello, Alice! and Hello, Bob! None

Why: it shows the difference between printing a value and returning it. print_message() shows text on the screen, but the value it hands back is None.

Learning points:

  • Printing is for people to read. Returning is for the program to use. Only a returned value can be stored in a variable or used in a calculation.
  • greet("Alice") is called without storing the result. That is fine: the returned None is simply thrown away.
  • This greet() replaces the greet() from Example 7, because a new def with the same name ties the name to the new function.

docs.title: 5.8.3 Summary table
docs.text:
Part Meaning def Starts a function definition Function name The name used to call the function Parameters Input names in the definition Arguments Actual values passed during the call : Ends the function header Indentation Marks the function body return Sends back a value and ends the function None What a function returns if it does not return anything else

Good habits:

  1. Use functions to avoid repeating code.
  2. Choose names that say what the function does, such as calculate_total or get_age.
  3. Keep each function short and give it one job.
  4. A function can call other functions.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.9 Function definition compared with function call
docs.text:
Function definition Function call What it does Creates the function Uses (runs) the function How it looks Starts with def The name followed by brackets, as in greet() Does the body run? No. Python only remembers the name and what the function should do Yes. Python jumps into the body, runs it, and comes back Order Must come first Must come after the definition. Calling a function before it is defined gives a NameError

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.10 Flow of execution
docs.text:
The order in which Python runs a program:

  1. It starts at the first statement that does something, which is not always the first line.
  2. It runs statements from top to bottom.
  3. A function definition does not interrupt this flow. Python just notes the function and moves on.
  4. The body of a function runs only when the function is called.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.11 Function calls as "detours"
docs.text:
A function call is like a short detour off the main road:

  1. The main flow pauses at the call.
  2. Python jumps to the function definition.
  3. It runs all the statements in the function body.
  4. It returns to the line after the call and carries on.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 9: Watching the detour
docs.text:
What it does: prints three lines: "Before calling greet()", "Inside greet()" and "After calling greet()".

How it does it: the numbers below are the line numbers of the code (turn on line numbers in Colab with Tools > Settings > Editor > Show line numbers, or press Ctrl + M, L).

Step Line What happens Output 1 1 and 2 The definition is read and stored. Nothing is printed 2 3 The main flow starts Before calling greet() 3 4 greet() is called. Python takes the detour 4 2 The body of greet() runs Inside greet() 5 4 The function ends. Python returns to the line of the call 6 5 The main flow carries on After calling greet()

Why are lines 1 and 2 not run first? They are a definition, like reading a recipe without cooking it. Python learns how to greet, but only does it when line 4 calls the function.

Learning point: this greet() takes no parameters, and replaces the earlier greet(name).

docs.title: 5.12 Nested function definitions
docs.text:
Python lets you define a function inside another function. The inner function is created only when the outer function runs. It does not run unless it is called, and at first it can only be called from inside the outer function. Sections 5.13.3 and 5.13.4 show examples.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.13 Scope, namespace and lifetime of variables
What is lifetime?
docs.text:
• The lifetime of a variable is how long it exists in memory: from the moment it is created to the moment it is destroyed.
  • When you write x = 3, Python (1) creates the object 3 in memory, and (2) ties the name x to it.
  • The name exists as long as the program can still reach it. When a function ends, its local names are no longer needed.
  • Python then frees the memory automatically, using reference counting and garbage collection. You never delete variables by hand in normal Python.

Scope and lifetime are covered in more depth in a later chapter. For now, you only need global and local variables:

Property Global variables Local variables Where defined Outside every function (usually at the top of the script) Inside a function body Born When the line that creates it runs When the function is called Dies When the program ends When the function returns or finishes Scope (visibility) Wide: can be read anywhere in the script, including inside functions Narrow: only inside the function where it was created Lifetime The whole run of the program Only while the function is running Main use Constants, or data shared by the whole program Temporary working values for one task Memory Stays until the program ends Freed as soon as the function ends Risk High: any part of the program can change it, which makes bugs hard to find Low: changes stay inside the function

Why this matters: local variables keep functions separate from each other, and let Python free memory as soon as a function is done. Too many global variables make a program harder to understand and to fix.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: A global and a local variable
docs.text:
What it does: defines a global msg and a function with a local name, calls the function, and then prints msg.

How it does it:

  1. msg = "Hello" is at the top level, so it is global.
  2. Inside my_function(), name = "Alice" is local.
  3. The function can see both, so it prints Hello Alice.
  4. After the call, print(msg) works, because msg is global.
  5. print(name) is commented out. Outside the function, name does not exist.

Learning point: remove the # from # print(name) and run the cell. You get NameError: name 'name' is not defined. Then put the # back.

docs.title: 5.13.1 Lifetime compared with scope
docs.text:
No. Property Scope (the "where") Lifetime (the "when") 1 Definition The part of the program where a name can be seen and used The time a variable stays in memory 2 Question it answers Can I see this variable from here? Does this variable still exist? 3 Decided by Where the variable is created in the code When the program enters and leaves a function 4 Words used Global scope, local scope, enclosing (non-local) scope Birth (creation) and death (clean-up) 5 Picture A pass: does it let you into this room (function)? A candle: how long until it burns out? 6 Typical error NameError: the name is not visible from here NameError: the name no longer exists

Both problems show up as the same error, NameError, which simply means "Python cannot find this name". There are two different reasons:

  1. A scope problem: the variable exists, but you are looking for it from a place that cannot see it. For example, a local variable cannot be seen from outside its function.
  2. A lifetime problem: the variable's function has already finished, so the variable is gone.

When Python meets a name, it looks for it in this order, and stops at the first place it finds it:

(These four places are often remembered as LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.)

Note:

  • You never need to free memory by hand.
  • Use long-lived global variables with care.
  • Loops and if blocks do not create a new scope in Python, unlike some other languages. A variable created inside a for loop still exists after the loop.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.13.2 Name clash in local and global scope
docs.text:
If the same name is given a value in two different scopes, which one does Python use? The rule is simple:

  • Inside the function, the local name wins. (There is a way to reach the global one, the global keyword; see "Beyond the Book", Extra 2.)
  • Outside the function, there is no clash, because the local name does not exist there.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 11: A local x hides the global x
docs.text:
What it does: has a global x = 'cat' and a local x = 'dog' inside f3(). It prints dog inside the function and cat outside.

How it does it:

  1. x = 'cat' creates a global x.
  2. Inside f3(), x = 'dog' creates a new, local x. It does not change the global one.
  3. Inside f3(), Python finds the local x first, so it prints dog. This is called shadowing: the local name hides the global one.
  4. After f3() ends, its local x is gone. print(x) at the top level finds the global x, which is still cat.

Learning point: assigning to a name inside a function makes it local to that function, even if a global of the same name exists.

docs.title: Example 12: Two local scopes in one global scope
docs.text:
What it does: has one global x and two functions, each with its own local x. It prints dog, then rat, then cat.

How it does it:

  1. The global x is 'cat'.
  2. f1() creates its own local x = 'dog' and prints it. When f1() ends, that x is gone.
  3. f2() creates a separate local x = 'rat' and prints it. It has no connection to f1()'s x.
  4. The last line prints the global x, which was never touched: cat.

Why: think of the global scope as a big box, and each local scope as a smaller box inside it. Inside a small box, you see the local x. Outside the small boxes, you see the global x.

docs.title: 5.13.3 Defining a function inside another function (nested functions)
docs.text:
A function defined inside another function is a nested function. Here, f1() is the enclosing (outer) function, and f2() is the enclosed (inner) function. Normally, the inner function can only be called from inside the outer one.

Inside f1(), the local x of f1() hides the global x. Inside f2(), the local x of f2() hides both the x of f1() and the global x.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 13: Three scopes, one inside another
docs.text:
What it does: has a global x, an x inside f1(), and an x inside f2(), which is nested in f1(). Each is printed from its own scope.

How it does it:

  1. f1() is called from the top level.
  2. Inside f1(), x = 'dog in f1()' is created and printed.
  3. f1() defines f2() and then calls it.
  4. Inside f2(), x = 'rat in f2()' is created and printed.
  5. Both functions end, their local names are gone, and the global x is printed.
Scope Value of x Printed by Global 'cat in global scope' the last line Enclosing: f1() 'dog in f1()' the print() inside f1() Local: f2() 'rat in f2()' the print() inside f2()

Learning points:

  • f2 exists only inside f1. Try calling f2() at the top level: you get a NameError.
  • Nested functions are useful, especially to build closures (Section 5.14), which is how tools such as decorators work. But keep them simple: deep nesting is hard to read.

docs.title: 5.13.4 Can a nested function be called from outside?
docs.text:
Yes, if the outer function returns the inner function. This hands the inner function to the outside world.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 14: Returning the inner function
docs.text:
What it does: f1() returns its inner function f2, the result is stored in nested, and nested() then runs f2.

How it does it:

  1. nested = f1() calls f1(). Inside, f2 is defined but not called.
  2. return f2 hands back the function itself. Notice: no brackets. return f2() would call f2 and return its result (None) instead.
  3. f1() is now finished, but nested refers to the function f2.
  4. type(nested) confirms it: <class 'function'="">.
  5. nested() calls it, and "Hello from f2!" is printed.

Why: in Python, functions are objects, just like numbers and strings. They can be stored in variables, passed around, and returned from other functions.

Learning point: the text in triple quotes just below each def line is a docstring. It describes the function. Try help(f1) in a new cell.

docs.title: 5.14 Nested functions and closures (an advanced idea)
docs.text:
A nested function becomes a closure when all three of these are true:

  1. the inner function uses a variable from the outer function,
  2. the outer function returns the inner function, and
  3. the inner function still has access to that variable later, even after the outer function has finished.

Think of a closure as a function carrying a "backpack". The backpack holds the variables from the place where the function was created, even when that place no longer exists.

Nested function Closure A function inside a function Yes Yes The inner function uses a variable of the outer one Optional Required The outer function returns the inner function No Yes The outer variables are remembered after the outer function ends No Yes

Why do we need closures? Sometimes we want to hand back both some data and a function that works on that data, and keep the data alive after the outer function ends. Returning just the data, or just a plain function, cannot do this.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 15: A closure remembers a name
docs.text:
What it does: makes two greeting functions, one for Alice and one for Bob, and calls them. They print "Hello, Alice!" and "Hello, Bob!".

How it does it:

  1. outer_greeter("Alice") runs. Its parameter name is "Alice".
  2. It defines inner_greeter(), which uses name, and returns it.
  3. outer_greeter has now finished, but greet_alice keeps name = "Alice" in its backpack.
  4. outer_greeter("Bob") does the same, making a separate function that remembers "Bob".
  5. Calling greet_alice() and greet_bob() prints each stored name.

Learning point: each call to outer_greeter() creates a new inner function with its own saved value. The two do not share anything.

docs.title: 5.14.1 The nonlocal keyword and its use in closures
docs.text:
nonlocal is a Python keyword. It is written as one word, with no hyphen. You use it inside a nested function to tell Python:

  • "Do not treat this variable as a new local variable."
  • "Use the variable of the same name in the nearest outer function."

Normally, if you assign to a variable inside a function, Python assumes it is local. nonlocal changes that.

Feature nonlocal global Refers to a variable in the nearest enclosing (outer) function the global (top-level) scope Typical use closures and nested functions shared data for the whole module Can it be used outside a nested function? No Yes

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 5.14.2 Using closures to keep state without global variables
docs.text:
State is data that a program remembers over time, or across several function calls. For example, a counter must remember whether it has reached 1, 2 or 3.

You could keep the count in a global variable, but that is usually a bad idea:

  • Unsafe: any part of the program can change a global by accident.
  • Cluttered: many globals make the top level of the code messy.
  • Hard to debug: in a large script, it is hard to find where a global was changed.

A closure is better. It gives a function its own "private memory" that lasts between calls, and that the rest of the program cannot touch.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 16: A counter with private memory
docs.text:
What it does: makes two separate counters, counter_a and counter_b, and calls them. Each keeps its own count. It also peeks at the hidden value stored inside counter_a.

How it does it:

  1. make_counter() sets count = 0 and defines counter().
  2. Inside counter(), nonlocal count says: "use the count of make_counter, not a new local one". Then count += 1 adds 1 and the new value is returned.
  3. make_counter() returns counter. Each call to make_counter() creates a fresh count, so counter_a and counter_b have separate counts.
  4. counter_a.__closure__[0].cell_contents looks inside the "backpack" of counter_a and finds the stored count.
Call counter_a's count counter_b's count Printed counter_a() 1 0 Counter A: 1 counter_a() 2 0 Counter A: 2 peek inside counter_a 2 0 The hidden value in counter_a is: 2 counter_b() 2 1 Counter B: 1 counter_a() 3 1 Counter A: 3

Learning points:

  • Private memory: each call to make_counter() makes a new, private count. That is why the two counters do not interfere.
  • No global clutter: you can make as many independent counters as you like from one function definition.
  • The re-binding rule: count += 1 means count = count + 1. It assigns to count, so without nonlocal, Python would treat count as a new local variable and stop with an UnboundLocalError. Try deleting the nonlocal line.
  • When nonlocal is not needed: (1) if you only read the variable without changing it, as in Example 15; or (2) if the variable holds a mutable object, such as a list, and you change the object's contents rather than re-assigning the name. "Beyond the Book", Extra 3 shows case (2). Even then, many programmers prefer nonlocal, because it makes the intention clear.
  • __closure__ is a special attribute that every function has. You rarely need it; here it simply proves that the count really is stored inside the function.

docs.title: 5.15 Function composition
docs.text:
Function composition means joining functions so that the output of one becomes the input of the next.

  • The order of working: in f(g(x)), the inner function g(x) runs first.
  • Data flow: the result of g(x) is passed straight into the outer function f().
  • Final result: whatever the outermost function returns.

Why use composition?

Benefit Meaning Modularity A big task is split into small functions Reuse The same small functions can be combined in different ways Easier testing Each small function can be tested on its own Readability "One function, one job" makes the logic easy to follow

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 17: f(g(x)) is not the same as g(f(x))
docs.text:
What it does: defines f(x) (add 10) and g(x) (multiply by 2), and shows that changing the order changes the answer.

How it does it:

Expression First step Second step Result f(g(5)) g(5) = 5 * 2 = 10 f(10) = 10 + 10 = 20 20 g(f(5)) f(5) = 5 + 10 = 15 g(15) = 15 * 2 = 30 30

Learning point: the order of composition matters, just as in maths.

docs.title: 5.16 A quick summary
docs.text:
• A name (or "tag") in Python points to an object in memory. When an object is no longer needed, Python frees its memory automatically.
  • Names live in a namespace. Each namespace has a scope: the part of the program where its names can be seen.
  • A name gets its scope when it is first assigned, usually with =. Unlike C++, Python has no way to declare a name without giving it a value.
  • A name assigned inside a function has local scope. It stops existing when the function ends. The same name can be used again in a different scope without any clash.
  • In a local scope, the local name wins over a global one of the same name. Outside the function, only the global name exists.
  • Parameters and variables made inside a function cannot be seen from outside. They are local.
  • The lifetime of a local variable lasts only while its function is running. So an ordinary function does not remember its local values from one call to the next (a closure is the exception, as Example 16 showed).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Beyond the Book
docs.text:
Three short extras. They are optional.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Extra 1: Repeatable random numbers with seed()
docs.text:
Section 5.7 said that the same seed always gives the same "random" numbers. This cell proves it. Both lines print exactly the same three numbers, every time you run the cell, on every computer.

This is very useful for testing, and for sharing results that others can check.

docs.title: Extra 2: The global keyword
docs.text:
Example 11 showed that assigning to x inside a function creates a new local x. If you really want a function to change a global variable, you must say so with the global keyword.

  • add_visit() changes the global visits, because of global visits.
  • Remove the global visits line and run the cell again: you get an UnboundLocalError, for the same reason as in Example 16.

Use global sparingly. For keeping state, a closure (Example 16) is usually the cleaner choice.

docs.title: Extra 3: A closure counter without nonlocal
docs.text:
Section 5.14.2 said that nonlocal is not needed if you change the contents of a mutable object instead of re-assigning the name. Here count is a list holding one number.

count[0] += 1 changes the item inside the list. The name count still points to the same list, so Python does not treat it as a new local variable.

This works, but it is a trick. Many programmers prefer the nonlocal version, because it states the intention clearly.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Functions, Part 2
docs.text:
def process_data(z):
    """
    Shows how Python handles different object types during function call.
    """
    if isinstance(z, int):  # Check if z is an integer (immutable)
        print(f"--- Processing Integer (Immutable) ---")
        print(f"Initial internal z: {z} (ID: {id(z)})")

        # This does NOT change the original 'a'.
        # It creates a new local variable 'z' pointing to 4.
        z = 4
        print(f"Modified internal z: {z} (ID: {id(z)})")

    elif isinstance(z, list):  # Check if z is a list (mutable)
        print(f"\n--- Processing List (Mutable) ---")
        print(f"Initial internal z: {z} (ID: {id(z)})")

        # This modifies the object in-place.
        # Both 'c' and 'z' point to the same memory ID.
        z.append(1)
        print(f"Modified internal z: {z} (ID: {id(z)})")

# --- Main Execution ---

# 1. Testing with an Integer
a = 5
print(f"Original 'a' before call: {a} (ID: {id(a)})")
process_data(a)
print(f"Original 'a' after call: {a} (Still 5!)")  # Out (5)

# 2. Testing with a List
c = [5, 4, 3]
print(f"\nOriginal 'c' before call: {c} (ID: {id(c)})")
process_data(c)
print(f"Original 'c' after call {c} (Updated to include 1!)")  #Out([5, 4, 3, 1])

Original 'a' before call: 5 (ID: 22522344)
--- Processing Integer (Immutable) ---
Initial internal z: 5 (ID: 22522344)
Modified internal z: 4 (ID: 22522312)
Original 'a' after call: 5 (Still 5!)

Original 'c' before call: [5, 4, 3] (ID: 140214289389056)

--- Processing List (Mutable) ---
Initial internal z: [5, 4, 3] (ID: 140214289389056)
Modified internal z: [5, 4, 3, 1] (ID: 140214289389056)
Original 'c' after call [5, 4, 3, 1] (Updated to include 1!)

Back to the Table of Contents

def reassign_list(z):
    z = [1, 2, 3] # This creates a NEW list. It does NOT change the original.

my_list = [9, 9, 9]
reassign_list(my_list)
print(my_list) # Output is still [9, 9, 9]

[9, 9, 9]

Back to the Table of Contents

# Example to illustrate parameters and arguments
def greet(name, message):  # Parameters: name and message
    print(message, name)
# Calling the function with arguments "Alice" & "Hi"
greet("Alice", "Hi") # Arguments "Alice" & "Hi" passed to parameters name & message

Hi Alice

Back to the Table of Contents

# Example demonstrating DEFAULT ARGUMENTS in Python

# Function definition with default arguments
def greet(name="Student", greeting="Hello"):
    # Print the greeting message
    print(greeting, name)

# Testing the function with different combinations of arguments

# 1. Both arguments supplied. Parameter 'name' takes supplied value "Alice"
# and parameter 'greeting' takes supplied value "Good morning".
# Default values are NOT used
greet("Alice", "Good morning")
# Output: Good morning Alice

# 2. Only the first argument supplied. Parameter 'name' takes supplied value "Bob".
# Parameter 'greeting' takes the default value "Hello" since it is not supplied.
greet("Bob") # Output: Hello Bob

# 3. No arguments supplied. Parameter 'name' takes default value "Student"
# Parameter 'greeting' takes default value "Hello". Both default values are used.
greet() # Output: Hello Student

Good morning Alice
Hello Bob
Hello Student

Rules for default parameters:

No. Rule 1 Parameters with defaults must come after all parameters without defaults 2 Once one parameter has a default, every parameter to its right must also have one 3 The default value is worked out once, when the def line runs, not at each call 4 So use immutable values (numbers, strings, None, tuples) as defaults. Avoid lists, dictionaries and sets (see Example 6)

Back to the Table of Contents

# Example 1 : Correct usage of default parameters

def calculate_price(price=100, tax_rate=0.10, discount=0):
    # All parameters have default values. This is perfectly valid.
    pass

def calculate_area(length, width, unit="cm"):
    # Only the last parameter has a default value. This is also valid.
    pass

def create_user(username, role="user", active=True):
    # Default values appear only on right side. Follows Python's rule correctly.
    pass

# Example 2 : Incorrect usage of default parameters. Following definitions
# are INVALID. Would raise a SyntaxError if uncommented.

# 'a' has a default value, but 'b' and 'c' do not. This violates Python's rule.
# def wrong_example1(a=1, b, c):  #
#     pass

# Function that raises numbers to a given power and sums them
# The first parameter (power) is the power to which numbers will be raised.
# The rest of the parameters (*values) are the numbers to be processed.
# We use *values to accept any number of numbers.
def sum_of_powers(power, *values):

    total = 0
    my_str = ""
    # Each number is raised to the specified power
    for value in values:
        total = total + (value ** power)
        # my_str is built up to show the expression being calculated. For example
        # if power=2 and values=(1,2,3), my_str is "1**2 + 2**2 + 3**2 + "
        my_str = my_str + str(value) + " ** " + str(power) + " + "

    my_str = my_str.rstrip(" + ")  # Remove the trailing " + " from the expression string
    return f"Power = {power}, Numbers = {values}, Expression → {my_str} = {total}"

# Factorial using Recursion. n! = n × (n-1) × (n-2) × ... × 2 × 1

def factorial_recursive(n):

    # ---------- BASE CASE ----------
    # When n is 0 or 1, the factorial is 1
    # This stops further recursive calls.
    if n == 0 or n == 1:
        print(f"Base case reached: factorial({n}) = 1")
        return 1

    # ---------- RECURSIVE CASE ----------
    # The function calls itself with a smaller value (n-1)
    print(f"Computing: {n} × factorial({n-1})")
    result = n * factorial_recursive(n - 1)  # Recursive call.

    # Show the value being returned after recursion unwinds
    print(f"Returning: {n}! = {result}")
    return result  # Return the computed factorial value to the caller

# Recursive function to compute the nth Fibonacci number

def fibonacci_recursive(n):
    # Returns the nth Fibonacci number using recursion.
    # There are 2 base cases: Fibonacci(0) = 0 and Fibonacci(1) = 1

    # -------- Base Case 1 --------
    # If n = 0, return
    if n == 0:
        return 0

    # -------- Base Case 2 --------
    # If n = 1, return 1
    elif n == 1:
        return 1

    # -------- Recursive Case --------
    # Compute the sum of the previous two Fibonacci numbers
    return fibonacci_recursive(n - 1) + fibonacci_recursive(n - 2)

# Tower of Hanoi using three lists representing towers A, B, C. Each list acts
# like a stack. In the list leftmost item is at bottom (Biggest) and rightmost
# is at top (Smallest). The script also counts and displays move numbers.

def print_towers(towers):
    """Display the current state of all three towers."""
    print(f"A: {towers['A']}   B: {towers['B']}   C: {towers['C']}")
    print("-" * 40)

def move_disk(towers, source, target, move_counter):
    # Move top disk from one tower to another also increment the move counter

    disk = towers[source].pop()     # Remove top disk from source
    towers[target].append(disk)     # Place disk on target

    move_counter[0] += 1            # Increment move count

    print(f"Move {move_counter[0]}: disk from {source} → {target}")
    print_towers(towers)

def hanoi_recursive(n, source, target, auxiliary, towers, move_counter):
    """
    Recursive solution to Tower of Hanoi.

    n         -> number of disks
    source    -> source tower (A/B/C)
    target    -> target tower (A/B/C)
    auxiliary -> auxiliary tower (A/B/C)
    towers    -> dictionary storing the towers
    move_counter -> list used to track number of moves
    """

    # -------- Base Case --------
    if n == 1:
        move_disk(towers, source, target, move_counter)
        return

    # -------- Recursive Case --------

    # Step 1: Move n-1 disks from source → auxiliary
    hanoi_recursive(n - 1, source, auxiliary, target, towers, move_counter)

    # Step 2: Move largest disk from source → target
    move_disk(towers, source, target, move_counter)

    # Step 3: Move n-1 disks from auxiliary → target
    hanoi_recursive(n - 1, auxiliary, target, source, towers, move_counter)

# Fibonacci using Memoization (Optimized Recursion)

memo = {0: 0, 1: 1}
# memo is a dictionary that will store previously computed Fibonacci values.
# It starts with the base cases: F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. As the recursive
# function computes new Fibonacci numbers, it will add them to this dictionary,
# allowing for fast retrieval in future calls.

def fib_memo(n):
    # Returns the nth Fibonacci number using memoization to optimize recursion.
    # It checks if value is already computed & stored in the memo dictionary.
    # If it is, it returns that value immediately. If not, it computes it
    # recursively, stores the result in the memo, and then returns it.

    # -------- Step 1: Check if value already exists in cache --------
    # If yes, return it immediately (very fast)
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]

    # -------- Step 2: Otherwise compute recursively --------
    # Break the problem into two smaller Fibonacci problems
    fib_n_minus_1 = fib_memo(n - 1)
    fib_n_minus_2 = fib_memo(n - 2)

    result = fib_n_minus_1 + fib_n_minus_2

    # -------- Step 3: Store the result in the cache --------
    memo[n] = result

    # -------- Step 4: Return the computed value --------
    return result

# This shows all Fibonacci values that were stored during execution
print("Memoization Cache Contents:", memo)

def food_checker(func):
    """
    A decorator that inspects function arguments (*args, **kwargs).
    """
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        # 1. Identify the food.
        # Since we are passing 'name' by position, args[0] is the name.
        # Since we are passing 'food' by keyword, it is in kwargs["food"].
        # Safely get 'food' from kwargs, default to "Unknown food" if not given
        # This prevents an error even if "food" is not provided.
        food = kwargs.get("food", "Unknown food")

        # 2. Perform the 'Check' logic
        unhealthy_foods = ["Chocolate", "Cakes", "Onions"]

        if food in unhealthy_foods:
            print(f"[WARNING] {food} is BAD for pets!")
        else:
            print(f"[INFO] {food} is safe. Proceeding...")

        # 3. Execute the original function
        return func(*args, **kwargs)

    return wrapper

@food_checker
def feed_pet(name, food="Bread"):
    print(f"Feeding {name} some {food}.")

# --- TEST CASES ---
# 'Tiger' goes to *args | food='Chicken' goes to **kwargs
feed_pet("Tiger", food="Chicken")  # Good food

# 'Kitty' goes to *args | food='Chocolate' goes to **kwargs
feed_pet("Kitty", food="Chocolate")  # Bad food

import sys

def fact_recursive(n):

    return result

docs.title: 6.1 Passing of variables in a function call
docs.text:
When you call a function and give it a variable, what does the function actually receive? Programming languages usually offer one of two answers:

Method What the function gets Can the function change the caller's variable? Call by value A copy of the value No. It only changes its own copy Call by reference A link to the same variable Yes. Changes show up outside the function too

Python does neither exactly. It uses pass by object reference (also called "call by sharing"): the parameter becomes a new name for the same object that the caller passed. What happens next depends on whether that object can be changed:

  • Immutable objects (int, float, str, tuple) cannot be changed in place. If the function "changes" one, Python makes a new object and moves only the local name. The caller sees no change. This looks like call by value.
  • Mutable objects (list, dict, set) can be changed in place. If the function changes the object, the caller sees the change, because both names point to the same object. This looks like call by reference.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: An integer and a list passed to the same function
docs.text:
What it does: passes an integer a = 5 and then a list c = [5, 4, 3] to process_data(). The function tries to change each one. The integer outside stays 5; the list outside becomes [5, 4, 3, 1].

How it does it:

  1. isinstance(z, int) checks whether z is an integer. isinstance(z, list) checks for a list. (isinstance(object, type) returns True or False.)
  2. Integer case: at the start of the call, z and a have the same id, so they point to the same object 5. Then z = 4 makes a new object 4 and moves z to it. The id of z changes. a is not touched.
  3. List case: z and c have the same id. z.append(1) changes that one list in place. The id stays the same, and c sees the new item.

Why: this is one of the most important ideas in Python. It explains why a function can change your list but not your number.

Learning points:

  • Compare the ids in the output. In the integer case the id changes after z = 4. In the list case the id never changes.
  • The ids in the saved output will not match yours. What matters is which ids are equal.

docs.title: 6.2 Understanding a function call in Python
docs.text:
• Each time a function is called, Python creates a new local scope for it (also called its execution context, or frame). It holds the parameters and local variables of that one call.
  • The local scope is thrown away as soon as the function finishes.
  • Think of it as a box inside a box: the caller is the outer box, and the running function is the inner box.
  • The function can read names from the outer scope. It can also change a mutable object that it was given.
  • But if it assigns to a parameter name (z = ...), it only moves its own local label. The caller's name is not affected.

A note on tuples: a tuple is passed in exactly the same way as everything else, as a reference to the same object. It "acts like" call by value only because a tuple cannot be changed. There is no special rule for tuples.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 6.3 Pass by value compared with pass by reference: C++ and Python
docs.text:
• In C++, a variable is like a box in memory with a fixed type. You declare the type in advance, and the box can only hold that type.
  • When calling a function in C++, you choose: pass a copy (call by value) or pass a reference to the original (call by reference, using &).
  • In Python, a variable is a name tag tied to an object. The tag has no type; the object does. (Python is dynamically typed. It is also strongly typed: it will not quietly mix types, as Chapter 1 showed.)
  • Python has only one way to pass arguments: it always passes a reference to the object. There is no copying.

Why does the original 5 not change, then? Because an integer object cannot be changed in place. When a function runs z = 4, Python does not overwrite the object 5. It finds or makes an object 4 and moves the local name z to it. The caller's name still points to 5.

Why pass a reference even for a small integer? Two reasons: (1) uniformity: everything is an object, so Python uses the same rule for all of them; and (2) efficiency: passing a reference to a 100 MB string is instant, but copying it would be slow.

Interning: Python also reuses small integers and short strings, so many names may point to the very same 5 object (see Chapter 3).

Feature C++ Python How arguments are passed You choose: copy or reference Always a reference to the object Immutable object (int, str) Usually copied Reference passed; "changing" it makes a new object and moves the local name Mutable object (list, dict) Reference used explicitly (&) Reference passed; the object can be changed in place

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 6.4 The "reassignment" trap
docs.text:
With a mutable object such as a list, there is one trap to watch for. Changing the list (z.append(...), z[0] = ...) affects the original. But reassigning the parameter with = just points the local name at a different object. The link to the original is broken, and the original is not changed.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: Reassigning a list parameter
docs.text:
What it does: passes my_list = [9, 9, 9] to a function that sets z = [1, 2, 3]. Afterwards my_list is still [9, 9, 9].

How it does it:

  1. At the start of the call, z and my_list point to the same list.
  2. z = [1, 2, 3] creates a new list and moves z to it.
  3. The function ends and the new list is thrown away. my_list was never touched.

Learning point: to change the caller's list from inside a function, change its contents (for example z[:] = [1, 2, 3] replaces all the items in place), or return the new list and let the caller assign it.

docs.title: 6.5 Parameters (function definition) compared with arguments (function call)
docs.text:
Every function has two sides: the definition, which creates it (its first line is the function header), and the call, which uses it.

Term Where it appears Meaning Picture Parameter In the function definition A placeholder name used inside the function An empty, labelled box Argument In the function call The actual value passed to the function The item you put in the box

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: Two parameters, two arguments
docs.text:
What it does: defines greet(name, message) and calls it with "Alice" and "Hi". It prints Hi Alice.

How: the arguments are matched to the parameters in order: "Alice" goes to name and "Hi" goes to message. The function prints message first, so the output is Hi Alice.

Learning point: swap the arguments (greet("Hi", "Alice")) and see what happens. Order matters for positional arguments (Section 6.9).

docs.title: 6.6 Function arguments: the basics
docs.text:
There are three main ways to hand data to a function:

No. Kind How the value reaches the parameter 1 Default arguments A preset value is used when the call gives none 2 Positional arguments Matched by order 3 Keyword arguments Matched by name

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 6.7 Default arguments (default values in the function definition)
docs.text:
Sometimes a parameter has almost the same value every time, and only now and then does the caller want something different. For this, you can give the parameter a default value in the function definition.

  • If the call gives a value for that parameter, that value is used.
  • If the call leaves it out, the default is used.
  • Default values are written in the definition, never in the call.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: A function with two default values
docs.text:
What it does: defines greet(name="Student", greeting="Hello") and calls it three ways.

Call name greeting Output greet("Alice", "Good morning") "Alice" (given) "Good morning" (given) Good morning Alice greet("Bob") "Bob" (given) "Hello" (default) Hello Bob greet() "Student" (default) "Hello" (default) Hello Student

Learning point: arguments are still matched from the left. With only one argument, it goes to name, not greeting. To give only a greeting, use a keyword: greet(greeting="Hi").

docs.title: Example 5: Correct and incorrect placement of default values
docs.text:
What it does: defines three valid functions, and shows two invalid ones as comments. There is no output. The functions only use pass because the point is the header line, not the body.

How:

Header Valid? Why calculate_price(price=100, tax_rate=0.10, discount=0) Yes Every parameter has a default calculate_area(length, width, unit="cm") Yes Only the last one has a default create_user(username, role="user", active=True) Yes Defaults are all on the right wrong_example1(a=1, b, c) No b and c have no default but come after a, which does wrong_example2(a, b=2, c) No c has no default but comes after b, which does

Why the rule? Python fills parameters from the left. If a parameter without a default came after one with a default, Python could not tell which value was meant for which parameter when some arguments are left out.

Learning point: remove the # signs in front of def wrong_example1(a=1, b, c): and its pass line, then run the cell. You get a SyntaxError (in Python 3.12 it reads "parameter without a default follows parameter with a default"). Put the # signs back afterwards.

docs.title: Problem with mutable default values
docs.text:
A default value is worked out only once, when Python runs the def line. The resulting object is stored inside the function and reused by every call that leaves that argument out.

  • For an immutable default (a number, a string, None), this is harmless: nothing can change it.
  • For a mutable default (a list, a dictionary, a set), it is a trap: if one call changes the object, the change is still there in the next call.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: The problem with a mutable default argument
docs.text:
What it does: calls add_number_to_list(2) and then add_number_to_list(3). You might expect [2] and then [3], but the second call gives [2, 3].

How it happens:

  1. When the def line runs, Python creates one empty list and stores it as the default for number_list.
  2. The first call appends 2 to that list: [2].
  3. The second call does not get a fresh list. It gets the same one, which already holds 2. Appending 3 gives [2, 3].

Learning point: the comment on the last line says "Should be 3". It means the result you would expect is [3], a list holding only 3.

docs.title: Example 7: The correct way: use None as the default
docs.text:
What it does: the same function, fixed. Now the two calls give [2] and [3].

How it does it:

  1. The default is None, which is immutable and safe.
  2. Inside the function, if number_list is None: checks whether the caller gave a list. If not, a new empty list is made for this call only.
  3. The number is appended and the list is returned.

Rule to remember: never use a mutable object as a default value. Use None, and create the object inside the function.

docs.title: 6.8 Passing arguments from the function call to the function definition
docs.text:
When a function is called, each argument must be matched to a parameter. Python matches them in two main ways:

  1. Positional arguments: matched by position.
  2. Keyword arguments: matched by name.

The full order in which Python fills the parameters is:

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 6.9 Passing arguments by position (positional arguments)
docs.text:
With positional arguments, the first argument goes to the first parameter, the second to the second, and so on.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: Positional arguments
docs.text:
What it does: shows three rules of positional arguments, using rivers, lakes and seas.

Rule What the code shows 1. Order matters ("Ganga", "Dal Lake", "Arabian Sea") gives the right result. ("Arabian Sea", "Ganga", "Dal Lake") still runs, but "Arabian Sea" becomes the river. Python cannot know the meaning is wrong 2. The number of arguments must match Too few arguments gives TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument. Too many gives TypeError: ... takes 3 positional arguments but 4 were given. Both are commented out 3. Defaults fill the gaps display_water_info("Ganga") uses the defaults for lake and sea. Giving more arguments replaces the defaults from the left

Learning points:

  • With positional arguments, mixing up the order is a logic error, not an error Python can catch.
  • The comments show commas between the items (River: Ganga, Lake : ...), but print() puts only spaces between its arguments. So the real output has no commas. Trust the output.
  • In one commented-out line there is a stray full stop after the closing bracket: display_water_sources("Nile", "Victoria").. If you uncomment it to see the TypeError, remove that full stop first, or you will get a SyntaxError instead.

docs.title: 6.10 Passing arguments by name (keyword arguments)
docs.text:
Positional arguments have a drawback: you must remember the order, and you cannot skip a parameter in the middle. (Some languages, such as Visual Basic, allow a call like f(a, , b, c), where the empty slot means "skip this one". Python does not.)

Python solves this with keyword arguments: in the call you write parameter_name=value, so Python knows exactly which parameter each value is for.

Keyword arguments let you:

  1. give the arguments in any order,
  2. make the call easier to read, and
  3. skip parameters in the middle, if they have default values.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 9: Keyword arguments: what is allowed and what is not
docs.text:
What it does: calls student_info(name, age, course) in several ways, correct and incorrect. The incorrect calls are commented out.

Rule Correct Incorrect (commented out) Error 1. Order does not matter student_info(age=20, course="Physics", name="Ravi") (none) 2. Names must match exactly name=..., age=..., course=... subject="Biology" TypeError: ... unexpected keyword argument 'subject' 3. A keyword cannot be repeated (one name=) name="Ravi", age=20, name="Amit" SyntaxError: keyword argument repeated 4. Positional arguments come first student_info("Kiran", age=23, course="Economics") student_info(name="Ravi", 20, "Physics") SyntaxError: positional argument follows keyword argument

Learning points:

  • A SyntaxError is found before the cell runs, so even one such line stops the whole cell. That is why the bad lines are commented out.
  • In Python 3.12 the message for rule 3 reads "keyword argument repeated: name". The wording changes a little between versions.

docs.title: 6.11 Mixing positional and keyword arguments
docs.text:
Python allows both styles in the same call, with one rule: all positional arguments must come before any keyword arguments.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: Three valid ways to call the same function
docs.text:
What it does: calls student_info() with all positional arguments, all keyword arguments, and a mix.

Style Valid only if All positional The number of arguments matches the parameters (unless some have defaults), and the order is right: 1st to name, 2nd to age, 3rd to course All keyword Every keyword matches a parameter name exactly, none is repeated, and none is for a parameter that does not exist. The order does not matter Mixed The positional arguments come first. Once you use a keyword argument, everything after it must also be a keyword argument

Learning points:

  • Positional arguments fill parameters from the left. Keyword arguments then fill the rest by name.
  • You can skip a parameter only if the definition gives it a default value.
  • A parameter cannot get two values. student_info("Ravi", name="Amit", ...) gives TypeError: ... got multiple values for argument 'name'.

docs.title: 6.12 Variable number of arguments (*args)
docs.text:
Sometimes you want a function that accepts any number of arguments. Python offers a special form for this:

def f(*args):
  • The * tells Python: collect all the extra positional arguments into one tuple, and give that tuple the name after the star.
  • args is only a habit. Any valid name works: *numbers, *values, *items.
  • Inside the function, args is an ordinary tuple. It is empty if no extra arguments were passed.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 11: Adding any number of values
docs.text:
What it does: calls add_numbers() with two, four, one and zero arguments, and prints the tuple it received and the total.

How it does it:

  1. *values collects all the arguments into a tuple, for example (2, 3).
  2. The for loop adds each item to total.
  3. The function returns an f-string showing the tuple and the total.
Call values total add_numbers(2, 3) (2, 3) 5 add_numbers(1, 2, 3, 4) (1, 2, 3, 4) 10 add_numbers(10) (10,) 10 add_numbers() () 0

Learning points:

  • A one-item tuple is printed as (10,), with a comma (see Chapter 2).
  • Python's own print() works this way: print(*objects, ...) accepts any number of values.

docs.title: 6.13 Combining fixed and variable arguments
docs.text:
You can put ordinary parameters before *args. The first arguments fill the ordinary parameters, and all the rest go into the tuple.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 12: Raise numbers to a power and add them
docs.text:
What it does: sum_of_powers(2, 1, 2, 3) works out 1² + 2² + 3² = 14, and shows the expression it calculated.

How it does it:

  1. The first argument goes to power. All the others go into the tuple values.
  2. The loop raises each value to power and adds it to total.
  3. At the same time it builds the text my_str, such as "1 ** 2 + 2 ** 2 + 3 ** 2 + ".
  4. my_str.rstrip(" + ") removes the trailing " + ".
  5. The f-string puts everything together.
Call power values Worked out Result sum_of_powers(2, 1, 2, 3) 2 (1, 2, 3) 1 + 4 + 9 14 sum_of_powers(3, 2, 3) 3 (2, 3) 8 + 27 35

Learning points:

  • Parameters before *values are required. sum_of_powers() with no arguments gives a TypeError.
  • rstrip(" + ") removes any of the characters space and + from the right end, one at a time, until it meets a different character. That is why it neatly removes " + ".
  • The comments write 1**2 without spaces, but the code puts spaces around **, so the real output shows 1 ** 2.

docs.title: 6.14 Summary of the different ways arguments can be passed
docs.text:
Table 1: how a function receives arguments (the definition side)

Parameter type Syntax in the definition Stored as Unlimited arguments? Example Positional parameters def f(a, b) separate variables No def add(a, b) Default parameters def f(a, b=10) separate variables No def area(length, width=1) Variable positional (*args) def f(*args) a tuple Yes def add(*values) Variable keyword (**kwargs) def f(**kwargs) a dictionary Yes def configure(**settings) Mixed def f(a, b, *args) variables and a tuple Partly def power_sum(n, *values)

Argument type Example call Matched by Order matters? Can skip parameters? Typical use Positional f(1, 2, 3) position Yes No Simple calls Keyword f(a=1, b=2) name No Yes, if they have defaults Clearer calls Leaving out defaulted arguments f(5) defaults fill the gaps Yes (for the positional part) Yes Optional settings Many positional values f(1, 2, 3, 4) packed into *args Yes Not applicable Passing many values Many keyword values f(x=1, y=2, z=3) packed into **kwargs No Yes Configuration-style inputs
