docs.title: 8.1 Introduction
docs.text:
So far we have written classes that stand alone. Python also lets you build a new class from an existing class. This is called inheritance. It is one of the main ideas of object-oriented programming, and most of this chapter is about it.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.2 What is inheritance?
docs.text:
• Inheritance means creating a new class from an existing class.
  • The new class reuses what the existing class already has, and can extend it with new things.
  • Think of a family tree. You may get your eye colour or your surname from your parents. In the same way, a child class (also called a subclass or derived class) gets attributes and methods from a parent class (also called a superclass or base class).
  • Goal: reuse code. You write the logic once in the parent and every child can use it.
  • The root of all classes: every class you write inherits from a built-in class called object, even if you do not say so.
  • The pass keyword: if the child should be exactly like the parent, with nothing new, the body of the child class is just pass.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Key characteristics of inheritance
docs.text:
Property What it means Code reusability You do not rewrite the same code for similar objects. Transitivity If B inherits from A, and C inherits from B, then C also has what A has. Overriding A child can change how a parent method works. For example, a dog speaks differently from a general animal. Method resolution Python looks for a method in the child first. If it is not there, it looks in the parent.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text:
The same two ideas have several names. You will meet all of them in books and on the web.

Term Meaning Parent class, superclass, base class The class that is inherited from Child class, subclass, derived class The class that inherits

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text:
Function What it returns Example type(obj) The exact class the object was made from type(c1) gives <class '__main__.child'=""> isinstance(obj, cls) True if obj was made from cls or from any subclass of cls isinstance(c1, Parent) gives True

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: type() and isinstance() with a parent and a child class
docs.text:
What the code does. It creates a class Parent and a class Child that inherits from it. Both classes are empty (pass). It makes one object of each: p1 from Parent and c1 from Child. Then it asks two kinds of questions: "What is the exact class of this object?" (type()), and "Does this object count as an instance of this class?" (isinstance()).

How it works. class Child(Parent): is the line that creates the inheritance. type() always gives the one class the object was made from. isinstance() is more generous. It also says True when the object's class is a child of the class you ask about.

Why it matters. A child object can be used anywhere a parent object is expected. isinstance() is the normal way to test this. It is better than comparing type(x) == SomeClass, because it also accepts subclasses.

Learning points

  1. c1 is a Child, and because Child inherits from Parent, c1 is also a Parent.
  2. The link is one way only. p1 is a Parent but not a Child. A parent does not know about its children.
  3. type() answers "exactly which class?". isinstance() answers "is it this kind of thing?".

The flowchart shows how isinstance() reaches its answer.

docs.title: 8.3 MRO (Method Resolution Order)
docs.text:
The MRO is the order in which Python searches classes for a method or an attribute.

When you call obj.method(), Python asks, in this order:

  1. Is the method in the object's own class?
  2. If not, is it in the parent class?
  3. If not, is it in the parent's parent, and so on?
  4. If it is found nowhere, Python raises an AttributeError.

Every class has an attribute __mro__. It is a tuple that lists the classes in the exact order Python will search them.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: Showing the MRO of object, Animal and Dog
docs.text:
What the code does. It prints the MRO of three classes: the built-in object, a class Animal (which inherits from object without saying so), and a class Dog that inherits from Animal.

How it works. ClassName.__mro__ is read like any other attribute. Python builds it when the class is created.

Why it matters. When a program calls the "wrong" method, the MRO tells you why. It is the map Python follows.

Learning points

  1. The MRO of object holds only object itself. It has no parent.
  2. Animal does not name a parent, but its MRO still ends with object.
  3. The MRO of Dog is Dog, then Animal, then object.
  4. The MRO is:
    • linear: it is one single list,
    • top-down: the child comes first, then the parents,
    • deterministic: it is always the same order,
    • ends at object: the last class is always object.

docs.title: 8.4 Role of the object class
docs.text:
object is the top-most class in Python. Every class inherits from it. You do not import it or create it, because it is built in. It gives every object a basic set of methods, so that any object can be (1) created, (2) initialised, (3) printed, and (4) compared.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Core methods inherited from object
docs.text:
Method Purpose When it is called What the default version does Returns __new__ Creates the object Before the object exists Allocates memory and returns a new instance the new object __init__ Initialises the object Just after the object is created Nothing None (it must not return anything else) __str__ Friendly text for users print(obj) or str(obj) <classname address="" at="" object=""> str __repr__ Exact text for developers repr(obj), or when the interpreter shows the object Same as the default __str__ str __eq__ Equality test obj1 == obj2 Compares identity, like is bool __hash__ Hash value When the object is a set member or a dictionary key Based on the object's identity int

Points to remember:

  • If __new__ does not return an instance of the class, __init__ is not called.
  • If you write your own __eq__, think about writing __hash__ too. Two objects that are equal must have the same hash.
  • If you write only __repr__, print() uses it as well, because the default __str__ falls back to __repr__.

The online resource has a problem on designing an animal management system that uses these ideas.

docs.title: 8.6 Inheritance as an "IS-A" relationship
docs.text:
Inheritance models an IS-A relationship. A subclass is a special kind of its superclass. It gets all the data and behaviour of the parent, and then it may keep them, add to them, or change them.

In simple words: if a Dog is a Pet, then anywhere your code expects a Pet, a Dog can be used and will work.

A quick test: say the sentence "A ___ is a ___." If it sounds right ("A Dog is a Pet"), inheritance fits. If it sounds wrong ("A Dog is a Collar"), it does not.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.7 What is super()?
docs.text:
super() is used inside a child class to call a method of the parent class.

In simple words, it means: "go to my parent and use its method."

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Why we need super()
docs.text:
If a child class writes its own __init__(), the parent's __init__() is not called automatically. Python does not do it for you (unlike Java or C++). So if you do not write super().__init__(...), the attributes that the parent's __init__() would have set will simply not exist in the child object.

With super() you can:

  1. reuse what the parent already does,
  2. avoid writing the same code twice, and
  3. keep the design clean. Each class looks after its own part.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
super().method_name(arguments)

Note that you do not pass self. super() already knows which object it is working for.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: What happens inside
docs.text:
When you call super().method(), Python:

  1. looks at the MRO of the object's class,
  2. finds the class that comes after the current class in that MRO, and
  3. calls method() from there.

So super() does not strictly mean "call my immediate parent". It means "call the next method in the MRO". In single inheritance these are the same thing. In multiple inheritance they can be different.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: super() in constructors and methods, over three levels
docs.text:
What the code does. It builds a chain of three classes: Pet, then Dog(Pet), then Puppy(Dog). Each class has its own __init__() and its own walk(). Each one prints a message and then calls the same method in the class above it with super(). Finally it prints the MRO of Puppy.

How it works.

  • Puppy.__init__ prints its message and calls super().__init__(name). That runs Dog.__init__.
  • Dog.__init__ prints its message and calls super().__init__(name). That runs Pet.__init__, which stores self.name.
  • walk() works the same way. Each class prints its own line and then passes the call up.

This passing of the call up the chain is called constructor chaining (for __init__) or method chaining (for other methods).

Why it matters. Each class only deals with its own part. Pet is the only class that sets name. If Pet changes, Dog and Puppy still work and get the change for free.

Learning points

  1. Look at the order of the messages. In Dog.__init__ and Puppy.__init__ the print() comes before super().__init__(), so the child's message appears first. If you swap the two lines, the parent's message appears first.
  2. self.name is set only in Pet, yet Dog.walk() and Puppy.walk() can use it. It is stored on the same object.
  3. The MRO of Puppy is Puppy, Dog, Pet, object. super() follows this list.

docs.title: Notes on Example 3
docs.text:
• Try it: remove the line super().__init__(name) from Dog, then run Dog("Tommy").walk(). You get an AttributeError, because self.name was never set. This is exactly the problem that super() solves.
  • super() without arguments works only inside a method of a class. Python fills in the class and the object for you.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.8 The four types of "IS-A"
docs.text:
A child class can relate to its parent in four ways.

No. Type What the child does How it thinks 1 Implicit (pass-through) It is an exact copy of the parent. The body is just pass. "I want exactly what the parent has, under a different name." 2 Extended (additive) It keeps everything and adds new methods or attributes. This is the most common type. "I am a version of the parent, with some extra tools." 3 Specific (replacement) It overrides a parent method with completely different logic. "I am a type of parent, but I do this task in my own way." 4 Cooperative (refinement) It overrides a method but also calls the parent version with super(), then adds its own work. "I add my own touch, but I still want the parent to do its normal job."

Where each type is used:

  • Pass-through is useful for giving a clear name to a role, even when the data is the same. For example, class Admin(User): pass lets your code tell admins apart from other users.
  • Replacement is used when the parent only has a default or dummy behaviour that is wrong for the child.
  • Cooperative is the most robust. If the parent's logic changes later (say, a bug fix), the child gets the change automatically.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: How the four types use the parent
docs.text:
Type Uses super()? Parent methods Child's role Pass-through No Used as they are None, just pass Extension No, or optional Used as they are Adds new methods or attributes Replacement No Hidden by the child's version Replaces the parent logic completely Cooperation Yes Called and extended Adds logic on top of the parent logic

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: The four types of IS-A inheritance
docs.text:
What the code does. It creates a base class Pet with __init__(), speak() and eat(), and then one child class for each type:

Class Type What it changes BasicPet Pass-through Nothing Retriever Additive Adds fetch() Cat Replacement Its own speak() prints "Meow!" instead of the generic sound Dog Cooperative Its own __init__() adds weight; its own speak() growls, calls Pet.speak(), then barks

It then makes one object of each and calls a method on it.

How it works. When p1.speak() runs, Python finds no speak() in BasicPet, so it uses the one in Pet. p3.speak() finds speak() in Cat first, so the Pet version is never reached. p4.speak() finds speak() in Dog, and that method calls super().speak() in the middle.

Why it matters. Most real class designs use these four patterns. Knowing their names helps you choose the right one and explain your design to others.

Learning points

  1. BasicPet("Rocky") works even though BasicPet has no __init__(). The one in Pet is used.
  2. Retriever still has speak() and eat() from Pet, as well as its new fetch().
  3. Cat never prints the generic sound. The parent method is hidden, not deleted: Pet.speak(p3) would still work.
  4. Dog needs super().__init__(name). Without it, self.name would not exist and speak() would fail.

docs.title: Notes on Example 4
docs.text:
• Try it: call p2.speak() and p3.eat(). Both work, because these methods are inherited without change.
  • A small point about the comments in the code: the comment for Retriever says it also has a breed, but the class only adds fetch(). The comment for Cat says it only purrs, but it prints "Meow!". The code itself is correct; only the comments are loose.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: What happens to __init__() when a derived object is made
docs.text:
There are three possibilities:

  1. The derived class has no __init__() of its own. The parent's __init__() is used automatically.
  2. The derived class has its own __init__(), but it does not call super().__init__(). Only the child's __init__() runs. It completely replaces the parent's, so the parent's attributes are never set.
  3. The derived class has its own __init__() and it calls super().__init__(). The object is set up partly by the child's __init__() and partly by the parent's.

In Example 4, BasicPet, Retriever and Cat are case 1, and Dog is case 3.

The online resource has a problem that brings together all the major properties of inheritance: IS-A, code reuse, MRO, overriding, polymorphism, super(), constructor behaviour, dynamic binding, encapsulation, extensibility and maintainability.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.9 Multiple inheritance
docs.text:
Multiple inheritance means a class inherits from more than one base class. The parent classes are listed inside the brackets, separated by commas.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 5: The syntax of multiple inheritance
docs.text:
What the code does. The book shows the line class DerivedClass(Base1, Base2, Base3):. On its own, that line cannot run, because Base1, Base2 and Base3 do not exist yet. So this cell first creates three tiny base classes, then uses the book's line, and finally prints the MRO.

Learning points

  1. The order of the parents in the brackets is the order Python searches them: Base1 first, then Base2, then Base3.
  2. DerivedClass gets hello() from Base1, bye() from Base2 and wave() from Base3.

docs.title: The problem with multiple inheritance, and the C3 rule
docs.text:
What if the same method exists in more than one parent? Python must pick one. It uses the MRO to decide.

Python 3 builds the MRO with an algorithm called C3 linearization. Old-style classes in Python 2 used a simple "depth-first, left-to-right" search. That simple search goes wrong for the diamond problem, where two parents share the same grandparent:

A pure depth-first search from Dog1 would visit Walker, then Pet (the grandparent), and only then Swimmer. That is not sensible, because Swimmer is closer to Dog1 than Pet is. C3 follows two rules:

  1. A child is always checked before its parents.
  2. Parents are checked in the order they are listed in the brackets.

So for class DerivedClass(Base1, Base2, Base3), Python checks the class itself, then Base1, Base2, Base3, and then goes on to their parents. A shared grandparent is checked only after all the classes that inherit from it.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.10 Example script for multiple inheritance
docs.text:
In this example we see how Python chooses a method when two parents both provide it.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: Walker, Swimmer, and the order of the parents
docs.text:
What the code does.

  1. Base class. Pet has a method info() that every child inherits.
  2. Two parent classes. Walker(Pet) and Swimmer(Pet) each define their own action(). Walker.action() prints "Walking..." and Swimmer.action() prints "Swimming...".
  3. Two child classes with multiple inheritance. Dog1(Walker, Swimmer) and Dog2(Swimmer, Walker). They have the same two parents, but in a different order. Neither child writes its own action().
  4. The test. It calls action() on a Dog1 object and on a Dog2 object, and prints both MROs.

How it works. For d1.action(), Python searches the MRO of Dog1: Dog1, Walker, Swimmer, Pet, object. It finds action() in Walker first and stops there. For Dog2, the MRO starts Dog2, Swimmer, so the Swimmer version runs.

Why it matters. With multiple inheritance, the order of the parent classes changes the behaviour. Swapping two names in the brackets makes the same call do something different.

Learning points

  1. The order of the parent classes matters.
  2. Python follows the MRO to find a method.
  3. The first match in the MRO is the one that runs. The search then stops.
  4. Methods of the base class (info()) are inherited by all.

docs.title: Notes on Example 6
docs.text:
• The comments in the code say that Walker and Swimmer "override Pet's action()". In fact Pet has no action() method. Walker and Swimmer each add a new action(). They do not override anything.
  • info() is never called in the script. Try it: add d1.info(). It prints "I am a Pet", found at the end of the MRO.
  • The online resource has a problem on using super() together with multiple inheritance, and on how the MRO controls the order of execution.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.11 Composition: the "HAS-A" relationship
docs.text:
Composition means that one class holds an object of another class as one of its attributes. The outer object does not become that other thing. It owns or uses it.

  • Rule of thumb: if you can say "Class A has a Class B", use composition.
  • Purpose: combine different pieces of behaviour without forcing them into a rigid family tree.
  • Examples: a Dog has a Collar. A Car has an Engine.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 7: A Dog that has a Collar
docs.text:
What the code does. It creates a small class Collar with one attribute, color. The class Dog does not inherit from Collar. Instead, Dog.__init__() makes a new Collar("Red") and stores it in self.collar.

How it works. d.collar is a full Collar object. So d.collar.color means: take the dog's collar, then take that collar's colour. Each dot moves one step into the object.

Why it matters. "A Dog is a Collar" is nonsense, so inheritance would be the wrong tool. Composition keeps the two classes separate. You can change Collar without touching the family tree of Dog.

Learning points

  1. Composition is built with an ordinary assignment inside __init__(): self.collar = Collar("Red").
  2. Dog does not get the methods of Collar. You reach them through the attribute: d.collar.something().
  3. Every Dog gets its own new Collar object.

docs.title: Notes on Example 7
docs.text:
• Here every collar is red, because "Red" is fixed inside Dog.__init__(). A more flexible design passes the colour in: def __init__(self, name, collar_color): and then self.collar = Collar(collar_color).
  • The online resource has a detailed note on composition, and a problem that compares three kinds of HAS-A link: composition (the part is created and owned by the whole), aggregation (the part exists on its own and is only shared), and dependency (one class only uses another for a moment, for example as a method argument).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: IS-A compared with HAS-A
docs.text:
Feature Inheritance Composition Relationship IS-A HAS-A Example A Dog is a Pet A Dog has a Collar Flexibility Less More

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.12 Abstract methods and abstract classes
docs.text:
An abstract method is a method that is declared but not implemented. It works as a placeholder. It tells every child class: "you must write this method yourself".

We need abstract methods when (1) every child class must follow the same rule (for example, "every pet can speak"), but (2) each child does it in its own way (a dog barks, a cat meows). In short, the parent decides what must exist, and the child decides how it works.

The simplest way to make an abstract method is to have it raise NotImplementedError. This is a built-in exception, made for exactly this purpose.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: An abstract method made with NotImplementedError
docs.text:
What the code does.

  1. Base class Pet. Its speak() has no real code. It only raises NotImplementedError("Subclass must implement speak()").
  2. Child class Dog. It writes its own speak(). This is called a concrete implementation. So Dog objects can safely call speak().
  3. Child class Cat. It does not write speak(). It inherits the version from Pet, which raises the error.
  4. Test. A Dog is created and speak() works. A Cat is also created with no problem. The call c.speak() is commented out, because it would stop the program.

The logic in four steps

  1. The parent defines the method, but it raises an error instead of doing work.
  2. The child inherits the method.
  3. If the child overrides the method with real code, calls succeed.
  4. If the child forgets to override it, calling the method crashes with NotImplementedError.

Learning points

  1. The parent defines the structure. Pet says that speak() must exist.
  2. The child must implement it. Dog does, so it works. Cat does not, so it fails.
  3. The error happens late, at run time. Python happily lets you create a Cat. The error appears only when speak() is actually called.

docs.title: Try it: calling speak() on the Cat
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It calls the method that the book leaves commented out. The try ... except catches the error so the notebook can carry on.

docs.title: 8.13 The abc module (the "new way" of making abstract classes)
docs.text:
abc stands for Abstract Base Classes. This module gives Python a proper way to define "blueprints" that other classes must follow.

  • Main goal: make sure a subclass provides a given interface, that is, a list of required methods.
  • Early failure: with NotImplementedError, the program fails only when the missing method is called. With abc, it fails the moment you try to create the object (c = Cat()).
  • Why use it?
    1. Enforcement: every object in your program really has the methods it claims to have.
    2. Clarity: other programmers can see at a glance which methods they must write.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.13.1 @abstractmethod
docs.text:
@abstractmethod is a decorator. As you saw in Chapter 7, a decorator changes the function written just below it.

Part What it does The flag @abstractmethod sets a hidden attribute on the function: __isabstractmethod__ = True. The guard The class ABC acts like a security guard. When you try to create an object, it checks the class and all its parents. If any method still carries the flag and has not been overridden with real code, the object is not created and you get a TypeError. pass in the body The body of an abstract method is usually just pass, because that code never runs. The method is there only to fix its name and parameters.

The usual pattern:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class SomeBase(ABC):          # 1. inherit from ABC
    @abstractmethod           # 2. mark each required method
    def required_method(self):
        pass

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 9: An abstract base class with @abstractmethod
docs.text:
What the code does. It imports ABC and abstractmethod from the abc module. Pet inherits from ABC and marks speak() as abstract. Dog writes its own speak(), so Dog() works. Cat does not, so Cat() would fail. That line is left commented out.

How it works. When Dog() is called, the guard finds that Dog.speak is a normal method, so the object is made. For Cat(), the guard finds that speak is still the abstract one from Pet, so it refuses.

Learning points

  1. A class with abstract methods must inherit from ABC, otherwise @abstractmethod has no effect.
  2. You cannot create an object from Pet itself either. Pet() also raises TypeError.
  3. The error now comes early, when the object is created, not later when a method is called.

docs.title: Try it: creating a Cat, and creating a Pet
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It runs the line the book leaves commented out, and then tries to create a Pet directly.

docs.title: 8.13.2 Abstract methods compared with NotImplementedError
docs.text:
Raising NotImplementedError is an informal way to make an abstract method. Using the abc module is the formal way.

raise NotImplementedError ABC and @abstractmethod Can you create the object? Yes, c = Cat() works No, c = Cat() raises TypeError When does the error appear? Only when the missing method is called As soon as the object is created Kind of failure Run-time failure Instantiation failure Needs an import? No Yes, from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

The online resource has a problem on designing a pet system with abstract classes, where every pet must have speak() and move(), and some pets can walk, some can swim, and some can do both (multiple inheritance).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.14 Real subclasses and virtual subclasses
docs.text:
A class can be related to another class in two ways.

1. Real subclass (normal inheritance)

  • A class inherits directly from another, with brackets: class Dog(Pet).
  • The child knows its parent, but the parent does not keep a list of its children.
  • A real subclass shows up in (1) __mro__, (2) issubclass(), and (3) isinstance().

2. Virtual subclass (registration)

  • The class does not inherit from the parent.
  • Instead, it is registered with a parent that is an ABC: Pet.register(RobotDog).
  • The child gets no code from the parent.
  • The link is logical, not physical. It only affects type checks.
  • This works only with abstract base classes.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Real and virtual subclasses side by side
docs.text:
Feature Real subclass Virtual subclass Inheritance Yes No Code reuse Yes No Appears in the MRO Yes No issubclass() True True isinstance() True True Needs an ABC No Yes Kind of link Physical Logical

Why use virtual subclasses? (1) To define a common interface. (2) To let classes that are not related still count as a particular type. This is useful in frameworks, plug-ins and APIs, where you want to accept a class written by someone else without changing its code.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: A real subclass and a virtual subclass
docs.text:
What the code does.

  1. Abstract base class. Pet(ABC) is empty. It is used only as a common type.
  2. Real subclass. Dog(Pet) inherits from Pet.
  3. Virtual subclass. RobotDog has no parent class. It is then registered with Pet.register(RobotDog).
  4. Type checks. issubclass() checks class against class, and isinstance() checks object against class. All four checks return True.
  5. MRO. Dog.__mro__ contains Pet. RobotDog.__mro__ would not, because there is no real inheritance.

Learning points

  1. After register(), Python treats RobotDog as a kind of Pet for type checks.
  2. RobotDog gets nothing from Pet. If Pet had a method, a RobotDog object could not use it.
  3. register() does not check anything. Python trusts you that RobotDog really provides what Pet promises.

docs.title: Notes on Example 10
docs.text:
• Try it: remove the # in front of the last line, print(RobotDog.__mro__). The output is (<class '__main__.robotdog'="">, <class 'object'="">). There is no Pet in it.
  • Notice abc.ABC in the MRO of Dog. Pet inherits from ABC, so ABC is part of the chain too.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.15 Registration
docs.text:
Registration is not about inheritance. It is about grouping, classifying and finding classes.

  • Inheritance says what you are.
  • Registration says how you are treated.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Why register classes?
docs.text:
1. To group unrelated classes. Two classes may share no code but behave in a similar way. For example, Dog and RobotDog below do not inherit from each other, yet both can be treated as "pets".
  2. Dynamic discovery. Instead of a long if ... elif chain that picks a class by name, the program keeps the classes in a dictionary and looks them up: registry[name]().
  3. Plug-in systems. Many real applications (for example, Django apps, Flask extensions and payment gateways) do not know all their classes in advance. The classes register themselves.
  4. Loose coupling. Without registration, the main program must know every class. With registration, classes add themselves and the main program stays clean.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 11: Grouping classes, and finding them with a registry
docs.text:
What the code does. Part A is the book's pair of unrelated classes, Dog and RobotDog. Parts B and C are not in the book. They turn the book's two short fragments (the if ... elif chain and registry[name]()) into code that runs, so you can compare them.

How it works. registry is an ordinary dictionary. Its keys are names and its values are classes, not objects. registry[name] gives back a class, and the () after it creates an object of that class.

Learning points

  1. A class is an object too. It can be stored in a dictionary like any other value.
  2. To add a new kind of pet, you add one entry to the dictionary. The code that uses it does not change.

docs.title: When to use registration and when to use inheritance
docs.text:
Situation Use You need shared code Inheritance You only need to classify classes Registration You need flexibility Registration You need a strict hierarchy Inheritance

The online resource has a problem on a pet registration system built in three ways:

Approach The idea Best for A. Manual registration The programmer keeps a list or dictionary and adds each class by hand. Beginners: simple and easy to follow B. Decorator-based registration A decorator adds the class to the registry when the class is defined. Large systems and frameworks C. Automatic registration with __init_subclass__() The base class records every subclass on its own. Nothing has to be done by hand. Large systems and frameworks

Approach C is shown in the "Beyond the Book" section at the end of this notebook.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.16 Containers in Python
docs.text:
A container is an object that holds several values.

Type Description Examples Key feature Sequence Stores items in order list, tuple, str Indexed by whole numbers (0, 1, 2 ...) Mapping Stores key-value pairs dict Indexed by keys

You can make your own container class. You do it by writing special methods, also called magic methods or dunder methods (short for "double underscore").

Method Purpose Called by __getitem__(self, key) Read a value obj[key] __setitem__(self, key, value) Store a value obj[key] = value

If a class defines:

  • __getitem__(), its objects can be read with square brackets, like a list;
  • __setitem__(), its objects can be written with square brackets.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 12: A custom container, PetStore
docs.text:
What the code does. PetStore keeps pet names in an internal list, self.pets, which starts as [None, None, None]. Because it defines __setitem__() and __getitem__(), you can use square brackets on a PetStore object, just as you would on a list. Each method prints a message, so you can see when Python calls it.

How it works. Python turns the bracket syntax into method calls:

You write Python actually runs store[0] = "Dog" store.__setitem__(0, "Dog") store[0] store.__getitem__(0)

Why it matters. This is how list, dict and many library types work inside. It lets your own classes feel like built-in types.

Learning points

  1. You never call __setitem__() or __getitem__() yourself. Python calls them when it sees the brackets.
  2. In the last three lines, "Getting pet at index ..." is printed before "Pet at ...". Python must work out store[0] (which prints its message) before print() can show the result.
  3. store[2] was never set, so it is still None.

docs.title: Notes on Example 12
docs.text:
• Try it: run store[5] = "Fish". You get an IndexError, because the list inside has only 3 places.
  • Try it: run len(store). You get a TypeError. A container usually also defines __len__(), so that len() works. Add def __len__(self): return len(self.pets) to the class and try again.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 8.17 __new__() compared with __init__()
docs.text:
Python creates an object in two steps:

Step Method Job 1 __new__(cls) Creates the object and returns it 2 __init__(self) Initialises the object, that is, fills in its attributes

The order is: (1) you call ClassName(), (2) Python calls __new__(cls), (3) __new__ returns the new object, (4) Python calls __init__(self) on it.

Note the first parameter. __new__ receives the class (cls), because the object does not exist yet. __init__ receives the object (self).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: watching the two steps
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. Both methods print a message so you can see the order. __new__ passes the real work to object.__new__ with super().

docs.title: 8.18 Metaclasses in Python
docs.text:
A metaclass is a class that creates other classes:

  1. a metaclass creates a class, and
  2. a class creates objects.

By default, Python uses type as the metaclass. type can be used in two ways:

Call Role Example type(obj), with 1 argument Inspector: gives the type of an object type(5) gives <class 'int'=""> type(name, bases, attributes), with 3 arguments Class factory: builds a new class see the cell below

So you have two options:

  1. Let Python create classes for you. This is the default. You do not need to know about metaclasses or about the three-argument form of type.
  2. Write your own metaclass by deriving it from type, and use it to create your classes. In effect, you change the "class factory" so that it builds custom classes.

Why would you want a custom metaclass? The usual reasons are:

  1. to enforce rules on classes (for example, every class must have a certain method),
  2. to register classes automatically, and
  3. to add methods or attributes to classes automatically.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: making a class with type()
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. The two definitions below build the same kind of class. The second one calls type directly, which is what Python does for you behind the class statement.

docs.title: 8.19 Namespaces in Python
docs.text:
A namespace is a container that maps names to objects. Think of it as a dictionary: the keys are the names you create, and the values are the objects in memory. Variables are names; objects are values.

Three key ideas:

  1. Unique identity: every object that exists has its own id().
  2. Mapping: the namespace links your variable name to that object.
  3. Independence: different namespaces can use the same name for different objects without any clash. A name inside one function has nothing to do with a name inside another.

So if three names var_name1, var_name2 and var_name3 refer to three objects, the namespace behaves like this dictionary:

namespace = {
    "var_name1": object1,
    "var_name2": object2,
    "var_name3": object3
}

Most user-defined classes and their objects keep their namespace in an attribute called __dict__.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: The four namespaces: LEGB
docs.text:
Python has four namespaces, nested one inside another:

Letter Namespace Where the names come from L Local Inside the current function (innermost) E Enclosing Inside an outer function, when functions are nested G Global The top level of the file (module) B Built-in Names Python provides, such as print and len (outermost)

Visibility rules: (1) an inner scope can see the names of the outer scopes; (2) an outer scope cannot see the names of an inner scope.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: A summary of the four namespaces
docs.text:
Question Answer Where is the variable created? Local: inside a function. Enclosing: inside an outer function. Global: at file level. Built-in: provided by Python. When is the namespace created? Local: when the function is called. Enclosing: when the outer function runs. Global: when the program (module) starts. Built-in: when the interpreter starts. How long does it live? Local: until the function ends. Enclosing: while the outer function runs (longer if a closure keeps it). Global: for the whole program. Built-in: always. Search order Local, then Enclosing, then Global, then Built-in. The first match wins. How can you see it? Local: locals(). Global: globals(). Built-in: the builtins module. What can an inner function reach? Its own locals, the enclosing names, the globals and the built-ins. This is why closures work. Can it be changed directly? Local: yes. Enclosing: only with nonlocal. Global: only with global. Built-in: it should not be changed. Shadowing The same name in an inner scope hides the outer one, but does not change it. Common mistakes Forgetting global or nonlocal; reusing a built-in name such as list or sum for your own variable. Name not found anywhere NameError

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 13: Reading and changing an object's namespace with __dict__
docs.text:
What the code does. It makes a class Dog with a class attribute species and an instance attribute name. It prints the namespace of the class and of the object. Then it adds an attribute and changes an attribute by writing straight into the object's __dict__.

How it works. d.__dict__ is a real dictionary. d.color and d.__dict__["color"] reach the same entry. The class has its own, separate __dict__, which holds species and the methods.

Learning points

  1. The object's __dict__ holds only instance attributes (name). species lives in the class's __dict__. When you read d.species, Python first looks in the object and then in the class.
  2. Writing into d.__dict__ has the same effect as a normal assignment such as d.color = "Brown". The normal way is clearer; this example only shows what happens inside.
  3. The class __dict__ output includes a memory address for __init__. Your address will be different.

docs.title: Try it: locals() and globals()
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. locals() gives the local namespace as a dictionary, and globals() gives the global one. Inside a function they are different. At the top level of a file they are the same dictionary.

docs.title: 8.20 Keywords: global and nonlocal
docs.text:
These two keywords control which variable an assignment changes.

Keyword Purpose Without it global Change a global variable from inside a function The assignment creates a new local variable nonlocal Change a variable of the enclosing (outer) function from inside a nested function The assignment creates a new local variable

nonlocal works only inside nested functions.

Note that these keywords are needed only for assignment. Just reading an outer variable works without them, thanks to LEGB.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 14: The effect of using and not using global and nonlocal
docs.text:
What the code does. It has two parts, and each part changes two variables: one with the keyword ("correct") and one without it ("wrong").

  • Part 1, global. test_global() assigns to pet_global_wrong without global, and to pet_global_correct after global pet_global_correct. After the call, the program prints both global variables.
  • Part 2, nonlocal. outer_function() has two local variables. The nested inner_function() assigns to pet_enclosing_wrong without nonlocal, and to pet_enclosing_correct after nonlocal pet_enclosing_correct. Back in the outer function, both are printed.

How it works. Inside a function, Python treats a name as local if the function assigns to it anywhere. global and nonlocal switch this off for the names they list.

Learning points

  1. Inside the functions, both "wrong" and "correct" variables show the new text. The difference only appears outside.
  2. After the calls, only the "correct" variables have changed. The "wrong" assignments made new local variables that disappeared when the function ended.
  3. global reaches the top level of the file. nonlocal reaches only the nearest enclosing function.

docs.title: Notes on Example 14
docs.text:
• Try it: inside test_global(), add the line print(pet_global_wrong) before the assignment to it. You get an UnboundLocalError. Python has already decided the name is local, because it is assigned later in the function.
  • Use global sparingly. Functions that change global variables are harder to test and to understand. Returning a value is usually better.

docs.title: Automatic registration with __init_subclass__()
docs.text: Python calls the special method __init_subclass__() of a base class every time a new subclass is created. The base class can use it to keep a registry, with nothing to do by hand. This is approach C from section 8.15.

docs.title: A read-only attribute with @property
docs.text: @property turns a method into something you read like an attribute, with no brackets. It is a clean way to compute a value on demand, or to protect an attribute from being changed.

docs.title: Saving memory with __slots__
docs.text: Normally every object has its own __dict__. If a class lists its attributes in __slots__, Python stores them in a fixed, smaller space instead, and no __dict__ is made. You then cannot add new attributes to the object. This is useful when a program creates millions of small objects.

docs.title: Cooperative super() in a diamond
docs.text: In a diamond, super() follows the MRO of the object, not the parent named in the class. So each class in the diamond runs exactly once, and the shared grandparent runs last.

def process_numbers(number, divisor):
    try:
        print("1. Performing division...")
        result = number / divisor  # may cause TypeError or ZeroDivisionError

    except ZeroDivisionError:
        print( f"divisor = {divisor} Error. Cannot divide by zero.")

    except Exception as e:  # Generic except for other exceptions like TypeError
        print("Generic Error:", e)

    else:  # Runs if no exception occurs
        print("No exception occurred")
        print("Result:", result)

    finally:  # Always runs, use for cleanup
        print(f"Finally block always executes. (divisor was {divisor})")

# Case 1: No Error

# Case 3: TypeError not specifically handled so Generic except will catch it

# This script demonstrates use of try-except-else-finally blocks for handling
# file operations. It has except blocks for errors like FileNotFoundError &
# PermissionError. It also has a generic except block to catch any other
# unforeseen exceptions. Using open() in 'r' mode is safer for reading
# files as it does not allow modifications, which can help prevent certain
# types of errors. The else block executes if no exceptions occur, and the
# finally block always executes regardless of whether an exception was raised
# or not, making it ideal for cleanup actions.

def myReader(fileName, mode='r'):
    try:
        print(f"1. Trying to open file in '{mode}' mode...")

        with open(fileName, mode) as f:
            content = f.read()

    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("Error: File not found")

    except PermissionError:
        print("Error: Permission denied")

    except Exception as e:
        print("Generic error (not caught by specific except blocks):", e)

    else:
        print("2. File read successfully")
        print("Content:\n", content)

    finally:
        print("3. File operation attempted")

# Test cases
print("Case 1: Valid file")
myReader("existing_file.txt")  # Make sure this file exists for the test
# Case 1 Output: try → else → finally. (No exceptions occur)

print("Case 2: File not found")
myReader("non_existent_file.txt")  # This file does not exist
# Case 2 Output: try → except(FileNotFoundError) → finally

print("Case 3: Permission denied")
myReader("/root/secret_file.txt")  # Assume file exists but not accessible
# Case 3 Output: try → except(PermissionError) → finally

print("Case 4: Invalid mode")
myReader("existing_file.txt", mode='non_existent_mode')  # Invalid mode → ValueError
# Case 4 Output: try → except(generic) → finally

# Step 1: Define custom exceptions
class ParentError(Exception):
    pass

class ChildError(ParentError):   # ChildError inherits from ParentError
    pass

# Case 1: Catch Child before Parent (Correct Order)
print("Case 1: Catch ChildError before ParentError")
for x in [ParentError, ChildError]:
    try:
        raise x()   # Raise ParentError or ChildError

    except ChildError:  # This will catch ChildError but not ParentError
        print("Caught ChildError")

    except ParentError: # ChildError already caught so only catches ParentError
        print("Caught ParentError")

# Case 2: Catch Parent before Child (Incorrect Order)
print("Case 2: Catch ParentError before ChildError")

for x in [ParentError, ChildError]:
    try:
        raise x()

    except ParentError:   # This will catch BOTH ParentError and ChildError
        print("Caught ParentError")

    except ChildError: # This NEVER executes ParentError catches both exceptions
        print("Caught ChildError")

Caught ParentError
Caught ChildError

class InsufficientBalanceError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, balance, withdraw):
        self.balance = balance
        self.withdraw = withdraw

    def __str__(self):  # Custom error message when the exception is printed
        return f"Balance {self.balance} is less than withdrawal {self.withdraw}"

# Function to simulate money withdrawal & show custom exception handling
def withdraw_money(balance, amount):
    try:
        if amount > balance:
            raise InsufficientBalanceError(balance, amount)

        print("Withdrawal successful")

    except InsufficientBalanceError as e:  # Handle custom exception
        print("Error:", e)  #Print __str__() of InsufficientBalanceError class

This notebook holds the code examples of Chapter 9. You do not need to type them. Run them, read the notes, and then change the code to see what happens.

Every program meets problems: a wrong input, a missing file, a division by zero. This chapter shows how Python reports such problems (exceptions), how your program can catch them and carry on, how to clean up with finally and with, and how to create your own exceptions.

  • A few short cells are marked Try it. They are not in the book. They let you see, safely, something the book describes in words.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • tell a syntax error apart from an exception;
  • use try, except and else so that a problem does not crash the program, and so that error handling stays separate from the normal logic;
  • catch several exceptions, either with separate except blocks or with one except and a tuple;
  • use a generic except carefully, as a last safety net for errors you did not expect;
  • use finally for clean-up work that must happen whether or not an error occurs;
  • use the with statement (a context manager) to handle files safely;
  • order except blocks so that a child exception is not hidden by its parent;
  • raise exceptions yourself with raise when data breaks a rule;
  • write your own exception classes, derived from Exception;
  • use as to get the exception object and read its details.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.1 Errors and exceptions
docs.text:
An error is a problem that stops a program from working correctly. Errors come in two broad kinds.

Syntax errors (parsing errors). Python cannot understand the code because it breaks the rules of the language. Python finds these while reading the file, before anything runs, so not a single line is executed. Common causes: (1) typing mistakes, (2) missing symbols such as : or ), (3) wrong indentation.

Exceptions (run-time errors). The code is valid, but something goes wrong while it runs, for example dividing by zero or reading past the end of a list. An exception interrupts the normal flow. If you handle it with try-except, the program can carry on.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Syntax error compared with exception
docs.text:
Feature Syntax error Exception When it occurs Before execution, while Python reads the code During execution Cause Code that breaks the rules of the language A problem in the logic or the data at run time Effect on the program The program does not start at all The program stops, unless the exception is handled Example A missing : after if x > 3 [1, 2][5] gives IndexError Can it be handled? No Yes, with try-except

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.2 The raise statement
docs.text:
So far, Python raised exceptions for us. With the raise statement you can raise an exception on purpose, when your own rule is broken. The syntax is:

raise ExceptionName("message")

The message tells the reader what went wrong. You can raise any built-in exception, such as ValueError, or one you wrote yourself (see section 9.12).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: Raising a ValueError for a negative age
docs.text:
What the code does. The class Pet checks the age it is given. If the age is negative, __init__() raises a ValueError instead of storing the bad value. The last line tries to create a pet with age -2.

How it works. raise stops __init__() at once. The lines that set self.name and self.age never run, and no Pet object is made. There is no try-except here, so the exception reaches the top level and Python prints a traceback.

Why it matters. It is better to refuse bad data early, with a clear message, than to store it and get strange results later.

Learning points

  1. raise is how your own code reports that a rule has been broken.
  2. ValueError is the right built-in exception when the type is correct (an integer) but the value is not acceptable.
  3. The red traceback below the cell is expected. Its last line reads ValueError: Age cannot be negative.

docs.title: Notes on Example 1
docs.text:
• Try it: change -2 to 3 and run the cell again. Nothing is printed, because the object is created without trouble.
  • To stop the program from crashing, the caller wraps the creation in try-except. You will learn how in the next section.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.3 The try-except-else block
docs.text:
Some code is risky: it may fail because of wrong user input, a missing file, a bad list index, and so on. If such a failure is not handled, the program stops abruptly. try-except lets you handle the failure gracefully.

The basic structure is:

try:
    # Risky code
except SomeException:
    # Code to handle error
else:
    # Runs only if no exception occurs

The flow of execution:

  1. Run the try block.
  2. Did an error occur?
    • Yes: Python looks for an except block that matches the exception. If one matches, it runs that block.
    • No: Python runs the else block.
  3. The program carries on after the whole try statement.

The role of else: (1) it runs only if no exception occurred, and (2) it keeps the normal logic apart from the error-handling logic.

If an exception occurs and no except block matches it, the exception is not handled. The same exception travels on to the code that called this code. If nothing handles it anywhere, Python prints a traceback and the program stops.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Multiple except blocks
docs.text:
One try block can have several except blocks, one for each kind of exception you want to treat differently.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: The shape of multiple except blocks
docs.text:
What the code does. This is the book's skeleton for multiple except blocks. Every block contains only pass, so the cell runs but prints nothing.

How it works. When an exception occurs in the try block, Python checks the except blocks from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. At most one except block runs.

Learning points

  1. Each except names the type of exception it handles.
  2. Try it: replace the first pass with int("abc"), and the pass under except ValueError: with print("Caught a ValueError"). Run the cell again.

docs.title: 9.4 Generic exception (except without a specific type)
docs.text:
A generic except block catches exceptions without naming a particular type. There are two forms:

Form What it catches except Exception as e: Every normal error (everything derived from Exception). e holds the exception object. except: (a "bare" except) Absolutely everything, including KeyboardInterrupt (pressing Ctrl+C) and SystemExit. This is rarely what you want.

Its main features: (1) it catches any error; (2) it acts as a safety net; (3) it is usually written after the specific except blocks; (4) it helps prevent a crash.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Advantages and disadvantages of a generic ("catch-all") except
docs.text:
Points Advantages Handles errors you did not expect. Prevents a crash, so the program can continue gracefully. Simple to write, with no need to list exception types. Useful as a final safety layer or fallback. Disadvantages Hides the real problem, so it is hard to know which error occurred. Makes debugging and tracking errors difficult. May catch errors you did not intend to catch, and so hide bugs. Makes the code less clear, because the handling is not explicit.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Good practice with generic exceptions
docs.text:
• Always write the specific except blocks first and the generic one last. The generic block is a last safety net, not your main way of handling errors.
  • Good places for a generic block: (a) logging systems, (b) programs used directly by people, where a crash would be unfriendly, (c) a final fallback at the top level of a program.
  • Do not use a generic block when (1) you know which exception to expect, or (2) the system is critical and precise handling matters.

The as keyword. In except SomeError as e:, the name e is a variable that refers to the exception object. You can then look inside it, for example print(e). Section 9.13 covers this in detail.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.5 try-except-else-finally without a generic exception
docs.text:
A finally block runs always: after the try block if all went well, after the except block if an error was handled, and even when an error is not handled.

If there is no generic except block, only the listed exceptions are handled. When an exception occurs:

  1. Python checks whether it matches one of the except blocks.
  2. If a match is found, that except block runs, then finally.
  3. If no match is found:
    • the finally block runs first,
    • then the exception carries on, Python prints its traceback,
    • and the program stops.

Points to note: (1) only the listed exceptions are handled; (2) finally always runs; (3) other exceptions stop the program; (4) there is no fallback, because there is no generic except.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: try-except-else-finally with one specific except
docs.text:
What the code does. process_numbers() divides number by divisor. It handles only ZeroDivisionError. It is called three times:

Case Call What happens Blocks that run 1 process_numbers(10, 2) No error; the result is 5.0 try, else, finally 2 process_numbers(10, 0) ZeroDivisionError, which is handled try, except, finally 3 process_numbers("10", 2) TypeError, which is not handled try, finally, then a traceback

How it works. In case 3, dividing a string by an integer raises TypeError. No except block matches it. Python still runs finally, prints "Finally block always executes", and then the exception stops the cell with a red traceback.

Why it matters. It shows the one job finally does that nothing else can: it runs even when the program is about to crash. That is why it is used for clean-up.

Learning points

  1. Compare the output of the three cases with the table above.
  2. In case 3, "Finally block always executes" is printed before the traceback.
  3. The red TypeError traceback at the end is expected.

docs.title: 9.6 try-except-else-finally with multiple except blocks and a generic except
docs.text:
Real programs meet many kinds of errors: invalid input, division errors, file errors and so on. A full try statement gives you (1) graceful handling with except, (2) clean normal logic with else, and (3) guaranteed clean-up with finally.

The typical structure (this is a pattern, not code that runs):

try:
    # Risky/ suspicious code
except ExceptionType1:  # Handle error 1
    # Handle error 1
except ExceptionType2:  # Handle error 2
    # Handle error 2
except:
    # Handle all remaining errors (generic)
else:
    # Runs if no error
finally:
    # Always runs

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Points to note about the blocks
docs.text:
Block Points try Holds the risky code. except Three possibilities: a single exception (handles one specific error), multiple except blocks (handle different errors separately), or a generic except (handles all errors). else Runs only if no exception occurred. Keeps the normal logic separate. finally Always runs. Used to close files and for other clean-up. Rules of execution Only one except block runs. Once an exception occurs, the rest of the try block is skipped. finally runs even if an error is not handled. A bare except: must be the last except block.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: Adding a generic except as a safety net
docs.text:
What the code does. This is Example 3 with one change: a generic block, except Exception as e:, is added after except ZeroDivisionError:. The third call now divides 10 by "a".

Case Call Blocks that run 1 process_numbers(10, 2) try, else, finally 2 process_numbers(10, 0) try, except ZeroDivisionError, finally 3 process_numbers(10, "a") try, generic except, finally

How it works. In case 3, TypeError does not match ZeroDivisionError, so Python moves on to except Exception as e:. TypeError is derived from Exception, so this block matches. e holds the exception, and printing it shows its message.

Learning points

  1. There is no traceback now. The program handles every case and carries on.
  2. The generic block comes after the specific one. If it came first, it would catch the ZeroDivisionError too, and the specific block would never run.
  3. finally can use the function's parameters. Here it prints the divisor in every case.

docs.title: 9.7 Context managers (the with statement)
docs.text:
A context manager is an object that (1) sets up a resource, for example opens a file, and (2) cleans it up automatically afterwards, for example closes the file. It is used with the with statement.

The basic syntax:

with open("file.txt", "r") as f:
    data = f.read()

Why use a context manager? To read a file you open it, read it and then close it. But if an exception happens after opening and before closing, the close() line is never reached and the file stays open. The with statement closes the file in every case.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Without and with a context manager
docs.text:
Without a context manager With a context manager f = open("file.txt") with open("file.txt") as f: data = f.read() data = f.read() f.close(): if an exception occurs before this line, the file stays open The file is always closed automatically, even after an error

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: creating two small files for the examples
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. Colab starts with an empty folder, so the examples that read file.txt and existing_file.txt would have nothing to read. The cell creates both files. You can see them in the Files panel on the left of the Colab window (the folder icon).

docs.title: Example 5: Reading a file with the with statement
docs.text:
What the code does. It is the book's basic syntax, plus one print() so you can see the result. It opens file.txt for reading ("r"), reads everything into data, and the file is closed as soon as the indented block ends.

Learning points

  1. as f gives the open file a name to use inside the block.
  2. You never write f.close(). After the block, f.closed is True.

docs.title: Example 6: What the with statement does inside
docs.text:
This listing from the book shows, in simplified form, what Python does for you when it runs a with statement. It is a sketch, not a program: fileName, mode, exc_type, exc_value and traceback are not defined, so it is shown here as text rather than as a code cell.

manager = open(fileName, mode)
# open() returns file object as a context manager
# The with statement automatically calls manager.__enter__() to get the file
# object and assigns it to f. It also ensures that manager.__exit__() is called
# to close the file, even if an exception occurs.
f = manager.__enter__()

try:
    content = f.read()
except:
    # Exception handling (outside)
    raise
finally:
    manager.__exit__(exc_type, exc_value, traceback)
    # exc_type, exc_value, traceback are the exception details if an exception
    # occurred, otherwise they are None.

How to read it.

Step Line Meaning 1 manager = open(fileName, mode) open() returns an object that can act as a context manager. 2 f = manager.__enter__() The start of the with block. For a file, __enter__() returns the file itself; this is the f after as. 3 the try block The body of your with block. 4 except: raise Any exception is passed on (re-raised) to the code outside. 5 finally: manager.__exit__(...) Always runs, so the file is always closed. The three arguments describe the exception, or are all None if there was none.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: calling __enter__() and __exit__() yourself
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It is a version of the sketch that runs. It uses the real file file.txt and passes None three times to __exit__(), which means "no exception happened". Never write code like this in practice; use with.

docs.title: 9.8 Using try-except to read a file
docs.text:
File handling is covered in detail in a later chapter, so you may skip this section for now.

File operations often fail. Common reasons: (1) the file does not exist, (2) permission is denied, (3) the path is wrong. Without handling, such an error ends the program abruptly. The usual pattern:

try:
    # File operation
except SomeException:
    # Handle error
else:
    # Runs if no error

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 7: try-except-else-finally for reading a file
docs.text:
What the code does. myReader() opens a file with with, reads it, and handles three kinds of problems:

except block Handles except FileNotFoundError: The file does not exist except PermissionError: The file exists but you may not read it except Exception as e: Anything else (generic safety net)

The else block prints the content only when the read succeeded, and finally always prints "3. File operation attempted".

It is tested with four cases:

Case Call Expected blocks 1 a file that exists try, else, finally 2 a file that does not exist try, except FileNotFoundError, finally 3 a file you may not read try, except PermissionError, finally 4 an invalid mode, 'non_existent_mode' try, generic except (ValueError), finally

How it works. open() raises a different exception for each problem, and Python picks the first except block that matches. An invalid mode raises ValueError, which is not listed, so the generic block catches it.

Why it matters. Opening files is one of the most common places for errors in real programs. Handling each case separately gives the user a clear message instead of a crash.

Learning points

  1. Specific blocks first, generic block last.
  2. with inside try closes the file, and try handles errors from open() itself.
  3. The 'r' mode only reads, so the file cannot be changed by mistake.

docs.title: Notes on Example 7
docs.text:
• Case 1 works because the "Try it" cell in section 9.7 created existing_file.txt. If you skipped that cell, case 1 prints "Error: File not found".
  • Case 3 in Colab: Colab runs your code as the administrator (the "root" user), who may read any file. The file /root/secret_file.txt does not exist there, so you see "Error: File not found" instead of "Permission denied". On your own computer, as an ordinary user, a protected file gives PermissionError.
  • The online resource has two projects on reading files from the internet: one with Python's urllib library, and one comparing it with the requests library.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.9 Handling multiple exceptions in a single except clause
docs.text:
One except block can handle several exception types. You list them as a tuple, inside brackets. This (1) reduces repeated code, and (2) groups related exceptions together.

try:
    # risky code
except (ExceptionType1, ExceptionType2, ExceptionType3):
    # common handling code
Use a tuple when Use separate except blocks when You want the same handling for all of them Different exceptions need different handling The exceptions are similar in nature You need a specific message for each You want simpler code

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: catching two exceptions with one except
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. to_number() turns a value into an integer. A string like "abc" raises ValueError, and a list raises TypeError. One except block with a tuple handles both. type(e).__name__ shows which one was caught.

docs.title: 9.9.1 Do not group a parent exception with its child
docs.text:
Exceptions are classes, arranged in a tree by inheritance. A child exception is a subclass of its parent, so catching the parent also catches all its children. Putting a parent and its child in the same tuple is valid, but the child adds nothing.

For example, ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of ArithmeticError:

Exception
 |
 +-- ArithmeticError
 |    +-- ZeroDivisionError
 |
 +-- ValueError
 |
 +-- TypeError

So except (ArithmeticError, ZeroDivisionError): does the same job as except ArithmeticError:.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: checking the family tree
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. issubclass() and __mro__ (from Chapter 8) show the parents of an exception. The last part catches a ZeroDivisionError with except ArithmeticError.

docs.title: 9.10 Built-in exceptions
docs.text:
Python's exceptions fall into two broad groups:

Category 1: application errors Category 2: system-level signals What they are Problems in your program's logic or data Events that control the running of the program Nature Expected and recoverable Not really "errors"; signals to stop, exit or interrupt Should you catch them? Yes, with try-except Usually not Examples Wrong input, file not found, division by zero The user presses Ctrl+C; the program calls exit() Base class Exception BaseException directly

This book deals only with category 1. The difference matters: application errors should be handled by the programmer, while system signals should normally be left alone so that the program can still be stopped.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Some common built-in exceptions
docs.text:
No. Exception Category Parent class Typical cause Example trigger Common handling 1 OSError System / I/O Exception Failure reported by the operating system Disk or file problem Check the path and permissions 2 FileNotFoundError File I/O OSError File missing open("x.txt") Ask for the correct file path 3 PermissionError File I/O OSError No permission Opening a protected file Change permissions 4 EOFError Input Exception No input available input() when input has ended Retry, or use a default value 5 ZeroDivisionError Arithmetic ArithmeticError Division by zero 10/0 Check the divisor first 6 ImportError Module Exception A name cannot be imported from math import xyz Check the name and the module 7 ModuleNotFoundError Module ImportError Module does not exist import xyz Install the module, or fix the name 8 IndexError Lookup LookupError Index out of range L[10] for a short list Check the length first 9 KeyError Lookup LookupError Missing key d['x'] Use d.get('x') 10 NameError Variable Exception Name not defined print(x) before x exists Define the variable 11 AttributeError Object Exception Missing attribute obj.x Check the object's attributes 12 IndentationError Syntax SyntaxError Wrong indentation Bad spacing Fix the code (it cannot be caught in the same file) 13 TypeError Type Exception Wrong type "5" + 2 Convert the types 14 ValueError Value Exception Right type, wrong value int("abc") Validate the input

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.11 Exception hierarchy in Python
docs.text:
Exceptions are organised as a tree: (1) some exceptions are parent classes, and (2) others are children (subclasses) of them. The tree helps you (1) group related errors, and (2) handle many errors with one except.

The root of the tree is BaseException. Every exception in Python inherits from it, directly or indirectly.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Direct subclasses of BaseException
docs.text:
Class Purpose SystemExit Raised when the program exits, for example by sys.exit() KeyboardInterrupt Raised when the user presses Ctrl+C (in Colab: the Stop button) GeneratorExit Raised when a generator is closed Exception Base class for all application-level errors

Two points to remember:

  • Derive your own exceptions from Exception, not from BaseException. BaseException also covers the system signals. Code that catches it may (1) stop the user from ending the program, and (2) interfere with signals such as Ctrl+C.
  • Parent before child is a mistake. If an except for the parent comes first, it catches the child too, and the child's except block is never reached.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 8: The order of except blocks for a parent and a child exception
docs.text:
What the code does. It creates two exceptions of its own: ParentError, derived from Exception, and ChildError, derived from ParentError. Then it raises each of them in turn, twice:

  • Case 1 (correct order): except ChildError comes before except ParentError.
  • Case 2 (wrong order): except ParentError comes first.

How it works. for x in [ParentError, ChildError]: loops over the two classes, and raise x() creates and raises an object of each one. For each exception, Python tries the except blocks from the top and stops at the first match. A ChildError is a ParentError, so except ParentError matches it.

Why it matters. Python gives no warning for the wrong order. The program runs, but one handler is silently dead.

Learning points

  1. Case 1 prints "Caught ParentError" and then "Caught ChildError". Each exception reaches its own block.
  2. Case 2 prints "Caught ParentError" twice. The except ChildError block never runs.
  3. Rule: always put the most specific (child) exception first.

docs.title: Parent and child, side by side
docs.text:
except clause Catches a ParentError? Catches a ChildError? except ParentError: Yes Yes (a child is a parent) except ChildError: No Yes

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Best practice
docs.text:
Practice Recommendation Catch specific exceptions first Yes Catch general exceptions later Yes except Exception at the end Optional except BaseException Avoid

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.12 User-defined (custom) exceptions
docs.text:
Sometimes the built-in exceptions do not describe an error in your program well. Python lets you define your own, called user-defined or custom exceptions.

Three facts to keep in mind:

  1. Exceptions are classes.
  2. When an exception is raised, it becomes an object.
  3. A custom exception is a class derived from Exception.

A custom exception must be raised explicitly, with raise. Creating an object of the class does not raise it. Python raises built-in exceptions such as ZeroDivisionError by itself, but it cannot know when your own rule has been broken. So you write:

raise MyException("message")

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.12.1 The role of __str__() in exceptions
docs.text:
__str__() is a special (dunder) method. It decides how an object is turned into text. It is used by (1) print(obj) and (2) str(obj). For an exception, it decides the message the user sees.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 9: A custom exception with its own __init__() and __str__()
docs.text:
What the code does. It brings together two ideas: raising a custom exception, and deciding how it is shown.

  1. InsufficientBalanceError is derived from Exception. Its __init__() stores two values, balance and withdraw. Its __str__() builds a clear message from them.
  2. withdraw_money(balance, amount) raises this exception when amount is larger than balance, and catches it in the same function.
  3. It is tested with a withdrawal that works (500 from 1000) and one that does not (1500 from 1000).

How it works, step by step

No. Point Explanation 1 Passing values when raising __init__() takes balance and withdraw, so the raise statement passes both: raise InsufficientBalanceError(balance, amount). They are stored as attributes of the exception object. 2 Creating the exception object raise creates an object of InsufficientBalanceError (so __init__() runs), throws it, and it travels to the nearest matching except block. 3 except ... as e e does not create a new object. It is a name for the same object that was raised. 4 __str__() print("Error:", e) calls e.__str__() automatically, so the user sees a clear message. 5 Without __str__() Python would use a default message, which is less helpful. __str__() is not required, but it is strongly recommended. 6 Flow of control When the exception is raised, the rest of the try block is skipped ("Withdrawal successful" is not printed), and control jumps to the matching except block. 7 The object carries data It can hold several values and a custom message. This is what makes custom exceptions powerful. 8 It is ordinary OOP InsufficientBalanceError is a class, and e is an object (instance) of it. 9 The type must match The block except InsufficientBalanceError: runs only for that type (or its subclasses). If nothing matches, the program stops with a traceback.

docs.title: Notes on Example 9
docs.text:
• Try it: print e.balance and e.withdraw inside the except block. The values stored by __init__() are available.
  • Try it: remove the whole __str__() method and run again. The message becomes Error: (1000, 1500), which is the default: the arguments given to the exception, shown as a tuple.
  • Many programmers also call super().__init__(...) inside a custom __init__(), passing a message. Then e.args holds that message too. It is good practice but not required here.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 9.13 The exception object
docs.text:
Exceptions are classes. When an exception occurs, an object of that class is created, and it holds useful information about the error.

When you write except SomeException as e:, e refers to that object.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 10: Looking inside an exception object
docs.text:
What the code does. It divides 10 by 0 on purpose, catches the ZeroDivisionError as e, and prints three things about it.

Expression What it gives Output here type(e) The class of the exception <class 'zerodivisionerror'=""> e.args A tuple of the arguments stored inside it ('division by zero',) str(e) The message, as text division by zero

finally then prints "3. Program continues".

Learning points

  1. e is an object of the class ZeroDivisionError.
  2. It contains (1) the type, which says what kind of error, (2) the arguments (args), which are its internal data, and (3) its text form, a message for the user.
  3. Lifetime: e exists only inside the except block. At the end of the block Python deletes the name e, so using it afterwards gives a NameError.

docs.title: Notes on Example 10
docs.text:
• Try it: add print(e) as a new line at the very end of the cell, outside the try statement. You get NameError: name 'e' is not defined, which confirms the lifetime rule.
  • If you need the exception later, copy it to another name inside the block: saved = e.

docs.text:

docs.title: Exception chaining with raise ... from
docs.text: When you catch one exception and raise another, raise NewError(...) from old_error keeps the link between them. The traceback then shows both, with the line "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception". The link is stored in __cause__.

docs.title: Adding a note to an exception (Python 3.11 and later)
docs.text: add_note() attaches extra information to an exception before it travels on. The notes appear at the end of the traceback and are stored in __notes__.

docs.title: Getting the traceback as text
docs.text: The traceback module can turn the current exception into the same text Python would print, without stopping the program. This is useful for writing errors to a log file.

docs.title: Ignoring one specific exception with contextlib.suppress
docs.text: Sometimes an error is expected and harmless, and you want to ignore it. contextlib.suppress is a context manager that does exactly that, in fewer lines than try-except-pass.

# Demonstrating file (1) pointer manipulation (2) reading (3) closing
# 1. Create and write some content first (so that reading works)
with open("demo.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3\n")  # Write multiple lines to the file

# 2. Now open the file for reading
with open("demo.txt", "r") as f:
    print("Initial pointer position:", f.tell())   # Output: 0

    # A. read() - read first 6 characters
    print("Using read(6):", f.read(6))  # Output: 'Line 1'
    print("Pointer after read:", f.tell())         # Output: 6

    # B. seek() - move pointer back to beginning
    f.seek(0)
    print("Pointer after seek(0):", f.tell())  # Output: 0

    # C. readline() - read one line
    print("Using readline():", f.readline())  # Output: 'Line 1\n'

    # D. readlines() - read remaining lines as list
    print("Using readlines():", f.readlines()) # Output: ['Line 2\n', 'Line 3\n']

# 3. File is automatically closed after 'with'
print("File closed automatically by with statement.")

# 4. Demonstrating close() explicitly (not recommended when using 'with')
f = open("demo.txt", "r")  # open file again
print("File opened again. Closed?", f.closed)  # Output: False

f.close()   # close()
print("After close(), Closed?", f.closed)  # Output: True
