docs.title: Chapter 10: File Operations in Python
docs.text:
This notebook holds the code examples of Chapter 10. You do not need to type them. Run them, read the notes, and then change the code to see what happens.

A program's variables live in RAM, and RAM forgets everything when the program ends. Files let you keep data. This chapter shows how to open, read, write and close files, how to move around inside a file, how text files differ from binary files, how to work with folders using the os module, how the three standard streams work, and how to save whole Python objects with pickle and json.

  • Before every example there is a text cell. It tells you what the code does, how it does it, why it matters, and what you should learn from it.
  • Some examples also have a text cell after them. Its heading starts with "Notes on Example" and the example number, so you always know which code cell it talks about.
  • A few short cells are marked Try it. They are not in the book. They let you see, safely, something the book describes in words.
  • At the end of every section there is a link that takes you back to the Table of Contents.
  • A short "Beyond the Book" section at the end adds a few extras. You can skip it on the first reading.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • tell the essential parameters of a function apart from the optional ones by reading its signature;
  • choose the right mode (r, w, a, x) for reading, appending or overwriting a file safely;
  • use with so that files are always closed, even after an error;
  • move the file pointer with seek() and find where it is with tell();
  • choose between read(), readline() and readlines(), keeping memory use in mind for large files;
  • add \n yourself when you use write() or writelines();
  • inspect the attributes of a file object, such as name, mode, closed and encoding;
  • tell text mode from binary mode (b), and handle bytes without damaging images or other media;
  • use the os module to find, create, rename, list and delete files and folders;
  • store Python objects with pickle, and exchange data in the web-friendly json format.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.1 Introduction
docs.text:
A file is a named place on a disk where data is stored permanently. RAM is volatile: it loses its contents when the power goes off. A disk is non-volatile. So we save our work in files.

Python gives you three kinds of tools for files: (1) built-in functions such as open(), (2) methods of the file object such as read() and write(), and (3) operating-system utilities in the os module.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.2 A small note on the function "signature"
docs.text:
From this chapter on we use many built-in and library functions. To read their documentation, you need to understand the word signature.

A function's signature tells you three things: (1) the name of the function, (2) the inputs it expects (its parameters), and (3) the order in which you must give them.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.2.1 The two faces of a function
docs.text:
When you look up a function such as open(), you may see it written in two ways. They are the same function, seen at two levels of detail.

The full signature The essential signature What it is The complete, technical definition from the official documentation. It lists every option the function offers. A simplified view, as seen in tutorials, textbooks and most real code. It shows only the parameters that matter for the usual task. Example open(file, mode='r', buffering=-1, encoding=None, errors=None, newline=None, closefd=True, opener=None) open(filename, mode, encoding) How to read it Anything with = (or, in older styles, anything inside [ ]) is optional. The value after = is the default, used when you say nothing. It leaves out options such as buffering or opener that most programmers never change.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.2.2 Mandatory and optional parameters
docs.text:
Mandatory parameters (no default) Optional parameters (default arguments) Meaning They have no default value. The function cannot work without them. If you leave one out, Python raises TypeError. They have a fallback value in the signature. If you give a value, Python uses it; if you do not, Python uses the default. How to spot them They come first and have no = sign. They come after the mandatory ones and are written name=value. Older manuals may write them in square brackets: func(required[, optional]). Example In round(number, ndigits=None), number is mandatory. You cannot round nothing. In round(number, ndigits=None), ndigits is optional.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.2.3 Comparison at a glance
docs.text:
Feature Mandatory (essential) Optional (secondary) Syntax parameter_name parameter_name=default_value Presence Must be given in every call Can be left out Placement Before the optional ones After the mandatory ones In documentation No = and no [ ] Marked with = or [...] Purpose Says what to act on Fine-tunes how to act

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: mandatory and optional parameters of round()
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. round() works with one argument or two. With no argument at all, it raises TypeError, because number is mandatory.

docs.title: 10.3 Types of files
docs.text:
Files come in two kinds:

Text files Binary files What they hold Characters, arranged in lines Raw bytes Examples .txt, .py, .csv, .json, .html Images, audio, video, PDF, .pkl Can you read them in a text editor? Yes No, they look like garbage

The online resource has a detailed comparison of text and binary files, and a table of all the important ideas in file handling.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.4 The file object (handle)
docs.text:
When you open a file, Python gives you back a file object, also called a file handle. You can do two kinds of things with it:

  1. call its methods, which perform actions, such as f.read();
  2. read its attributes, which give information, such as f.name.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.5 File handle methods
docs.text:
The methods can be grouped by what they are for:

No. Category Methods Purpose 1 File control and good practice open, close, with, truncate Life cycle of the file 2 Pointer control seek, tell Moving around 3 Reading read, readline, readlines Input from the file 4 Writing write, writelines Output to the file 5 Buffer control flush Performance

(Strictly, open() is a built-in function and with is a statement, but they belong to the same life cycle.)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.6 The file object and good practice
10.6.1 open()
docs.text:
open() is where every file operation starts. It opens a file and returns a file object. The mode decides what you are allowed to do: 'r' to read, 'w' to write, 'a' to append, and so on.

Its essential signature is open(file, mode='r', encoding=None).

Two warnings:

  • Read mode 'r': if the file does not exist, Python stops with FileNotFoundError.
  • Write mode 'w': if the file already exists, its content is thrown away at once, before you write anything. Be careful with 'w'.

In practice open() is used together with with, so that the file is closed automatically.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Summary of the modes
docs.text:
Mode Purpose Must the file exist? Overwrites existing data? Where writing starts 'r' Read only (text) Yes No Not applicable 'rb' Read only (binary) Yes No Not applicable 'r+' Read and write (text) Yes No Beginning 'rb+' or 'r+b' Read and write (binary) Yes No Beginning 'w' Write only (text) No (creates it) Yes (clears it) Beginning 'wb' Write only (binary) No (creates it) Yes (clears it) Beginning 'w+' Write and read (text) No (creates it) Yes (clears it) Beginning 'wb+' or 'w+b' Write and read (binary) No (creates it) Yes (clears it) Beginning 'a' Append only (text) No (creates it) No End of file 'ab' Append only (binary) No (creates it) No End of file 'a+' Append and read (text) No (creates it) No End (for writing); use seek() to read 'ab+' or 'a+b' Append and read (binary) No (creates it) No End (for writing); use seek() to read 'x' Create a new file (text) Must NOT exist No Beginning 'xb' Create a new file (binary) Must NOT exist No Beginning

An easy way to remember them: the letter says what (r read, w write, a append, x exclusive create), + adds the other direction, and b means binary.

The online resource has a full study of open(): its parameters (file, mode, encoding, errors, buffering), the methods and attributes of the file object, and errors such as FileNotFoundError, PermissionError, UnicodeDecodeError, and writing a string in binary mode.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.6.2 close()
docs.text:
close() closes the file and frees the resources the operating system gave to it. After that, the file object cannot be used for reading or writing.

Always close files. If you do not, data may be lost or resources may leak. In modern Python you rarely call close() yourself, because with does it for you.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.6.3 with (context manager)
docs.text:
with is the recommended way to work with files. It closes the file automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens inside the block. So always prefer

with open("notes.txt") as file:
    ...

to calling open() and close() by hand.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.7 Control operations
docs.text:
Every open file has a file pointer (also called the cursor or position). It marks where the next read or write will happen. Reading moves the pointer forward.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.7.1 tell()
docs.text:
tell() returns the current position of the pointer, counted from the beginning of the file. It shows how much of the file has been read or written. It is handy when you read in parts, or when you are debugging.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.7.2 seek()
docs.text:
seek(offset) moves the pointer to a given position, so you can re-read data or skip part of the file. The most common use is seek(0), which goes back to the start.

Use seek() with care. A wrong position can make you skip data, or overwrite the wrong part of the file.

The full signature is seek(offset, whence=0). whence says where the offset is counted from: 0 the start, 1 the current position, 2 the end. In text mode only seek(0), a value returned by tell(), or seek(0, 2) (go to the end) are safe.

The online resource has a study of seek(offset, whence) and how it behaves in text and binary files.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.8.1 read()
docs.text:
read() with no argument reads the whole file into one string. read(n) reads at most n characters. It is simple and convenient for small files. For a very large file, reading everything at once can use a lot of memory, so use it only when you know the file is a manageable size.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.8.2 readline()
docs.text:
readline() (singular) reads one line each time it is called. The line includes its newline character \n. It is useful when each line is one record, such as one entry in a log. It is often used in a loop. When the end of the file is reached, it returns an empty string ''.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.8.3 readlines()
docs.text:
readlines() (plural) reads all the remaining lines and returns them as a list of strings, one element per line. It is convenient but can use a lot of memory for big files. For large files, loop over the file directly: for line in file:. Use readlines() only when you really need all the lines in a list.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Summary of the read methods
docs.text:
Method What it does Returns read() Reads the entire file One string read(n) Reads up to n characters One string readline() Reads one line One string (ends with \n, or '' at the end of the file) readlines() Reads all remaining lines A list of strings

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: Reading, moving the pointer, and closing
docs.text:
What the code does.

  1. It creates demo.txt with three lines, so there is something to read.
  2. It opens the file for reading and shows where the pointer is, then uses read(6), seek(0), readline() and readlines() one after another, printing the position as it goes.
  3. After the with block, the file is closed automatically.
  4. Finally it opens the file again without with, to show closed before and after calling close() by hand.

How it works. Each read starts where the pointer is and moves it forward. read(6) takes the six characters Line 1 and leaves the pointer at 6. seek(0) sends it back to the start, so readline() reads the first line again, this time with its \n. readlines() then takes everything that is left.

Why it matters. Knowing where the pointer is explains most surprises in file reading, such as "why did my second read() return nothing?" (answer: the pointer was already at the end).

Learning points

  1. A new file object starts at position 0.
  2. readline() keeps the \n. That is why there is an empty line in the output after "Using readline(): Line 1". print() adds its own newline as well.
  3. readlines() returned only lines 2 and 3, because line 1 had already been read.
  4. f.closed tells you whether a file object is closed.

docs.title: Notes on Example 1
docs.text:
• Try it: add one more print(f.read()) just after the readlines() line, inside the with block. It prints an empty string, because the pointer is already at the end of the file.
  • Try it: change f.read(6) to f.read(3). You get Lin, and tell() gives 3.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.9.1 write()
docs.text:
write(string) writes one string to the file and returns the number of characters written. That number can be used to check the write.

write() does not add a newline. If you want separate lines, put \n at the end of each string yourself. And remember: in 'w' mode the old content of the file is gone.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.9.2 writelines()
docs.text:
writelines(list_of_strings) writes every string in a list (or any sequence of strings) to the file. It is handy when you have many lines at once.

writelines() does not add newlines between the items either. Each string must already end with \n if you want it on its own line. Beginners often forget this and find everything on one long line.

write() writelines() Takes One string A list (or other sequence) of strings Adds \n? No No Returns Number of characters written None

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: write() and writelines()
docs.text:
What the code does. It opens write_demo.txt in 'w' mode, writes two lines with write() and two more with writelines(), and lets with close the file.

How it works. Every string ends in \n, so the file ends up with four separate lines. The file is created if it does not exist; if it exists, its old content is erased first.

Learning points

  1. The cell prints nothing. Writing to a file does not show anything on the screen. The "Try it" cell below reads the file back so that you can see the result.
  2. 'w' replaces the whole file every time you run the cell. You will never see the lines twice.

docs.title: Try it: reading back what Example 2 wrote
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It opens write_demo.txt and prints it. Then it writes again without \n, to show what goes wrong.

docs.title: Try it: append mode and exclusive-create mode
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. 'a' adds to the end and keeps what was there. 'x' creates a file but refuses if it already exists, so it can never destroy data.

docs.title: 10.10 File object attributes
docs.text:
Attributes give information about an open file. You read them without brackets: f.name, not f.name().

Attribute What it tells you Notes name The name (or path) used to open the file Useful in logs and when a program handles many files. It only repeats the name; it does not check that the file exists. mode How the file was opened: 'r', 'w', 'a' ... Useful when debugging, for example to catch a file opened for reading by mistake. It is for inspection only. closed True if the file is closed, False if it is open Reading or writing a closed file raises ValueError. Check this when you manage files without with. encoding The encoding used to turn bytes into text, such as utf-8 Text files only. A wrong or missing encoding can garble special characters or raise errors. newlines The kind of line ending met so far: '\n', '\r\n' ... None until a line ending has been read. Mainly useful when files move between Windows and Linux. buffer The binary buffer underneath the text file Used internally by Python. Advanced; you rarely need it. errors How encoding errors are handled: 'strict', 'ignore', 'replace' Matters for files with broken or mixed encodings. Treat it as advanced.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 3: Looking at the attributes of a file object
docs.text:
What the code does. It writes attr_demo.txt with encoding="utf-8", opens it again for reading (without with), and prints each attribute. It reads one line first, so that newlines has something to report. Finally it closes the file and prints closed again.

How it works. The attributes are set when the file is opened, except newlines, which is filled in as lines are read, and closed, which changes when close() is called.

Learning points

  1. f.mode is r because that is the mode passed to open().
  2. The line "Newlines encountered:" looks empty, and is followed by a blank line. The value is really the newline character '\n', and printing a newline just moves to the next line. Try it: change that line to print("Newlines encountered:", repr(f.newlines)) to see '\n' spelled out.
  3. f.buffer shows a BufferedReader. A text file is a layer over a binary file.

docs.title: 10.11 Summary of file object attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Meaning Type Example Typical value Important notes name Name of the file String f.name "a.txt" Shows the file path or name mode Mode in which the file was opened String f.mode "r", "w" Helps debugging closed Whether the file is closed Boolean f.closed True / False Important for safety encoding Encoding used String f.encoding "utf-8" Text files only newlines Line endings met so far String, tuple or None f.newlines '\n', '\r\n' Useful across platforms buffer Underlying binary buffer Object f.buffer A buffer object Advanced use errors How encoding errors are handled String f.errors "strict" Rarely used

The online resource studies three more methods that tell you what a file object can do: readable(), writable() and seekable().

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.12 Binary files (and how they compare with text files)
10.12.1 open(), close() and with
docs.text:
The core operations, open(), close() and with, work in exactly the same way for text files and binary files. Only the mode changes:

  • text: "r", "w", "a"
  • binary: "rb", "wb", "ab"

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.12.2 tell() and seek()
docs.text:
Aspect Text file Binary file tell() A position marker; not always an exact byte count, because of encoding The exact byte position seek() Limited: only positions from tell(), or 0, are safe Precise control, to any byte Accuracy Depends on the encoding Fully reliable

Binary files give precise control. Text files depend on the encoding.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.12.3 Modes
docs.text:
Type Modes Text 'r', 'w', 'a', 'r+' Binary 'rb', 'wb', 'ab', 'rb+'

The binary modes are simply the text modes with a b added.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: a binary file, byte by byte
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It writes bytes to hello.bin, reads them back, and uses seek() and tell(). Notice the b in front of the strings: these are bytes, not str. The last part shows that writing a normal string to a binary file fails.

docs.title: 10.13 Methods for binary files
docs.text:
The methods for binary files are the same as for text files. What changes is the type of the data: bytes instead of str.

No. Method In binary mode, compared with text mode 1 open() with b Opens the file for bytes instead of text. Used for images, PDFs and audio. A common mistake is forgetting the b, which damages the data. 2 read() Returns a bytes object (b'...'), all of it or part of it. Used to copy files and to process media. The output is not meant for humans. 3 readline() Reads bytes up to and including b'\n'. Rarely used, and only when the binary file happens to be organised in lines. 4 readlines() Returns a list of bytes objects, split at b'\n'. Of little use with binary data; avoid it for large files. 5 write() Must be given bytes, for example f.write(b"Hello"). Giving it a str raises TypeError; encode the string first. 6 writelines() Writes a list of bytes objects. Every element must be a bytes object. 7 close() The same as for text files. Better to use with. 8 tell() Returns the exact byte position. Very reliable in binary mode. 9 seek() Moves the pointer to a byte offset. Precise; good for random access. 10 flush() Forces the buffered bytes onto the disk. Useful for live logging. The same as in text mode. 11 truncate() Cuts the file at a byte position. Anything after it is lost.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.14 Attributes in binary files
docs.text:
A file opened in binary mode is a different kind of object (a BufferedReader or BufferedWriter). It has the basic attributes, but not the ones about text.

No. Attribute In binary mode 1 name Same as in text files: the file name. 2 mode Shows modes such as 'rb' or 'wb'. The b confirms binary mode. 3 closed Same as in text files: True or False. 4 encoding Not available. Accessing f.encoding raises AttributeError. Binary files do not use an encoding. This is a key difference from text files. 5 newlines Not available (AttributeError). Binary data has no idea of lines. 6 buffer Not available. buffer belongs to a text file object and gives access to the binary buffer underneath it. A binary file object is itself that buffer. 7 errors Not available (AttributeError). There is no decoding, so there are no decoding errors.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: attributes of a binary file
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It checks each attribute of a file opened with 'rb'. getattr(f, name) reads an attribute whose name is held in a string.

docs.title: 10.15 Key differences between text and binary files
docs.text:
No. Feature Text files Binary files 1 Data type str bytes 2 Encoding Required Not used 3 read() gives "Hello" b"Hello" 4 write() takes str bytes 5 tell() / seek() Position marker, limited Exact byte position 6 Newlines Important Not relevant 7 encoding attribute Present Not available 8 errors attribute Present Not available

Golden rules:

  1. Text files use strings.
  2. Binary files use bytes, and the mode has a b.
  3. For exact control of positions, use binary mode.
  4. If a file's content looks garbled, the wrong mode (or the wrong encoding) was probably used.

In short: text files are friendly to people and depend on the encoding; binary files are friendly to machines, precise and efficient.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.16 Some useful functions of the os module
docs.text:
The os module lets Python talk to the operating system, especially about files and folders: renaming files, changing the current folder, listing a folder, and so on. You must import it first: import os.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.17 Important functions
docs.text:
Function Purpose Parameters Returns Key behaviour Points to watch os.rename(src, dst) (file management) Rename a file or folder src: current name, dst: new name None Renames within the same file system The source must exist, otherwise FileNotFoundError. May overwrite dst, depending on the operating system. os.chdir(path) (navigation) Change the current working folder path: the target folder None Changes the base for relative paths A bad path gives FileNotFoundError. It affects every later file operation. os.getcwd() (debugging, path checks) Get the current working folder None str (a path) Returns the absolute path of the current folder Always returns a string; normally no error. os.listdir(path='.') (viewing content) List files and folders path (optional) list of names Returns all entries, files and folders The order is arbitrary. A bad path gives FileNotFoundError.

The example below also uses a few more functions:

Function What it does os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True) Creates a folder (and any missing parent folders). With exist_ok=True, no error if it already exists. os.path.join(a, b) Joins parts of a path with the right separator for the system (/ on Linux and Mac, \ on Windows). os.path.exists(path) True if the file or folder exists. os.path.isfile(path) True if the path is an existing file (not a folder). os.remove(path) Deletes a file. os.rmdir(path) Deletes a folder, which must be empty.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 4: Working with files and folders using os
docs.text:
What the code does. It goes through eight steps: find the current folder, create test_dir, write sample.txt inside it, check that the file exists, rename it to renamed.txt, list the folder, delete the file, and finally delete the folder.

How it works. os.path.join("test_dir", "sample.txt") builds the path test_dir/sample.txt. Each later step uses such paths. The clean-up at the end (steps 7 and 8) leaves the folder as it was, so you can run the cell again and again.

Why it matters. Real programs often need to create folders for output, check that input files exist, and tidy up afterwards.

Learning points

  1. In Colab the current folder is /content.
  2. os.rmdir() only removes an empty folder. That is why the file is deleted first.
  3. Checking with os.path.exists() or os.path.isfile() before acting avoids errors.

docs.title: Notes on Example 4
docs.text:
• Try it: put a # in front of the two lines of step 7 and run the cell. Step 8 then fails with OSError: Directory not empty. Remove the # again and run the cell twice (the second run cleans up).
  • The online resource covers more os functions: os.remove(), os.rmdir(), os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True) and the os.path utilities.

docs.title: 10.18 Python I/O stream objects
docs.text:
When a Python program runs, three standard streams are created for it automatically: (1) standard input (stdin), (2) standard output (stdout), and (3) standard error (stderr). They connect the program with the user and the operating system. They live in the sys module.

A stream is a flow of data. An input stream brings data into the program; an output stream carries data out of it.

Stream Purpose Direction Example use Main use Important notes sys.stdin (line buffered; read(), readline()) Takes input, normally from the keyboard Outside to program input(), sys.stdin.readline() User input, file input Blocking: it waits for input sys.stdout (line buffered; write()) Shows normal output Program to outside print(), sys.stdout.write() Results, logs print() adds a newline for you; write() does not sys.stderr (write()) Shows error messages Program to outside Error messages, exceptions Debugging, error reports Kept separate from normal output

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.19 Do's and don'ts
docs.text:
Do: (1) use print() in normal programs; (2) use sys.stdout when you need finer control; (3) use sys.stderr for errors.

Don't: (1) confuse the sys module with the os module; (2) forget the \n in sys.stdout.write(); (3) mix too many methods without need.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 5: Using the three standard streams
docs.text:
What the code does. It writes a prompt with sys.stdout.write(), reads a line with sys.stdin.readline(), greets the user with sys.stdout.write(), and writes a message to sys.stderr.

How it works. sys.stdout.write() is the low-level version of print(): it writes exactly the string you give it, with no newline added. readline().strip() reads a line and removes the newline at its end.

Learning points

  1. write() needs explicit \n characters, unlike print().
  2. The stderr message appears with a light red background in Colab, so that errors stand out.
  3. The number 34 at the end is the value returned by the last line: sys.stderr.write() returns the number of characters written, and Colab shows the value of the last line of a cell.

docs.title: Notes on Example 5
docs.text:
• In Colab, sys.stdin.readline() does not wait for you. Colab has no keyboard stream connected to sys.stdin, so the call returns an empty string at once. That is why the output says just "Hello". Run the code as a script on your own computer (for example python streams.py in a terminal), and it will wait for you to type your name.
  • In Colab, use input() to read from the keyboard. It shows a text box under the cell. For example: name = input("Enter your name: ").

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.20 Pickling and unpickling
docs.text:
Pickling is also called serialisation or flattening. The key ideas:

  • Python objects cannot be written to a file as they are. They must first be turned into a sequence of bytes.
  • Pickling turns a Python object into a byte stream.
  • Unpickling turns the byte stream back into the original object.
  • Why? (1) To store complex Python objects (lists, dictionaries, objects of your own classes), (2) to save the state of a program, (3) to pass data between programs.
  • Persistence means that data survives after the program ends. Data in RAM is lost when the program stops; files and databases make it persistent.

Python has a standard library module called pickle for this. To use it, write import pickle.

  • To pickle (write): (1) open the file in 'wb' mode, (2) call pickle.dump(obj, file).
  • To unpickle (read): (1) open the file in 'rb' mode, (2) call pickle.load(file).
Operation Function File mode Purpose Returns Pickling pickle.dump(obj, file) 'wb' Save an object None Unpickling pickle.load(file) 'rb' Load an object The original object

Important points:

  1. Use pickling for Python objects only; other languages cannot read it.
  2. Always open pickle files in binary mode.
  3. Use with.
  4. Never open a pickle file in text mode.
  5. Never edit a pickle file by hand.
  6. Never unpickle data from a source you do not trust. A pickle file can be built to run harmful code when it is loaded.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 6: Pickling and unpickling a dictionary
docs.text:
What the code does. It pickles the dictionary {'a': 1, 'b': 2} into data.pkl, unpickles it into new_data, prints both, and finally prints the raw bytes of the file.

How it works. pickle.dump(data, f) writes the bytes that describe the dictionary. pickle.load(f) reads those bytes and builds a new dictionary with the same content.

Learning points

  1. new_data equals data (new_data == data is True), but it is a different object (new_data is data is False).
  2. The raw bytes are not meant to be read by people. Only pickle understands them.
  3. Your raw bytes may differ slightly from the sample in the comment; they depend on the pickle protocol version.

docs.title: 10.21 JSON for data storage
docs.text:
• JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation.
  • It is a text-based format for storing and exchanging data.
  • It is easy for people to read, and almost every language and system understands it. Example: {"name": "Alice", "marks": 90}.
  • Python provides the json module. To use it, write import json.

JSON is used in (1) web APIs (REST APIs), (2) data exchange over the internet, (3) configuration files, and (4) NoSQL databases such as MongoDB.

Security: JSON is plain text, so data sent over a network can be read if it is intercepted. The solution is to send it over an encrypted connection (HTTPS, which uses SSL/TLS).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.21.1 Serialisation and deserialisation with JSON
docs.text:
Function Direction Works with Returns Common use json.dump(obj, file) Python to JSON A file None Saving data to a .json file on disk json.dumps(obj) Python to JSON A string A JSON-formatted str Sending data over a network, or printing it json.load(file) JSON to Python A file A Python dict or list Reading a .json file json.loads(string) JSON to Python A string A Python dict or list Reading JSON received as text

A way to remember: the functions ending in s work with strings.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Try it: the four json functions
docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It converts a dictionary to a JSON string and back, and then to a .json file and back. Notice how Python's True becomes JSON's true, and that the file is plain text you can open in the Files panel.

docs.title: 10.22 JSON compared with pickle
docs.text:
Feature JSON Pickle Format Text Binary Readability Readable by people Not readable Security Safe to load Unsafe: loading can run code Language support Almost every language Python only Data types Basic: dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None Almost any Python object Used in APIs Yes No Speed Moderate Faster File size Larger Smaller

Points to remember about JSON: (1) use it for data exchange and in APIs; (2) keys must be strings in double quotes, as in {"key": value}; (3) it cannot store complex objects (such as objects of your own classes) directly; (4) do not send sensitive data without encryption; (5) do not use it for binary data.

The online resource has a comparative study of JSON and pickle: serialising with both, and comparing performance, security and portability.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 10.23 Project
docs.text:
The online resource has a project on inserting data at any position in a file. Python can overwrite ('w') or append ('a'), but it has no direct way to insert data at the beginning or in the middle of a file. The project explains why (files are read and written in sequence), and designs two algorithms: (A) copying into a temporary file while inserting the new data, and (B) reading the file into a list, changing the list, and writing it back.

docs.title: Reading a big file one line at a time
docs.text: Looping over a file object reads one line at a time, so even a huge file uses very little memory. This is the memory-safe way to count lines.

docs.title: Paths the modern way: pathlib
docs.text: The pathlib module treats a path as an object. The / operator joins parts of a path, and the object has handy methods for reading and writing.

docs.title: Two styles of error handling: LBYL and EAFP
docs.text: LBYL ("look before you leap") checks first. EAFP ("easier to ask forgiveness than permission") just tries and handles the error. Python programmers usually prefer EAFP, because the file could disappear between the check and the open().

import numpy as np

vector = np.array([90, 85, 70, 60])                  # 1 student, 4 subjects
matrix = np.array([[90, 85, 70],
                   [60, 75, 80],
                   [55, 65, 95],
                   [88, 92, 79]])                     # 4 students, 3 subjects
tensor = np.array([matrix, matrix + 5])               # 2 classes stacked

for name, a in [("vector", vector), ("matrix", matrix), ("tensor", tensor)]:
    print(f"{name}: ndim = {a.ndim}, shape = {a.shape}")

print("Class 1, student 2, subject 0:", tensor[1, 2, 0])

matrix: ndim = 2, shape = (4, 3)
tensor: ndim = 3, shape = (2, 4, 3)
Class 1, student 2, subject 0: 60

import time
import numpy as np

n = 1_000_000
numbers = list(range(n))
array = np.arange(n)

start = time.perf_counter()
total_list = sum(x * x for x in numbers)
t_list = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
total_np = np.sum(array * array)
t_np = time.perf_counter() - start

print("Same answer?", total_list == total_np)
print(f"List : {t_list:.4f} s")
print(f"NumPy: {t_np:.4f} s")
print(f"NumPy was about {t_list / t_np:.0f} times faster")

Same answer? True
List : 0.0329 s
NumPy: 0.0037 s
NumPy was about 9 times faster

docs.title: Chapter 11: NumPy
docs.text:
This notebook holds the code examples of Chapter 11. You do not need to type them. Run them, read the notes, and then change the code to see what happens.

NumPy is the library that makes Python fast with numbers. This chapter starts with the ideas behind it (vectors, matrices and tensors), then shows how to create arrays, pick out parts of them, reshape and join them, and do arithmetic on whole arrays at once. It ends with linear algebra: solving equations, eigenvalues, and the Singular Value Decomposition, used here to compress an image.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why a NumPy ndarray is faster and uses less memory than a Python list (one continuous block of memory, handled in C);
  • describe vectors, matrices and tensors, use zero-based indexing, and follow the "axis 0 is rows, axis 1 is columns" rule;
  • create arrays with np.array, zeros, ones, eye, arange and linspace;
  • index and slice with arr[i, j], including several dimensions at once, and know when you get a view and when a copy;
  • use broadcasting and universal functions to do arithmetic on arrays of different shapes;
  • build coordinate grids with np.meshgrid for 3D plots and surfaces;
  • use np.linalg for matrix operations and for solving systems of linear equations;
  • compute and interpret eigenvalues and eigenvectors;
  • understand what the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) does, and use it to compress an image with the PIL library.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction to NumPy and array creation
docs.text:
Python, together with packages like NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib, is a powerful, free alternative to MATLAB for scientific computing. NumPy stands for "Numerical Python". It is the basic package for numbers in Python. It gives you large, multi-dimensional arrays and matrices, and a big library of fast mathematical functions that work on them.

Many other libraries are built on top of NumPy:

Library Built on NumPy for Pandas Data analysis SciPy Scientific computing Scikit-learn Machine learning Matplotlib Data visualisation TensorFlow, Keras Deep learning

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 11.2 What is NumPy?
docs.text:
NumPy (Numerical Python) is a core library for scientific computing. It supports large multi-dimensional arrays and matrices, and a collection of functions that work on them efficiently. It is the foundation of most data science libraries, such as Pandas, SciPy and Scikit-learn.

It was created by Travis Oliphant in 2005, by combining two older libraries, Numeric and Numarray.

Characteristic Description Open source Free to use and distribute High performance Written in C, optimised for speed Memory efficient Stores data in one continuous block of memory Interoperable Works well with other Python libraries Multi-dimensional Supports arrays of any number of dimensions

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text:

Method Command Best for pip pip install numpy General use conda conda install numpy Anaconda users From source python setup.py install Advanced users requirements.txt pip install -r requirements.txt Setting up a whole project

docs.title: 11.4 Understanding vectors, matrices and tensors
docs.text:
Vectors, matrices and tensors come from mathematics. It is worth understanding them first, because a NumPy array is simply a software version of a mathematical tensor. Once you know the shapes, NumPy code becomes easy to follow.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Matrix
docs.text:
Think of a matrix as a spreadsheet. It has rows and columns, and the data sits where a row meets a column (a cell).

Zero-based indexing. In Python and NumPy, rows and columns are counted from 0. So the top-left cell has the index (0, 0). A table of 3 rows and 4 columns has rows 0 to 2 and columns 0 to 3. Each cell's address is the pair (row_number, column_number).

Data and addresses. If a matrix is called X, the data in row i and column j is written Xi,j. In Python code this becomes X[i, j].

Column 0 Column 1 Column 2 Column 3 Row 0 X0,0 X0,1 X0,2 X0,3 Row 1 X1,0 X1,1 X1,2 X1,3 Row 2 X2,0 X2,1 X2,2 X2,3

An example. Suppose you keep the marks of all the students in a class. By convention, each student is a row and each subject is a column.

  • A row is one "entity". In databases, rows are also called tuples or records.
  • A column is one "feature". In databases, columns are called fields or attributes.

With 3 students and 4 subjects you get 3 rows (index 0 to 2) and 4 columns (index 0 to 3). Then Xi,j holds the marks of the (i+1)th student in the (j+1)th subject. The index is one less than the count, because counting starts at 0.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Axis 0 and axis 1
docs.text:
In a matrix, axis 0 runs down the rows (top to bottom), and axis 1 runs across the columns (left to right).

Be careful: this is not the school geometry picture, where the x-axis goes left to right and the y-axis goes bottom to top. In data science and matrix algebra, the first index is always the row (going down), and the second is the column (going right).

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Row vectors and column vectors
docs.text:
• Row vector: a class with only one student gives a table with a single row and many columns: [X0,0 X0,1 X0,2 X0,3]. So a vector is a matrix with a single row: one entity with many features.
  • Column vector: now look at one subject for all students. That is a single column, with one value per row. A column vector is often written as a row with a "T" (transpose) mark.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Heterogeneous and homogeneous data inside the cells
docs.text:
In a spreadsheet, a teacher may put marks in some columns and text (such as "Boy/Girl" or an address) in others. That is heterogeneous (mixed) data. A mathematical matrix, and so a NumPy array, holds homogeneous data: every cell has exactly the same type (all integers, or all floats). If you mix text and numbers, NumPy turns everything into text.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Tensors
docs.text:
When there are more than 2 dimensions, the object is called a tensor. Take the school example further. Every class has the same subjects, and the teacher prints one spreadsheet of marks per class. Stacking these sheets on top of each other gives a 3D block: a tensor. The new direction, the stack, becomes axis 0; rows become axis 1, and columns axis 2.

Object Dimensions Example shape Meaning Vector 1 (4,) one row of 4 marks Matrix 2 (4, 3) 4 students, 3 subjects Tensor 3 (2, 4, 3) 2 classes, each with 4 students and 3 subjects

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text: This cell is not in the book. ndim gives the number of dimensions (axes) and shape gives the size along each axis.

docs.title: 11.5 Python lists and NumPy speed: the "why"
docs.text:
Python lists are flexible, but they are not built for heavy maths. The main difference is how data is stored in memory.

  • Python lists: a list is really an array of pointers. Each item can be a different type (an integer, a string, a boolean), so Python stores each one as a separate object somewhere in memory and keeps a pointer to it. Jumping around memory makes loops slow.
  • NumPy arrays: strictly homogeneous. Because NumPy knows the type of every element, it stores the data in one continuous block of memory, as a C array. The processor can then work through the data very fast, without checking the type of each element.

In short, a NumPy array (ndarray) (1) holds elements of one data type (dtype), (2) keeps them in contiguous memory, which is very fast, and (3) supports vectorised operations, with no loops needed.

Aspect Python list NumPy array Memory storage Scattered locations One contiguous block Data type Can mix types One data type Operation speed Slow for large data Optimised C-level operations Element-wise operations Need loops Built-in vectorisation Memory overhead High (a full object per element) Low (fixed-size elements)

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.text: This cell is not in the book. It adds up the squares of one million numbers, first with a list and a loop, then with a NumPy array. Your times will differ, but NumPy is usually many times faster.

docs.title: 11.6.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Most arrays are created in one of five ways:

Way Functions 1. From existing data np.array(), np.asarray(), np.fromiter(), np.fromfunction(), np.loadtxt() 2. Basic arrays np.zeros(), np.ones(), np.full(), np.empty(), np.zeros_like(), np.ones_like(), np.full_like() 3. Sequences np.arange(), np.linspace(), np.logspace() 4. Special matrices np.identity(), np.eye(), np.diag(), np.indices(), np.meshgrid() 5. Random arrays np.random.rand(), np.random.randint(), np.random.randn(), np.random.choice(), np.random.uniform()

Beginners usually start with a handful of them: np.array(), np.zeros(), np.ones(), np.full(), np.arange() and np.linspace(). These cover most real tasks.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: The common creation functions
docs.text:
Function and purpose Input Example Key property Typical use np.array(): turn Python data into an array A list, tuple or nested list np.array([1, 2, 3]) Works out the dtype automatically Converting existing data np.zeros(): array of zeros A shape np.zeros((3, 2)) The default type is float Starting values np.ones(): array of ones A shape np.ones((2, 3)) Machine learning, matrices np.full(): array of one constant value A shape and a value np.full((2, 2), 9) Default or fixed values np.arange(): sequence by step size Start, stop, step np.arange(0, 10, 2) Like range(), but returns an array Number sequences np.linspace(): evenly spaced numbers Start, stop, how many np.linspace(0, 1, 5) Includes the end value Plotting, interpolation np.eye(): identity matrix Size np.eye(3) 1 on the diagonal, 0 elsewhere Linear algebra np.random.rand(): random floats Dimensions np.random.rand(3) Values in [0, 1) Simulations

SciPy is built on top of NumPy, so an array made with np.array() can be passed straight to any SciPy function. The array-creation functions themselves live in NumPy, not in SciPy.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Signatures of some common creation functions
docs.text:
Signature What it does numpy.array(alist) Makes an array (of type ndarray) from a list. Note that numpy.array is a function; the object it creates is an ndarray. numpy.zeros((N, M), dtype=float) An array of the given shape, here N x M, filled with 0. numpy.ones((N, M), dtype=float) An array of the given shape, here N x M, filled with 1. numpy.eye(N, M=None, dtype=float) A 2D array with 1 on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere. If M is left out it equals N, giving a square matrix. numpy.transpose(a, axes=None) Swaps the dimensions of array a. With no axes, the order of the dimensions is reversed, so a 2 x 5 matrix becomes 5 x 2. numpy.arange(start, stop, step) Like Python's range(), but start, stop and step may be decimals. numpy.random.random((N, M)) An N x M array of random numbers in [0, 1): 0 can appear, 1 never does. numpy.random.randint(X, Y, (N, M)) An N x M array of random integers from X up to, but not including, Y.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: The basic ways of creating arrays
docs.text:
What the code does. It creates arrays in five ways: (1) from Python data (a list, a tuple, a nested list), (2) filled with a default value (zeros, ones, full), (3) as sequences (arange, linspace), (4) as a special matrix (eye), and (5) with random numbers (rand, after seed).

How it works. Each function returns a new ndarray. NumPy picks the data type for you: whole numbers give an integer array, and anything with a decimal point gives a float array.

Learning points

  1. np.array([10, 20, 30, 40]) gives integers, but the tuple (1.5, 2.5, 3.5) gives floats.
  2. np.zeros(5) prints [0. 0. 0. 0. 0.]. The dot shows the values are floats, the default type.
  3. A shape of several dimensions is given as a tuple: np.ones((2, 3)).
  4. np.arange(0, 10, 2) stops before 10. np.linspace(0, 1, 5) includes 1.
  5. np.random.seed(0) makes the "random" numbers the same on every run.

docs.title: Example 2: Working on the whole array at once
docs.text:
What the code does. It builds a list of squares with a list comprehension, turns it into an array, and then adds, multiplies, raises to a power and divides the whole array in one step each.

How it works. An arithmetic operator between an array and a number is applied to every element. No loop is written; NumPy runs the loop in C.

Learning points

  1. np_array + 10 would fail on a list ([0, 1, 4] + 10 is a TypeError), but works on an array.
  2. * on a list repeats it; on an array it multiplies each element. Compare [1, 2] * 2 with np.array([1, 2]) * 2.
  3. Division / always gives floats, shown with a dot: [0. 0.5 2. ...].

1. Read the question and write your own answer first, in a new cell.

  3. Change the numbers and run it again. That is where the learning happens.

Answers that use random numbers give different values every time. If you want the same values as this notebook, add np.random.seed(0) before the random call.

docs.title: Q1. Reverse an array with slicing
docs.text:
Question. Create a 1D NumPy array containing the numbers from 10 to 49. Then, reverse this array using slicing.

What the answer does. np.arange(10, 50) builds the 40 numbers from 10 to 49 (the stop value 50 is not included). arr[::-1] then reads them backwards.

How it works. The full slice syntax is [start : stop : step]. With start and stop left out, the slice covers the whole array, and a step of -1 means "move one place at a time, from right to left".

Learning points

  1. arange(10, 50) gives 40 numbers, not 41. The stop value is always excluded.
  2. arr[::-1] is a view, not a copy. It shares memory with arr.
  3. Try it: arr[::-2] gives every second number, backwards.

docs.title: Q2. A 3 x 3 matrix with reshape
docs.text:
Question. Create a 3x3 matrix with values ranging from 0 to 8 using np.reshape.

What the answer does. np.arange(9) makes the flat sequence 0 to 8, and .reshape(3, 3) arranges it in 3 rows of 3.

Learning points

  1. The rule of reshaping: the number of elements must stay the same. Here 3 x 3 = 9.
  2. NumPy fills the new shape row by row: 0 1 2, then 3 4 5, then 6 7 8.
  3. reshape returns a new view; arange(9) itself is unchanged.

docs.title: Q3. An identity matrix with 5 on the diagonal
docs.text:
Question. Initialize a 5x5 identity matrix and change all the diagonal elements to 5.

What the answer does. np.eye(5) gives a 5 x 5 matrix with 1 on the diagonal and 0 everywhere else. Multiplying the whole matrix by 5 turns each 1 into a 5 and leaves the zeros as they are.

Why it is written this way. It avoids a loop: one broadcast multiplication does the whole job.

Learning points

  1. np.eye() always gives floats, so the output shows 5. and 0..
  2. This trick works only because everything off the diagonal is 0.

docs.title: Notes on Q3
docs.text: If the matrix had other non-zero values, multiplying would change them too. The direct way to write on the diagonal is np.fill_diagonal(), which changes the array in place:

docs.title: Q4. Minimum, maximum and memory address
docs.text:
Question. Generate a 10x10 array with random values. Find the minimum and maximum values and their memory addresses.

What the answer does. np.random.rand(10, 10) gives 100 random floats between 0 and 1. data.min() and data.max() return the smallest and largest. data.ctypes.data gives the memory address where the array's block of data starts.

How it works. A NumPy array keeps all its values in one continuous block of memory. ctypes.data is the address of the first byte of that block.

Learning points

  1. min() and max() without an axis look at the whole array.
  2. The address is a large number, and it is different every time you run the cell.
  3. The address printed here is the start of the array, not the address of the smallest or largest value. The Notes cell below shows how to work those out.

docs.title: Notes on Q4
docs.text: To reach the address of a particular element, start at the array's address and add its position times the size of one element. argmin() and argmax() give the positions.

docs.title: Q5. A border of ones
docs.text:
Question. Create a 2D array with 1 on the border and 0 inside.

What the answer does. It starts with a 5 x 5 array of ones, then sets the inside to 0 in a single assignment.

How it works. x[1:-1, 1:-1] means "all rows except the first and the last, and all columns except the first and the last". Assigning 0 to that slice changes the original array, because a slice is a view.

Learning points

  1. Negative indexes count from the end: -1 is the last row or column.
  2. Assigning a single number to a slice fills the whole slice with it.
  3. Try it: change np.ones((5, 5)) to np.ones((6, 4)). The same line still works.

docs.title: Q6. A checkerboard pattern
docs.text:
Question. Create an 8x8 matrix and fill it with a checkerboard pattern (0s and 1s) using slicing.

What the answer does. It starts with an 8 x 8 array of zeros and then writes 1 into two sets of positions: odd rows with even columns, and even rows with odd columns.

How it works. check[1::2, ::2] selects rows 1, 3, 5, 7 and columns 0, 2, 4, 6. check[::2, 1::2] selects rows 0, 2, 4, 6 and columns 1, 3, 5, 7. Together they cover exactly the black squares of a chessboard.

Learning points

  1. A slice can be used on both sides of the equals sign.
  2. dtype=int keeps the output as 0 and 1 rather than 0. and 1.
  3. Try it: swap the two assignments around, so that the top-left square becomes 1.

docs.title: Q7. Kilograms to pounds by vectorization
docs.text:
Question. Convert an array of weights [70.5, 80.2, 65.0] from kilograms to pounds (1kg = 2.2lb) using vectorization.

What the answer does. It multiplies the whole array by 2.2 in one step.

Why it matters. With a Python list you would need a loop or a list comprehension. With an array, one operator does the work for every element, in fast C code.

Learning points

  1. array * number is an element-wise operation. No loop is written.
  2. The result is a new array; weights_kg is unchanged.
  3. The exact factor is 2.20462, so this answer is a rounded conversion.

docs.title: Q8. View compared with copy
docs.text:
Question. Demonstrate the "View vs Copy" behavior by slicing an array and modifying the slice. Verify the original array.

What the answer does. It slices the first three elements and changes one of them, then prints the original array to show that it changed too. It then takes a .copy() of the same slice, changes that, and prints the original again to show that this time nothing changed.

How it works. A basic slice does not move any data. It only records where to look, so the slice and the original share the same memory. .copy() makes a real second copy of the data.

Learning points

  1. After slice_view[0] = 99, the original starts with 99.
  2. After safe_copy[1] = 88, the original still shows 2 at that position.
  3. Rule of thumb: slicing gives a view; fancy indexing (a list of positions) and boolean masking give a copy.

docs.title: Q9. The inner sub-matrix
docs.text:
Question. Given a 4x4 matrix, extract the inner 2x2 sub-matrix.

What the answer does. matrix[1:3, 1:3] keeps rows 1 and 2 and columns 1 and 2, which is the 2 x 2 block in the middle.

Learning points

  1. In a slice 1:3, the row or column numbered 3 is not included.
  2. The same effect can be written as matrix[1:-1, 1:-1], which works for any even size.
  3. The result is a view, so changing it would change matrix.

docs.title: Q10. Normalising a matrix to the range 0 to 1
docs.text:
Question. Normalize a random 5x5 matrix so that all values lie between 0 and 1.

What the answer does. It applies the min-max formula (x - min) / (max - min) to every element at once.

How it works. rand_arr.min() and rand_arr.max() are single numbers, so they are broadcast across the whole matrix. After the calculation the smallest value becomes exactly 0 and the largest exactly 1.

Learning points

  1. Normalising puts different measurements on the same scale. It is a common first step in machine learning.
  2. The shape does not change; only the values do.
  3. If every value were the same, max - min would be 0 and you would get a division-by-zero warning.

docs.title: Q11. Common values in two arrays
docs.text:
Question. Create a script to find the common values between two NumPy arrays.

What the answer does. np.intersect1d(arr1, arr2) returns the values that appear in both arrays.

Learning points

  1. The result is sorted and holds each common value only once.
  2. Related functions: np.union1d() (everything in either array), np.setdiff1d() (in the first but not the second), and np.in1d() or np.isin() (a True/False mask).
  3. Try it: np.isin(arr1, arr2) gives [False False True True True].

docs.title: Q12. Fifty points from 0 to 2 pi, and their sines
docs.text:
Question. Generate 50 evenly spaced numbers between 0 and 2π and calculate their sine values.

What the answer does. np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 50) gives exactly 50 points, including both ends. np.sin(x) then works on all 50 at once.

Why linspace and not arange? Here the number of points matters, not the step size. That is what linspace is for.

Learning points

  1. np.pi is NumPy's value of pi.
  2. np.sin is a universal function (ufunc): it is applied to every element.
  3. Some values print in scientific notation, such as 1.22464680e-16 for sin(2 pi). That is a rounding error; the true value is 0.

docs.title: Notes on Q12
docs.text: These are exactly the values you need to draw a sine curve:

docs.title: Q13. The sum of each column
docs.text:
Question. Create a 5x5 matrix and find the sum of each column.

What the answer does. matrix.sum(axis=0) adds the values going down each column, and gives one number per column.

How it works. The axis says which direction to collapse. Axis 0 is the row direction, so the rows disappear and five column totals remain.

Learning points

  1. axis=0 gives column totals; axis=1 gives row totals.
  2. The shape shrinks from (5, 5) to (5,).
  3. matrix.sum() with no axis adds every element: 300.

docs.title: Q14. Replacing values with a boolean mask
docs.text:
Question. Replace all values in a 1D array that are greater than 50 with the value 0 using Boolean Masking.

What the answer does. It first builds a mask, arr > 50, which is an array of True and False, and then uses that mask on the left of an assignment, so only the True positions are changed.

Learning points

  1. A mask has the same shape as the array it came from.
  2. arr[mask] = 0 changes the array in place. There is no copy.
  3. The same result with np.where would be arr = np.where(arr > 50, 0, arr), which builds a new array instead.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# GROUP A: SERIES WITH DEFAULT INDEX (0, 1, 2, 3...)

# Method 1: From List
s1 = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40])
print("From List:\n", s1) # Index will be 0, 1, 2, 3 by default

# Method 2: From DataFrame Column
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2, 3], 'B': [4, 5, 6]})  # Create simple DataFrame
s6 = df['A']  # This creates a Series from column 'A' of the DataFrame
print("\nFrom DataFrame Column:\n", s6)  # Index will default to 0, 1, 2

# Method 3: From a function (List Comprehension)
s7 = pd.Series([x**2 for x in range(5)])  # Series with 0, 1, 4, 9, 16
print("\nFrom Function:\n", s7)  # Index defaults to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

# GROUP B: SERIES WITH CUSTOM INDEX (Labels explicitly defined)

# Method 4: From List with Custom Index
s2 = pd.Series([100, 200, 300], index=['a', 'b', 'c'])
print("\nWith Custom Index:\n", s2) # Custom index labels are 'a', 'b', 'c'

# Method 5: From Dictionary
# Note: In dictionaries, the keys automatically become the custom index labels
data_dict = {'Name': 'John', 'Age': 25, 'City': 'NYC'}
s3 = pd.Series(data_dict)
print("\nFrom Dictionary:\n", s3)  # The keys ('Name', 'Age', 'City') become the index

# Method 6: From NumPy Array with Custom Index
arr = np.array([1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5])
s4 = pd.Series(arr, index=['w', 'x', 'y', 'z'])
print("\nFrom NumPy Array:\n", s4) # Custom index labels are 'w', 'x', 'y', 'z'

# Method 7: From Scalar Value
# Note: Creating a Series from a scalar REQUIRES you to specify the index
# so Pandas knows how many times to repeat the value.
s5 = pd.Series(5, index=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
print("\nFrom Scalar:\n", s5)  # Even though it looks like default numbers, the index was explicitly provided

Two points about the next example:

Point Why ?raw=true on a GitHub link A normal GitHub link shows you a web page about the file. Adding ?raw=true asks GitHub for the file itself, which is what Pandas needs. StringIO Functions such as read_csv() and read_json() expect a file. StringIO wraps a piece of text so that it behaves like a file held in memory. Use it when the data is already a string in your program.

import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

# A. From CSV (Web URL)
# Loading the popular penguin dataset from a public CSV
csv_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/master/penguins.csv"
df_csv = pd.read_csv(csv_url)

# B. From Excel (Your GitHub Resource)
# NOTE: For GitHub files, always add '?raw=true' to the end of the URL
xl_url = "https://github.com/ag999git/001-Python-book-2026/blob/main/resources/palmer_penguins.xlsx?raw=true"
df_xl = pd.read_excel(xl_url)

# C. From JSON (Data String)
# We use StringIO to wrap the text so Pandas treats it like a file
json_str = '[{"Species": "Adelie", "Island": "Torgersen"}]'
df_json = pd.read_json(StringIO(json_str))

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 1. Create the raw data (List of Dictionaries of sales records)
# Each sale record has shop name, item sold, & sale amount.
sale_data = [
    {'Shop': 'Shop1', 'Item': 'Item1', 'sale': 90},
    {'Shop': 'Shop2', 'Item': 'Item2', 'sale': 100},
    {'Shop': 'Shop3', 'Item': 'Item3', 'sale': 50},
    {'Shop': 'Shop4', 'Item': 'Item1', 'sale': 80},
    {'Shop': 'Shop1', 'Item': 'Item2', 'sale': 70},
    {'Shop': 'Shop2', 'Item': 'Item1', 'sale': 100},
    {'Shop': 'Shop3', 'Item': 'Item3', 'sale': 200},
    {'Shop': 'Shop1', 'Item': 'Item1', 'sale': 200}
]

# 2. Create DataFrame in "long" format (one row per sale record).
sale_df = pd.DataFrame(sale_data)
print("Original Data:\n", sale_df)

# 3. Create Pivot Table with fill_value=0 so Nan →0
# This makes visualizing 'stack' and 'unstack' much easier.
pv = sale_df.pivot_table(index='Shop', # Index will be the Shop names
                        columns='Item', # Columns will be the Item names
                        values='sale',  # Values will be the 'sale' amounts
                        aggfunc=np.sum, # aggfunc is sum.
                        fill_value=0)  # NaN → 0 →visualing stack/unstack
print("pivot table:→\n", pv)

# 4. stack(). Moves Column Labels (Item1, Item2, Item3)→ Index as row labels,
# creating a Series with a MultiIndex. Wide → Long format. The 'Shop' index
# remains, and the 'Item' column labels become part of the new MultiIndex.
stacked_data = pv.stack()
print("\n--- After stack() (Wide -> Long) ---\n", stacked_data)

# 5. unstack(). 'Item' level of MultiIndex → to columns & return to original
# pivot table. Transform "Long" data into "Wide" data (DataFrame format).
unstacked_data = stacked_data.unstack()
print("\n--- After unstack() (Long -> Wide) ---\n", unstacked_data)

# 6. You can also unstack the 'Shop' index to flip the table entirely so that
# 'Shop' becomes the columns and 'Item' becomes the index.
flipped_table = stacked_data.unstack('Shop')
print("\n--- After unstacking 'Shop' ---\n", flipped_table)

docs.title: Chapter 12: Pandas, an open source data analysis and manipulation tool
docs.text:
This notebook holds the code examples of Chapter 12. You do not need to type them. Run them, read the notes, and then change the code to see what happens.

Pandas is the library that turns Python into a data analysis tool. It gives you two structures, the Series (one column) and the DataFrame (a whole table), and hundreds of methods for loading, cleaning, summarising and reshaping data.

docs.title: How this notebook is arranged
docs.text:
• Each code example from the book is in its own code cell.
  • Before every example there is a text cell. It tells you what the code does, how it does it, why it matters, and what you should learn from it.
  • Some examples also have a text cell after them. Its heading starts with "Notes on Example" and the example number, so you always know which code cell it talks about.
  • A few short cells are marked Try it. They are not in the book. They let you see something the book describes in words.
  • At the end of every section there is a link that takes you back to the Table of Contents.
  • A short "Beyond the Book" section at the end adds a few extras. You can skip it on the first reading.

docs.title: How to run the code
docs.text:
1. Click inside a code cell.
  2. Press Shift + Enter, or click the round Run button on the left of the cell.
  3. The result appears just below the cell.

Run the cells from top to bottom. Pandas, NumPy, Seaborn and Matplotlib are already installed in Colab.

Some cells need the internet. They read files from public web addresses, or load a Seaborn dataset. Colab has an internet connection, so they work there. If a cell fails with a connection error, the website may be busy or the file may have moved. Run the cell again later, or use another of the examples.

Warnings in pink boxes. A few cells print a FutureWarning. That is Pandas telling you that a way of writing something will change in a later version. The code still runs correctly. The notes explain each one.

docs.title: How to read the flowcharts
docs.text: The steps are numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. When the flow splits into two paths, one path uses the letter A (2A, 3A ...) and the other uses the letter B (2B, 3B ...). A long chain of steps is folded onto a second row: follow the arrow down and back to the left.

docs.title: Learning objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain what a dataset is, in terms of rows, columns and data types;
  • tell numerical, categorical and boolean data apart, and say what you may do with each;
  • load real datasets with Seaborn: penguins, tips and flights;
  • say how Pandas differs from NumPy: labels, mixed types and tables;
  • use the two core structures, the Series (1D) and the DataFrame (2D), and know that the old Panel (3D) has been removed and that MultiIndex replaces it;
  • create a Series and a DataFrame from lists, dictionaries, NumPy arrays and external files;
  • understand the index: default and custom, unique and non-unique;
  • read the DataFrame attributes: shape, columns, index, dtypes and values;
  • follow the four-pillar workflow: inspect, analyse, clean and then use special tools;
  • select, filter, group and aggregate data;
  • find and handle missing data with isna(), dropna() and fillna();
  • reshape data with pivot_table(), crosstab(), stack() and unstack();
  • combine datasets with concat() and merge();
  • work with dates: conversion, a datetime index and resampling;
  • read and write files: CSV, HTML, JSON and Excel;
  • draw simple plots straight from a DataFrame.

A note from the author. Pandas is huge and it changes fast. The book builds the ideas and the core skills. Longer examples, advanced topics, full scripts and datasets are in the online resource that goes with the book.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction to datasets in Pandas
docs.text:
A dataset is a collection of data arranged in a structured form, nearly always as rows and columns:

  • Rows are individual observations, also called records.
  • Columns are the variables, also called features or attributes.

You can picture a dataset as (1) an Excel sheet, (2) a database table, or (3) a CSV file. In Pandas a dataset is loaded into a DataFrame.

Why do we need datasets? Without data there is nothing to analyse. Datasets let us (1) find patterns and trends, (2) calculate and summarise, (3) test ideas, (4) draw charts, and (5) train machine learning models.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 12.2 Types of data in a dataset
docs.text:
When a dataset is loaded, every column gets a data type (dtype). Getting the type right matters, because it decides (1) which operations are possible, (2) which analysis makes sense, and (3) which charts are suitable.

Category Sub-type Description Example Pandas dtype What you can do What you should not do Numerical Continuous Measured values, any value in a range Height, temperature, price float64 Mean, sum, correlation, regression, histograms, scatter plots Treat as categories without a reason Discrete Counted whole numbers Number of students, books int64 Counting, aggregation, bar charts, basic statistics Use fractional operations where they have no meaning Categorical Nominal No natural order Gender, city, colour object or category Grouping, counting (value_counts()), bar charts Mean, median and other arithmetic Ordinal Has a logical order Rank, size (S/M/L), rating category Sorting, ranking, ordered comparisons Treat as purely numeric, such as averaging ranks blindly Boolean Binary Only two values Yes/No, True/False bool Filtering, logical operations, counting Complex mathematical analysis Temporal Date and time Time-based values Date, timestamp datetime64 Time-series analysis, trends, resampling, line plots Treat as plain text, or ignore the order

Pandas is powerful because it holds all these types together in one structure.

Why use built-in datasets? While learning, ready-made datasets are better than made-up numbers: (1) they are clean and ready to use, (2) they come from the real world, and (3) they let you compare your results with other people's. This chapter uses three datasets from the Seaborn library.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: 12.2.1 The penguins dataset
docs.text:
The penguins dataset holds physical measurements of penguins from three species and three islands in Antarctica. It is a modern alternative to the classic iris dataset.

Its columns are:

Column Meaning species Type of penguin: Adelie, Chinstrap or Gentoo island Island where the penguin was observed bill_length_mm Length of the beak, in millimetres bill_depth_mm Depth of the beak, in millimetres flipper_length_mm Flipper length, in millimetres body_mass_g Body mass, in grams sex Male or female

It is good for learning (1) grouping and aggregation, (2) pivot tables, (3) comparing species, (4) scatter and pair plots, and (5) handling missing values. Because it mixes categorical columns (species, island, sex) with numerical measurements, it suits DataFrames, groupby() and pivot tables very well.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 1: Loading the penguins dataset
docs.text:
What the code does. It imports Seaborn under the usual name sns, downloads the penguins dataset into a DataFrame, and prints the first five rows with head().

How it works. sns.load_dataset() fetches a small, well-known CSV file from the Seaborn data repository on the internet and hands it back as a Pandas DataFrame.

Learning points

  1. head() shows the first 5 rows by default. Use head(3) for three.
  2. Row 3 shows NaN in four columns. NaN means "not a number", the marker for a missing value. Real data usually has some.
  3. The first column of the printout, 0 1 2 3 4, is the index, not a column of the data.

docs.title: 12.2.2 The flights dataset
docs.text:
The flights dataset records the number of airline passengers each month from 1949 to 1960. It is one of the best datasets for time-series work, pivot tables and reshaping.

Column Meaning year Year of travel month Month name passengers Number of passengers that month

It suits (1) pivot tables, (2) cross-tab style summaries, (3) heatmaps, (4) stack() and unstack(), (5) trend analysis, and (6) seasonal patterns. Each row is one month of one year, so it is ideal for showing how long data is reshaped into a wide table.

Back to the Table of Contents

docs.title: Example 2: Loading the flights dataset
docs.text:
What the code does. It loads the flights dataset and prints the first five rows.

Learning points

  1. This is long format: one row per month, with the year repeated twelve times.
  2. month is a category, year and passengers are numbers. Section 12.11 shows how a pivot table turns this into a year-by-month table.

docs.title: 12.2.3 The tips dataset
docs.text:
The tips dataset is one of the most used datasets in data analysis. It records restaurant bills and the tips that customers left.

Column Meaning total_bill Total bill amount, in dollars tip Tip given by the customer sex Gender of the customer smoker Whether the customer is a smoker (Yes/No) day Day of the week (Thur, Fri, Sat, Sun) time Time of the meal (Lunch or Dinner) size Number of people at the table

It is useful for studying (1) bill amount against tip, (2) group size against tip, and (3) smoking and non-smoking behaviour.

Concept Example with this dataset Pivot tables Average tip by day and time Cross-tab Count of smokers against non-smokers Grouping Mean bill by gender Visualisation Bar plots, box plots, heatmaps

Back to the Table of Contents
